title: ACEs and resilience: what childhood adversity scores can and cannot tell you
parentQuestions: What are ACEs and should I worry about my child's score?
Will my own difficult childhood harm my kids?
What protects children from stress and trauma?
Влияет ли тяжёлое детство родителей на ребёнка?
whatToKnow: The ACE study (Felitti 1998, about 9,500 adults) found that more types of childhood abuse and household dysfunction went with higher adult risks for many diseases and behaviors. The CDC treats ACEs as a prevention priority and emphasizes safe, stable, nurturing relationships. A 2021 study found ACE scores forecast group differences but predict an individual's later health poorly. Positive childhood experiences (Bethell 2019: for example feeling supported by family, safe at school) were linked with much lower odds of adult depression across ACE levels.

whatToDo.action: Build one steady, warm bond: respond to cries, play, and keep routines. This is the main protective factor.
Be a safe base: ask about the day, listen without judgment, and keep a predictable home.
Help the child have a trusted adult outside the family (teacher, relative, coach) and friendships.
If you had a hard childhood, build your own support (partner, friend, counselor) and tell your pediatrician if it weighs on you.

seeClinicianIf: If you suspect a child is being harmed or is unsafe, contact child-protection services or emergency services immediately. Speak to the pediatrician or a psychologist if a child shows lasting changes after a frightening event, or if you feel unable to cope.
evidenceNote: Population-level associations are well documented (Felitti 1998), but ACE scores are retrospective, count categories equally, and are poor individual predictors (Baldwin 2021). Positive childhood experiences (Bethell 2019) come from one cross-sectional state survey.

Baldwin et al 2021, Population vs individual prediction of poor health from ACE screening, JAMA Pediatr, PubMed
Bethell et al 2019, Positive childhood experiences and adult mental and relational health, JAMA Pediatr, PubMed

title: ADHD signs and when it can be assessed
parentQuestions: Is my 5 year old hyperactive or normal?
At what age can ADHD be diagnosed?
Who can diagnose ADHD?
whatToKnow: The AAP clinical guideline covers children from 4 to 18. Core signs are inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that cause problems in more than one setting. CDC says there is no single test; a pediatrician, psychologist or psychiatrist evaluates, with hearing and vision checks to rule out other causes. Families can ask the school system for an evaluation for children 3 and older.

whatToDo.action: Note when, where and how often; ask teacher and caregivers for their view.
Ask the pediatrician for a structured evaluation; do not accept a diagnosis from a single short visit.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent attention or hyperactivity problems at home and school that affect learning or friendships, or injuries from impulsive risk-taking.
evidenceNote: AAP guideline page (4 to 18) and CDC. Preschool-level energy is normal; only persistent, impairing patterns count.

sources.title: AAP: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), clinical guideline page
CDC: Diagnosing ADHD

title: Adoption: telling your child their story
parentQuestions: When should I tell my child they are adopted?
What words should I use about birth parents?
My child keeps asking about their birth mother
whatToKnow: AAP says adoption should not be a secret, and children who are not told often sense they are different. Preschool is a good time to start, with a simple, honest account, and children grasp adoption gradually. AAP advises using the word adoption early, saying birth parents made a loving decision such as an adoption plan, and avoiding 'given up' or 'put up'. Repeated questions are normal. AAP describes typical stages: ages 5 to 7 worry about parents leaving, 7 to 9 grow curious about birth parents, and 9 to 12 care about appearance and fitting in. A life book can hold the story.

whatToDo.action: Tell the story simply and warmly, and keep the word adoption in daily talk.
Add details a bit at a time, including hard facts when the child can take them in.
Say that the placement was not the child's fault, and stay calm about questions.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician or a counsellor if distress about the story is long-lasting or disrupts school or sleep.
evidenceNote: AAP guidance from two HealthyChildren pages; Child Welfare Information Gateway confirms adoption brings joy and also loss, grief and identity issues and that families may need support. Open or closed adoption affects what contact is possible.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): When to Tell Your Child About Adoption
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Respectful Ways to Talk about Adoption, Dos and Don'ts

title: Age and fertility for both partners
parentQuestions: Is 35 too late to have a baby?
Does the father's age matter?
How quickly does fertility decline?
whatToKnow: Most couples where the woman is under 40 conceive within a year of regular unprotected sex. A review of guidelines found that those naming an age placed the decline between 30 and the late 30s, and that few address counselling well. NHS miscarriage guidance lists age 35 or older and a father aged 45 or older as risk factors. A systematic review links older fatherhood with lower semen quality and a modest rise in some conditions, but not with miscarriage.

whatToDo.action: Talk with a clinician if you are 35 or older or if either of you has a health condition.

whatToDo.when: If it is taking longer than expected (see the not-conceiving topic)
whatToDo.action: Ask a clinician sooner rather than later if either of you is older or has a known condition.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician early if cycles are irregular, there are known conditions, or previous pregnancy losses.
evidenceNote: Age effects are real but individual. The father-age findings are associations; the review calls some of them controversial.

title: AI chatbots and children
parentQuestions: Can my child talk to ChatGPT?
Are AI companions safe for kids?
whatToKnow: The AAP says chatbots are not built with children in mind and can give false, harmful or inappropriate answers; young children may attach to human-like bots. Advice: talk about which bots they use, review chats together, explain bots do not care or check facts, avoid oversharing, and use AI in common areas.

whatToDo.action: Ask calmly what they use and why.
No private details to a bot; use in shared rooms.

seeClinicianIf: Child withdrawing from people and preferring a bot, or hearing harmful content.
evidenceNote: AAP guidance (opened); area is new and evidence limited.

title: Alcohol, smoking and medicines when trying and when pregnant
parentQuestions: Is any alcohol safe in pregnancy?
I smoked before I knew I was pregnant, what now?
Can I take paracetamol or herbal remedies?
Do I stop my regular medicine?
whatToKnow: CDC says no amount of alcohol has been shown to be safe in pregnancy, and that stopping at any point still helps. The NHS says stopping smoking at any stage lowers the risk of stillbirth and early birth, and nicotine replacement can be used if needed. Paracetamol is the first-choice painkiller, and the UK medicines regulator says it is not linked to autism. Herbal and homeopathic products are not automatically safe, and regular medicines should not be stopped suddenly without advice.

whatToDo.action: Stop alcohol and ask for help with quitting smoking, including for the partner.

whatToDo.when: If you drank or smoked before knowing
whatToDo.action: Stop now, keep your visits, and tell the midwife without worry.
Check with a pharmacist, midwife or doctor first.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a clinician if you cannot cut down alcohol or smoking, or if you take medicines for epilepsy, mental health, diabetes or blood pressure.
evidenceNote: CDC and the NHS are consistent. The paracetamol statement is from the UK regulator as reported on the NHS page.

parentQuestions: Does my child need an action plan at school?

whatToKnow: NHS says asthma usually starts in childhood; use the reliever as instructed and call emergency if it does not help. Food allergy signs range from hives and swelling to anaphylaxis; with an adrenaline injector use it right away and call emergency. Share plans with school staff.

whatToDo.action: Give the school a written plan and medicines.
See a doctor within 2 days (NHS).

title: Allowance and money lessons
parentQuestions: Should I pay my child for chores?
How to teach saving?
whatToKnow: The AAP says whether to give an allowance is a family choice. If you do, tie it to chores and give real spending responsibility. Ages 7 to 8 can use stickers and three jars (save, spend, share); 9 to 11 save toward goals; 12 to 13 make real spending choices.

whatToDo.action: Use jars; start with small amounts.
Let them make mistakes safely.

evidenceNote: Parenting writers disagree on pay for chores; the AAP gives one family-based view.

title: Autonomy at 2: feeding and toileting battles
parentQuestions: Why does my toddler refuse everything?
whatToKnow: Control struggles at meals and the potty overlap with Erikson's autonomy period. Power struggles prolong problems; offering choices and staying calm works better than pressure.

whatToDo.action: Offer limited choices; do not turn it into a contest.

evidenceNote: Draws on AFP toilet training review (stool refusal rises with pressure).

title: Anaphylaxis and using an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen)
parentQuestions: What does anaphylaxis look like in a child?
When do I use the EpiPen?
Do I still go to hospital after using it?
whatToKnow: Anaphylaxis is a life threatening allergic reaction that usually starts within minutes of food, medicine or an insect sting (NHS). Signs include swelling of lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or hard breathing, wheeze, a hoarse voice, feeling faint, blue, grey or pale skin, and a child who is limp or floppy. NHS says use an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector at once if you have one, even if symptoms seem mild, then call for emergency help.

whatToDo.action: Use the auto-injector following the instructions on the device, then call your local emergency number and say you think it is anaphylaxis.
Lay the child down with legs raised, or sit up if breathing is hard. Do not let them stand or walk.
NHS says if symptoms have not improved after 5 minutes use a second auto-injector.
Carry 2 auto-injectors, check expiry dates, practise with a trainer device and teach carers.

seeClinicianIf: Call 911 (or your local emergency number) and go to the ER for any sign of anaphylaxis, even after the auto-injector, because treatment in hospital is needed. NHS says people usually stay 2 to 12 hours. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS and St John Ambulance agree. Training of carers on the device matters; a trainer injector is recommended by NHS.

sources.title: NHS: Anaphylaxis
St John Ambulance: Anaphylaxis

title: Anger and fights
parentQuestions: My child hits when angry
How do I teach calm?
whatToKnow: The AAP page says parents' own calm matters most. Teach steps to acknowledge the feeling, calm the body (breathe, walk away, safe outlet), then think and talk. Walking away from a fight can take more courage than staying.

whatToDo.action: Model calm and rehearse the steps when calm.
Talk to the pediatrician if struggles continue.

seeClinicianIf: Frequent aggression or injuries.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

title: Dog and animal bites
parentQuestions: My child was bitten by a dog, what do I do?
Does a bite need antibiotics or a rabies shot?
When do I go to the ER after a bite?
whatToKnow: Any bite that breaks the skin needs cleaning to lower the infection risk. NHS says to wash with soap and warm water, press firmly with a clean cloth if bleeding heavily, then cover with a clean dressing. A doctor may close the wound, give antibiotics, and check tetanus and rabies risk. Bites on the hands, feet, face or head, and bites from a person, should be seen by a health service.

whatToDo.action: Wash with soap and warm water, press to stop bleeding, pat dry and cover with a clean dressing.
Contact a doctor or health line for bites on hands, feet, face or head, bites from a person, anything left in the wound, or if tetanus status is unclear.
If a part such as a finger or ear is torn off, wrap in clean tissue, put in a plastic bag with ice around it and take it to hospital.

seeClinicianIf: Go to the ER or call your local emergency number if the wound is large or deep or bleeding cannot be stopped. See a doctor for signs of infection (hot, swollen, smelly, leaking, fever) or a risk of rabies. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen for emergencies.
evidenceNote: NHS and St John Ambulance agree. Neither opened page covers how to prevent dog bites, so this topic does not.

sources.title: NHS: Animal and human bites
St John Ambulance: Human and animal bites

title: Antibiotics: when they help and when they do not
parentQuestions: Does my child need antibiotics for a cold?
Why won't the doctor prescribe antibiotics?
Are antibiotics harmful for kids?
whatToKnow: CDC says antibiotics treat certain bacterial infections such as strep throat, whooping cough and urinary tract infections. They do not work on viruses, so they do not treat colds, most sore throats other than strep, flu or most bronchitis. CDC adds that some bacterial sinus and ear infections can clear up without them. Side effects can include rash, diarrhea and allergic reactions, and CDC says side effects are the most common reason for medication-related emergency visits in children.

whatToDo.action: Ask what the diagnosis is, whether it is likely viral or bacterial, and what to do to ease symptoms.
Give them as directed by the doctor or pharmacist, and ask what to watch for.
Do not use leftover antibiotics or ask for them 'just in case'.

seeClinicianIf: Contact the doctor if symptoms get worse, a fever persists, or after starting antibiotics there is a rash, swelling of the face or lips, breathing difficulty (call your local emergency number or go to the ER for the last two), or severe diarrhea.
evidenceNote: CDC states the points above. NHS cold, cough and sore throat pages say the same for those illnesses.

sources.title: CDC: About antibiotic use and resistance
NHS: Common cold
NHS: Sore throat

title: Apgar score
parentQuestions: What do the Apgar numbers mean?
Does a low score predict problems?
whatToKnow: The Apgar score rates heart rate, breathing, muscle tone, reflex response and colour at 1 and 5 minutes, each 0 to 2, for a maximum of 10. Most babies score above 7, and hands and feet often stay bluish at first, so a 10 is uncommon. It alerts staff when a baby needs help but does not predict long-term health, development or intelligence.

whatToDo.action: Ask what the scores were if the team has not said.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the team to explain any score under 7 and what follow-up is planned.
evidenceNote: AAP and ACOG agree on its use and limits.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: Apgar Scores

title: Attachment parenting (Sears) versus attachment theory
parentQuestions: Do I have to babywear and co-sleep to bond with my baby?
Is extended breastfeeding good for attachment?
Is bed sharing safe if I follow attachment parenting?
Is attachment parenting the same as attachment theory?
whatToKnow: Attachment parenting is a popular movement associated with William and Martha Sears and Attachment Parenting International, whose eight principles include feeding with love and respect, nurturing touch and safe sleep. It borrows the word from attachment theory but is a separate set of practices, and there is no evidence that babywearing, bed sharing or extended breastfeeding are required for secure attachment; responsiveness is what matters. The AAP advises against bed sharing under any circumstances for infants and recommends room sharing for at least 6 months; the AAP also supports breastfeeding to 2 years or longer if mother and child both want it. Babywearing is a separate question: choose a safe carrier with the baby's airway visible.

whatToDo.action: Share a room, but put the baby in their own firm, flat sleep surface; if you feed or comfort the baby in your bed, return the baby to their own space before you sleep.
Use a carrier or cuddles if you enjoy them, but do not feel guilty if you cannot; warm, responsive care in other ways counts.
Breastfeed as long as you and the baby wish; ask a lactation consultant for support; formula or earlier weaning does not prevent secure attachment.
Read the AAP safe sleep summary together with your partner and pediatrician, especially if one parent smokes, drinks or takes sedating medicine.

seeClinicianIf: Questions about safe sleep set-ups, premature or low birth weight babies, or breastfeeding problems; ask the pediatrician or a lactation consultant.
evidenceNote: The practices are a lifestyle movement. The AAP's no-bed-sharing recommendation conflicts with the movement's co-sleeping advice, while some researchers and groups advocate harm-reduction advice for families who choose to bed share. Evidence that the practices cause secure attachment is lacking.

Policy Statement: Breastfeeding and the Use of Human Milk

title: Attachment theory: what it says and what it does not
parentQuestions: Is my baby securely attached to me?
Will daycare damage our bond?
Did I miss a bonding window after a C-section or NICU stay?
Can grandparents or a nanny be attachment figures too?
Привязанность к матери: что значит надежная привязанность?
Will not picking up my baby spoil them?
Does attachment parenting matter?
whatToKnow: Bowlby proposed that infants form bonds with caregivers who act as a secure base, and Ainsworth's Strange Situation (about 12 to 18 months) sorted babies into secure, anxious-resistant and avoidant, with disorganized added later. Secure attachment is linked to responsive, sensitive care. The theory does not claim a fixed bonding window at birth, that daycare by itself breaks attachment, that a child has only one attachment figure, or that an attachment style is destiny. The large NICHD study found child care alone did not undermine infant-mother attachment; risk rose mainly when care was poor or unstable and maternal sensitivity was low. Intervention trials show that attachment can be improved: a meta-analysis found sensitivity-focused programs moderately improved parenting and security, and the ABC program showed effects on child-reported security at age 9 in high-risk families.

whatToDo.action: Respond warmly to crying and cues, hold and comfort; you do not need to be perfect, repairing after missed cues counts.
Be a safe base: stay close while the child explores, welcome them back after separations, keep goodbyes short and predictable.
Pick stable, consistent caregivers, plan a gradual settling-in, keep a short goodbye ritual.
Many caregivers (father, grandmother, nanny, teacher) can be attachment figures; encourage consistent, warm relationships with several people.
Ask the pediatrician or a perinatal mental health service about evidence-based parent programs such as Circle of Security or ABC; do not self-diagnose attachment problems.
Respond warmly and consistently; repair after ruptures.
Share caregiving; fathers can be primary attachment figures.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent difficulty bonding, a parent with prolonged low mood, anxiety or loss of interest in the baby, a baby who seems extremely withdrawn or indiscriminately overly friendly, or family stress, trauma or placement changes; ask the pediatrician about parent-infant support. Never label a child's attachment yourself.
evidenceNote: Attachment research is large and peer-reviewed, though classification tools were built in Western samples and temperament and culture shape results. Circle of Security is a widely used program, but this entry cites only the meta-analysis and the ABC trial.

title: Autism signs that appear later
parentQuestions: My child is fine at home but struggles socially at school
Can autism be missed until school age?
Can girls be missed?
whatToKnow: NHS lists signs in older children such as few close friends, rude-seeming remarks, literal understanding of sarcasm, need for strict rules, rituals, trouble with changes (including school transitions), and notes that girls may mask signs. Signs are not proof; assessment is by a specialist team after referral.

whatToDo.action: Speak to your GP or pediatrician and the school's special needs coordinator.
Keep routines predictable and prepare for changes.

seeClinicianIf: Marked difficulties with social communication, repetitive behaviors, or distress at change that interferes with daily life.

title: Autism signs and M-CHAT at 18 and 24 months
parentQuestions: Is my toddler autistic?
What is M-CHAT?
whatToKnow: AAP recommends autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months and developmental screening at 9, 18, 30 months. CDC lists early signs by age: not responding to name at 9 months, few gestures at 12, not sharing interest at 15, not pointing at 18. M-CHAT-R/F is a validated parent questionnaire; screening is not a diagnosis.

whatToDo.action: Ask for M-CHAT-R/F and complete it honestly.
Ask for a referral and request early intervention evaluation.

seeClinicianIf: Any signs above, loss of words or social skills, or a sibling with autism.

title: Erikson: autonomy vs shame and doubt (1 to 3 years)
parentQuestions: How do I help my toddler be independent?
whatToKnow: Erikson proposed toddlers need chance to do things themselves; ridicule or too much control fosters shame. Modern research supports that supported autonomy helps self-regulation but does not support the stage as a strict sequence.

whatToDo.action: Offer two choices; let child do small tasks like dressing, even if slow.

evidenceNote: APA describes Erikson's second stage, about 1.5 to 3 years, where self-reliance grows when children develop at their own pace and doubt can follow excessive criticism or control. It is a theory description; no empirical test was opened.

parentQuestions: Is a used crib or seat safe?
How do I check recalls?
whatToKnow: Rules cover resale too, and you cannot tell from looking whether a crib is compliant. Check recalls, hardware, and avoid nests, pods and bumpers for sleep.

whatToDo.action: Search recall lists by model.
Check the label and fit of any seat before use.

parentQuestions: Is a sling safe for a newborn?
How should the baby sit in a carrier?
Can I feed in the sling?
whatToKnow: The Lullaby Trust says there is no reliable evidence slings cause SIDS, but infants, especially under 4 months, have died when airways were blocked. The T.I.C.K.S. rules are Tight, In view, Close enough to kiss, Keep chin off chest, Supported back. Hands free feeding in a sling is unsafe.

Take baby out to feed.

title: BCG vaccine at birth
parentQuestions: Why is BCG given in the maternity hospital?
What is the scar or bump?
Is BCG needed where tuberculosis is rare?
whatToKnow: WHO recommends one BCG dose for all healthy newborns in countries with high TB incidence or leprosy burden, and allows low-incidence countries to vaccinate only high-risk babies. It can be given with the hepatitis B birth dose, and WHO does not recommend repeat BCG. BCG is not for babies with HIV unless on stable treatment, or those exposed to immunosuppressive treatment in the womb or through breast milk.

whatToDo.action: Ask which vaccines are planned and tell staff about any maternal treatment during pregnancy.
Ask the pediatrician what local reaction at the injection site to expect and how to care for it.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if the site swells, drains pus for a long time, or the glands in the armpit become large.

title: Bed sharing, couch and armchair: what the risks are
parentQuestions: Can I sleep with my baby in bed?
Is it okay to fall asleep with the baby on the sofa?
What if I breastfeed at night?
Is co-sleeping dangerous?
whatToKnow: Sleeping on a sofa or armchair with a baby is a recognised risk factor. NHS advice is not to share a bed if the baby was born early or small, or if anyone smokes, drinks alcohol or takes drowsy medicines. CDC recommends room sharing.

whatToDo.action: Feed in bed with pillows and bedding cleared away, or in a spot where you will not doze off with the baby on a sofa; put the baby back in their own sleep space after feeding.
If you might fall asleep, decide beforehand where the baby is safest.

whatToDo.when: If you may fall asleep with baby
whatToDo.action: Prepare a safe adult bed or move baby to their own surface, never a sofa.
No alcohol, smoke, or sedatives if bed-sharing happens.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a pediatrician or midwife for help if exhaustion is making it hard to stay awake while feeding.
evidenceNote: Guidelines are consistent against sofas and in the high-risk situations; a minority of experts argue for harm-reduction advice about planned bed sharing, but the official bodies here do not recommend it.

Bedtime takes two hours

parentQuestions: How much sleep does my toddler need?

Encourage daytime drinking, regular toilet trips including before bed, waterproof covers; do not punish or routinely wake. An alarm or medicine may be suggested. ADHD and constipation can contribute.

Ask the doctor at 5 to 6 years or if daytime wetting.

parentQuestions: Does my child need a helmet?
Which helmet is right?
whatToKnow: The AAP says a helmet on every ride, a bicycle-certified helmet, replace after a crash or if outgrown, ride with traffic, learn hand signals, and avoid riding at dusk. Adults should model use. Bike-related head injuries cause about 26,000 US emergency visits a year per AAP.

Feet touch the ground; no oversized bikes.

title: Raising a bilingual or trilingual child
parentQuestions: Will two languages confuse my child?
Should we speak Russian, Kazakh and English at home?
My child mixes languages
Will two languages delay my child's speech?
whatToKnow: The AAP says using more than one language does not cause communication delay or disorders, milestones are the same, and mixing languages is normal. Children usually separate their languages by about 3. If a problem exists it shows in all languages. Keeping the home language does not prevent learning the school language and helps academic skills.

Ask for assessment in all the child's languages.
Each parent speaks the language they are most fluent in; keep both rich.
Ask for evaluation in both languages.

title: Birth order: do firstborns and youngest children differ in personality?
parentQuestions: Does birth order shape personality?
Are firstborns smarter?
Will my second child be more relaxed than my first?
Правда ли, что старший ребёнок всегда ответственнее, а младший избалован?
whatToKnow: Large studies in the US, UK and Germany (over 20,000 people) found no consistent birth-order effects on the Big Five personality traits. They did find a tiny decline in measured IQ from firstborn to later-born, and a small decline in self-rated intellect. A second study of narrower traits (trust, patience, risk taking) also found nothing meaningful. Differences you see between your children are mostly temperament, age gap and how you parent each.

whatToDo.action: Treat each child as an individual; avoid labels like 'the responsible one' or 'the baby' that children can grow into.
Give each child one-on-one time regularly, even 10 minutes a day, and ask what they enjoy.
Give older children age-appropriate duties without making them a second parent.
Compare yourself with your own earlier parenting, not children with each other.

evidenceNote: Strong data for a null effect on personality and a very small effect on intelligence (Rohrer 2015, PNAS; Rohrer 2017, specification-curve analysis). Adult self-reports were used, so family-specific effects in individual homes are not excluded.

title: Childbirth education classes: do they help?
parentQuestions: Do we need antenatal classes?
Hypnobirthing or standard classes?
Is a refresher class useful for a second baby?
Should I have a doula?
Can my husband be with me?
Are antenatal classes worth it?
whatToKnow: NHS antenatal classes usually start 8 to 10 weeks before the due date, run weekly for about 2 hours and cover labor, relaxation, delivery methods, newborn care and emotional wellbeing. They are free on the NHS, and refresher classes suit second babies. NICE says to offer all women education on the signs of labor, including how Braxton Hicks differs from active labor and how to contact the team. A Cochrane review (9 trials, last updated 2007) found the effects of general antenatal education on birth outcomes remain largely unknown.

whatToDo.action: Book a class that includes the partner; note that many fill up early.
Attend, and practice the breathing, positions and signs-of-labor lists at home.

whatToDo.when: If it is a second baby
whatToDo.action: Take a refresher or review notes, especially if the gap is long.
Decide who will be with you and check hospital rules.
Book an antenatal class and attend with your partner.

evidenceNote: Classes are recommended by NICE and offered by the NHS, but trials of general education are small and show unclear effects on birth outcomes. Their value is knowledge, confidence, and meeting other parents.

title: Writing a birth plan: preferences, flexibility, and what helps
parentQuestions: Do I need a birth plan?
What should be in it?
What if the plan changes?
Which positions are best in labour?
Are routine procedures like enema or shaving needed?
whatToKnow: The NHS describes a birth plan as a way of letting the team know your wishes, with a checklist: place of birth, who is with you, positions, pool, skin-to-skin before the cord is cut, trainee presence, pain relief, feeding and vitamin K. It stresses that things may change and the midwife will help with the safest choice. NICE says to discuss and record choices early, and that you may change your mind at any time. A 2026 meta-analysis of randomized trials found birth plans linked with more normal vaginal births and more early breastfeeding, but the review itself only says plans 'may be associated' with better outcomes.

whatToDo.action: Read the checklist, talk with your partner, and discuss choices with your midwife or doctor.
Write it as one page with your top 3 priorities; share it with the team and keep a copy in your bag.
Treat it as a conversation: ask 'what are my options and what happens if we wait?'
Write your preferences on one page and discuss with your midwife.
Move, stay upright and change position as comfortable.

evidenceNote: NHS and NICE recommend discussing and recording choices; the effect of written plans on outcomes comes from trials of modest size and quality.

title: Biting and hitting
parentQuestions: How do I stop my toddler biting?
whatToKnow: Biting and hitting are common at 1 to 3 as language is limited and emotions are strong. Respond calmly: stop the act, comfort the hurt child, name the feeling, and offer an alternative. Avoid biting back or hitting.

whatToDo.action: Say 'no biting, that hurts'; move away; teach words or gentle touch.
Watch triggers like fatigue and crowded play.

title: Bleeding, miscarriage and hiding early pregnancy
parentQuestions: Is spotting normal?
Why do people wait 12 weeks to tell anyone?
What causes miscarriage?
whatToKnow: Light bleeding is common early on and does not always mean a miscarriage, but any bleeding should be checked with a maternity unit or doctor. The NHS defines miscarriage as loss before 24 weeks and lists risk factors such as age 35 or older, smoking, heavy caffeine or alcohol, and some medical conditions. It often has no known cause. Heavy bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain or fainting are emergencies.

whatToDo.action: Call your maternity unit, early pregnancy unit or local health advice line.
Go to emergency care.

seeClinicianIf: Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding soaking a pad, severe abdominal or shoulder pain, or feeling faint.
evidenceNote: NHS is clear on when to call; many causes are unknown and nothing parents did is a typical cause.

How to teach consent?

whatToDo.action: Use real names; ask before hugs.
Review the rules at bath time and before new activities.
Use real names; teach 'my body belongs to me'.
Tell the child they will never be in trouble for telling you.

parentQuestions: When can my child stop using a booster?
Is it safe in the front seat?
whatToKnow: The AAP says use a belt-positioning booster until the adult belt fits, typically about 4 feet 9 inches and 8 to 12 years; most children do not fit a seat belt alone until 10 to 12. All children under 13 should ride in the back seat.

whatToDo.action: Switch to a booster.
Check fit before stopping.

evidenceNote: AAP (opened); local law may differ.

title: Bottle, sippy cup and open cup
parentQuestions: When to stop bottles?
Sippy cup vs open cup?
whatToKnow: From about 6 months offer water in a free-flowing, non-valved cup or open cup; valved sippy cups keep drink on the teeth and slow learning to sip. Bottles are fine for milk but not for juice or sugary drinks. Many guidelines suggest moving away from bottles around 12 to 18 months.

whatToDo.action: Introduce an open or free-flowing cup with meals.
Phase out bottles, starting with daytime feeds.

seeClinicianIf: Child cannot swallow drinks without coughing or choking repeatedly.

title: Braxton Hicks or real labor contractions?
parentQuestions: How do I know if these are real contractions?
What is the difference between Braxton Hicks and labor?
Contractions stopped when I lay down, is that normal?
How do I know it is labour?
When should I go to the hospital?
What are Braxton Hicks?
whatToKnow: Braxton Hicks contractions are practice tightenings that can start weeks before labor. They tend to be irregular, stay weak or fade, and often stop when you rest, drink water or change position. True labor contractions come in a pattern, get closer together and stronger over time, keep going when you rest, and are often felt first in the back and then the front. ACOG notes that sometimes only a cervical check can tell the difference.

whatToDo.action: Learn the comparison table with your partner: pattern, closer together, stronger, not easing with rest or position.
Drink a glass of water, empty your bladder and lie down or walk for 30 to 60 minutes; note whether they fade.
Time them from the start of one to the start of the next for an hour and write down length and gap.
Ask your midwife or doctor at which pattern they want you to call, and save the maternity unit phone number.
Know your hospital route and number.
Time them and call.

seeClinicianIf: You are not sure, they are getting stronger or closer together, or any urgent sign appears (waters breaking, bleeding, less baby movement, contractions before 37 weeks).
evidenceNote: ACOG and NHS describe the same distinguishing features; NICE tells services to teach this difference antenatally. The signs are guides, not a test, and a cervical exam is the only certain check.

title: Breastfeeding basics: latch, positions, early days
parentQuestions: How do I know the latch is right?
Is it normal that it hurts?
How soon after birth do I start?
whatToKnow: WHO recommends starting within an hour of birth with skin to skin contact and exclusive breastfeeding for about 6 months. A good latch is a wide mouth, chin touching the breast, more areola above the top lip than below, and no pain after the first few sucks. Nearly all mothers can produce enough milk.

whatToDo.action: Skin to skin and a first feed as soon as possible.
Ask a midwife or lactation consultant to watch a feed.

seeClinicianIf: Seek help early for nipple pain at every feed, cracked or bleeding nipples, or a baby who seems unsatisfied after feeds.

title: Sore nipples, engorgement and mastitis
parentQuestions: Why do my nipples hurt?
What is engorgement?
How do I know it is mastitis?
whatToKnow: Sore nipples are usually from positioning and attachment and fixable with help; do not stop breastfeeding. Engorgement can occur when milk comes in or when feeds are missed. Mastitis is a swollen, hot, painful breast, sometimes with flu like symptoms, usually managed by continuing to feed and getting help.

whatToDo.action: Get a feed observed and adjust positioning.
Keep feeding or expressing, use cold compresses and pain relief, and ask a clinician if it is not improving.

seeClinicianIf: Seek care for fever, red hot wedge shaped area, symptoms lasting more than a day or two, or feeling very unwell.

title: Broken bone or sprain? What to look for
parentQuestions: Is my child's arm broken or just sprained?
Should I give ice and rest?
When does an injury need an X-ray?
whatToKnow: Both injuries cause pain, swelling and bruising. NHS says a crack when it happened, a limb that changed shape or points at an odd angle, numbness or tingling, or skin that turns blue or grey or feels cold are signs of a possible broken bone. St John Ambulance adds that a limb may look shorter, twisted or bent, with a grating feeling, and that open fractures and long bones need emergency transfer.

whatToDo.action: Keep the child still, support the injured part above and below, and remove rings, watches or anything that wraps the limb.
Cover with a sterile dressing or clean non-fluffy cloth and press around, not on, the bone.
NHS suggests protect, rest, ice for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, compression and elevation for the first 2 to 3 days. Do not heat for the first couple of days.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number or go to the ER if you heard a crack, the part changed shape, is numb, tingling, blue, grey or cold, there is an open wound, or a thigh, hip, back, neck or pelvis injury is possible. Ask a doctor the same day if the child cannot put weight on it, pain is severe or getting worse, or it is not improving. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS (sprains) and St John Ambulance (fractures) agree on the warning signs. Neither page is specific to children, so ask a doctor early when the child is young.

title: Bronchiolitis and RSV in babies and young children
parentQuestions: My baby has a cold and is breathing fast, is it bronchiolitis?
Is RSV dangerous?
When do I go to hospital with a wheezy baby?
whatToKnow: NHS says bronchiolitis is a common chest infection of babies and children under 2, usually caused by RSV, and almost all children get it at least once before 2. It starts like a cold, then may bring a cough, faster breathing, feeding difficulty and wheezy or crackly breathing, worst around days 3 to 5. There is no specific treatment and most children recover at home, but some need hospital. Risk is higher under 6 months, with prematurity, or with heart, lung or immune conditions.

whatToDo.action: Keep your child upright when awake, offer small frequent feeds or extra drinks, and check on them at night.
Do not smoke around the child, do not sponge them with cool water, and no aspirin under 16.
Wash hands, clean toys, keep newborns away from people with colds. NHS lists the RSV vaccine in pregnancy for baby protection in the first 6 months.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says to call your local emergency number (911 in the US) or go to the ER for difficulty breathing, pauses in breathing, blue or grey skin, tongue or lips, or a floppy child who will not wake or stay awake. Ask for urgent help if the cold is worsening, feeding is much reduced, there has been a dry nappy for 12 hours, or you are worried. Open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS gives these steps and says to trust your own judgement if your child seems seriously unwell.

NHS: Croup

title: Burns and scalds: what to do in the first minutes
parentQuestions: My child touched something hot, what do I do?
Should I put butter or ice on a burn?
When does a burn need the ER?
whatToKnow: Cool a burn or scald straight away under cool running water for 20 minutes. NHS says to start within 3 hours, and if there is no running water use cool bottled water or a wet towel. Take off clothing and jewellery near the burn unless stuck to it, then lay cling film loosely over the cooled burn. St John Ambulance says do not use ice, creams or gels, and NHS adds no butter or oils, no sticky plasters and do not burst blisters.

whatToDo.action: Hold the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, remove nearby clothing and jewellery unless stuck, and keep the child warm elsewhere on the body.
Cover loosely with cling film lengthways, not wrapped around a limb. A clean plastic bag works for a hand or foot per St John Ambulance.
No ice, butter, oils, creams or gels, and do not burst blisters.

seeClinicianIf: Go to the ER or call your local emergency number if the burn is very large or deep, is on the face, genitals or bottom, or was caused by acid, a chemical or electricity (NHS). Phone the doctor or health line if you are unsure what to do for a child. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen for these cases.
evidenceNote: NHS and St John Ambulance agree on 20 minutes of cool running water and on avoiding ice and greasy products.

title: Button battery swallowed or in the nose or ear
parentQuestions: My child swallowed a button battery, what do I do?
Who do I call?
Should I give anything to drink?
whatToKnow: Poison Control says a button battery stuck in the esophagus can cause a tissue burn through an electric current and severe damage can happen in as little as 2 hours. Most batteries pass in the stool, but you cannot tell in advance. Call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 1-800-498-8666 or a poison center at 1-800-222-1222 immediately, and do not induce vomiting. Batteries in the nose or ear can also cause permanent injury.

whatToDo.action: Call the battery hotline (US) or your emergency number. Have the battery's identification number from the package ready if you can.

Do not induce vomiting. Do not eat or drink on your own initiative. Do not use ear or nose drops if a battery is in the ear or nose. Poison Control mentions a honey step only under their guidance, so ask them.
Watch for fever, stomach pain, vomiting or blood in the stool and report at once.

seeClinicianIf: Go to the ER immediately if a battery may be stuck, or call your local emergency number if the child has trouble breathing or chokes. Poison Control says an x-ray is usually needed right away. Pain or discharge from the nose or ear can mean a battery there. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen. We did not open a Kazakhstan hotline.
evidenceNote: Poison Control page opened (National Capital Poison Center). It covers button batteries only; we did not open a source on magnets, so no magnet advice is included.

title: Coffee and tea in pregnancy
parentQuestions: How much coffee can I drink while pregnant?
Is tea or cola counted?
Does caffeine cause miscarriage?
whatToKnow: The NHS advises no more than 200 mg of caffeine a day, which is roughly two mugs of instant coffee, and counts tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate. A recent review found links between higher caffeine intake and pregnancy loss and low birth weight, often dose dependent, but studies disagree and no single safe dose is established. Keeping under 200 mg is a cautious middle position.

whatToDo.action: Count all sources and stay under 200 mg a day.
Skip them; they add caffeine fast.

seeClinicianIf: Ask if you feel palpitations, severe heartburn or cannot sleep despite cutting back.
evidenceNote: The 200 mg limit is an official UK precaution. Research reviews report conflicting results and no agreed dose.

title: Critical congenital heart disease pulse oximetry screen
parentQuestions: What is the oxygen test on the foot?
Can a heart defect be missed?
whatToKnow: A painless sensor measures oxygen on the right hand and a foot once the baby is at least 24 hours old. A reading under 90%, or two readings an hour apart under 95% or differing by more than 3 points between hand and foot, counts as a fail and leads to a clinician evaluation, usually including an echocardiogram. Passing does not rule out every heart defect.

whatToDo.action: Ask that the test is done before discharge and that the result is recorded.
Watch for the symptoms listed below.

seeClinicianIf: Seek urgent care for fast or laboured breathing, blue or grey lips or skin, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness.

title: Cesarean birth: planned, unplanned, and previous cesarean
parentQuestions: What happens in a cesarean?
How long is recovery?
Can my partner be there?
Can I try a vaginal birth after a cesarean?
When is a caesarean needed?
Can I choose a caesarean?
Is VBAC safe?
whatToKnow: In a cesarean, spinal or epidural anesthesia usually keeps you awake so you can see your baby straight away and your partner can be with you; general anesthesia is used when regional is not possible. The NHS says the operation takes about 40 to 50 minutes and the baby is delivered in 5 to 10 minutes, while ACOG says the hospital stay is usually 2 to 4 days and the abdomen takes a few weeks to heal. NICE says to offer and facilitate early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding help. ACOG says people with a previous cesarean may choose a repeat cesarean or a trial of labor, depending on the incision type, hospital and other risks.

whatToDo.action: Ask your doctor what would make a cesarean likely, and ask the unit about partner presence and skin-to-skin in the operating room.
Attend the pre-op visit, learn the fasting rules, and pack loose clothes and cotton underwear.
Take pain relief as advised, move gently, and ask partner and family for help while you limit activity.

whatToDo.when: If you had a previous cesarean
whatToDo.action: Get your operation notes and discuss options for this birth by 34 to 36 weeks.
Ask whether a caesarean is likely and what recovery involves.
Discuss VBAC options early.

seeClinicianIf: After a cesarean, contact your doctor right away for fever, chills, leg pain, leaking or draining from the incision, heavy bleeding, worsening pain or shortness of breath.
evidenceNote: NHS, ACOG and NICE agree on the procedure and recovery; length of stay differs by country. Birth after a previous cesarean is a shared decision.

title: Child with a disability or delay: early intervention
parentQuestions: Who can ask for an early intervention evaluation?
Do I need a doctor's referral?
Is it free?
whatToKnow: CDC says early intervention means services and supports for babies and young children with developmental delays or disabilities and their families, such as speech, physical and occupational therapy. In the US each state runs its own program with its own eligibility rules. You, your child's doctor, or another care provider can request an evaluation, and you do not need a doctor's referral. Under age 3 contact your state early intervention program; from age 3 contact a local public elementary school for a preschool special education evaluation. ECTA says Part C of IDEA covers infants and toddlers from birth to age 2 and their families, services are at no cost except where state law allows fees, and a written plan (IFSP) is reviewed every 6 months.

whatToDo.action: Write down what you see and ask for an evaluation in writing or by phone, even while you wait for the doctor.
Ask for the eligibility rules in your area, and ask how family needs are assessed.
Keep the plan, review it every 6 months, and tell the team about stress at home.

seeClinicianIf: Tell the pediatrician about any developmental concern at any age, including if your child seems behind even for the corrected age.

title: Licensing, ratios and group size: what to check
parentQuestions: Does childcare have to be licensed?
How many babies per caregiver is okay?
How do I check a daycare's inspection record?
whatToKnow: ChildCare.gov says licensing is the main way US states regulate child care, sets minimum health and safety rules rather than guaranteeing quality, and that not all care is licensed (some is legally exempt). The AAP page lists recommended maximums: for 12 months 3 children per staff member in a group of up to 6; for 13 to 35 months 4 per staff and up to 8; for 3-year-olds 7 per staff and up to 14; for 4 and 5-year-olds 8 per staff and up to 16. For family child care the AAP recommends no more than six children per adult including the caregiver's own, and no more than two under age 2; state rules often allow more.

whatToDo.action: Use your state's child care search to see license status, inspection reports, valid complaints and whether the license was ever suspended or revoked.
Count the adults and children in the room and compare with the AAP numbers; ask what happens when a staff member is sick.

whatToDo.when: If a program is not licensed
whatToDo.action: Ask whether it is legally licensed-exempt and why, and weigh that.

evidenceNote: Ratio numbers are the AAP recommendations as printed on HealthyChildren; actual legal ratios are set by each US state and are often looser, which the AAP page says. ChildCare.gov did not give numbers on the pages we opened.

title: Settling in at daycare: a practical drop-off plan
parentQuestions: How do I make daycare drop-off easier?
My baby cries when I leave, what do I do?
How do I prepare my child for starting childcare?
whatToKnow: The AAP says that before about 7 months babies usually adjust to a consistent caregiver, from 7 to 12 months expect stranger anxiety, and at 12 to 24 months separation anxiety peaks. Its advice by age: for 7 to 12 months, delay or ease in gradually if you can, keep a short goodbye routine, say goodbye and leave quietly; for 12 to 24 months be understanding but firm, reassure that you will come back, and do not return once you have left unless you are prepared to stay. It also says starting child care is often harder on the parents than on the child.

whatToDo.action: Visit with your child, show that you like and trust the caregiver, let your child bring a photo or small toy, and read a picture book about child care.
Keep a short, same-every-day goodbye; if you are able, ease in with shorter days.
Arrange a meeting first; sudden changes can upset a child even when the new person is kind.

seeClinicianIf: If distress does not ease over several weeks, or your child stops eating, sleeping or playing in a lasting way, raise it with your pediatrician.
evidenceNote: AAP advice, not trial-based. The 'several weeks' threshold for asking the doctor is our wording, not a figure on the AAP pages.

title: Types of childcare: in-home, family childcare, center, relative
parentQuestions: Daycare, nanny or a childminder at home: what are the choices?
What is the difference between family child care and a center?
Can grandparents be the childcare?
whatToKnow: The AAP page describes three basic types: in-home care (a caregiver comes to your home), family child care (a provider cares for children in their own home) and center-based care (a church, employer, school or government program such as Head Start). In-home care offers more individual attention and less exposure to illness but skilled providers can be hard to find; family child care can feel more home-like; centers offer structure and trained staff. The AAP also says the quality of care matters more for brain development than the type, and that cost and convenience often drive choices even though they say little about quality.

whatToDo.action: List what matters most: hours, location, group size, cost, and whether your child does better in a small home group or a larger group of similar-aged children.
Share current guidance with them (back sleeping, car seat, medicines out of reach) and ask them to give the people at drop-off a phone number, as the AAP grandparent tips suggest.
Plan for a backup for sick days and caregiver absences.

evidenceNote: Types and trade-offs are from AAP and ChildCare.gov pages. No page we opened ranks one type as best; the AAP says quality matters more than type.

title: Childcare visit checklist: what to look for and ask
parentQuestions: What should I ask when touring a daycare?
What should I look for during a visit?
How do I know a daycare is good?
whatToKnow: ChildCare.gov suggests visiting several programs and asking whether staff made you feel welcome, whether children are happy and busy with age-suited activities, and whether you feel your child would be safe. The AAP adds: written policies on illness, medication, nutrition, discipline and media; a visiting policy that lets you see all areas your child will use; children supervised by sight and sound including at nap time; CPR-certified caregivers; car seats if the center transports children; and a health professional who consults regularly. It points to a 38-indicator checklist from Child Care Aware of America for a structured score.

whatToDo.action: Ask: licensed or legally exempt, space for your child, hours, cost, whether they accept state assistance if you use it.
Ask about caregiver training and tenure, discipline, how often you get feedback, how illness and medication are handled, and whether you can contact current parents.
The AAP nutrition checklist asks whether bottles are held rather than propped, how pumped milk is handled, how allergies and choking are managed, and screen time rules.
Weigh how you felt on calls and visits; check inspection reports for the shortlist.

evidenceNote: Checklist items are from AAP and ChildCare.gov pages. The 38-indicator checklist is only linked from AAP; we did not open it.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Choosing a Child Care Center
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Your Child Care Checklist
ChildCare.gov: Simple Steps for Finding and Choosing Child Care

title: Childproofing basics for 0 to 3 months
parentQuestions: What do I need to baby proof now?
Can the baby fall from the changing table?
whatToKnow: At this age risks are falls, hot drinks, sleep hazards and being left unattended on raised surfaces. NHS advises changing nappies on a mat on the floor or never turning away on a table, and holding the bottle and baby at feeds.

whatToDo.action: Never leave the baby on a raised surface.
Keep hot drinks away.

seeClinicianIf: Seek urgent advice after any fall from a height.
evidenceNote: NHS pages.

sources.title: NHS: Baby and toddler safety
NHS: How to change your baby's nappy

title: Choking first aid: baby versus child
parentQuestions: What do I do if my baby is choking?
Back blows or chest thrusts?
Does my child need the ER after choking?
whatToKnow: Choking first aid differs by age. St John Ambulance: for a baby under 1 who cannot breathe, cry or cough, lay the baby face down along your thigh with the head supported and give up to five back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to five chest thrusts with two thumbs on the breastbone one finger's breadth below the nipple line. For a child, encourage coughing, then up to five back blows leaning the child forward, then up to five abdominal thrusts from behind. Do not sweep the mouth. If the child can cough, speak or cry, let them cough and watch closely.

whatToDo.when: Baby under 1, cannot breathe, cry or cough
whatToDo.action: Five back blows, then five chest thrusts, repeat, and call for emergency help if not cleared. Take the baby with you to make the call.

whatToDo.when: Child, cannot breathe, cough or make noise
whatToDo.action: Five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts, checking the mouth after each. Do not finger sweep.
Move on to CPR (see the CPR topic).
See the choking-prevention topic and take a certified first aid course, which AAP recommends.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number if the object has not cleared, and stay with the child. St John Ambulance says every baby who received chest thrusts, and every child who received abdominal thrusts, should be seen in hospital even if the blockage has cleared. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen while you act.
evidenceNote: St John Ambulance gives the steps and AAP gives the warning signs and says to learn first aid. Techniques are taught best by a trained instructor; this page is not a substitute for a course.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Choking prevention for babies and children
St John Ambulance: Choking baby (under one year old)
St John Ambulance: Choking child

title: Choking prevention and first aid
parentQuestions: What foods can my toddler choke on?
whatToKnow: Gagging is normal; choking is silent and needs first aid. Under 4 avoid whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, hard raw carrot and apple, hot dog rounds; cut food small and sit the child down to eat. Learn infant and child choking first aid.

whatToDo.action: Stay with the child while eating; no eating in car seat or running.
Take a first-aid class.

seeClinicianIf: Any choking episode with coughing that persists, noisy breathing afterward, or blue lips: emergency and check-up.
evidenceNote: NHS lists foods to avoid and gag vs choke; AAP choking page failed to open.

sources.title: NHS: Your baby's first solid foods

title: Where to give birth: hospital, birth centre or home
parentQuestions: Is home birth safe?
How do I choose a maternity hospital?
What is a midwifery unit?
whatToKnow: The NHS says you can give birth at home, in a midwife-led unit or in hospital, and that birth is generally safe in any of them for low-risk women. In the large English Birthplace study, the main safety outcome did not differ significantly by place overall, but for first-time mothers planned home birth had a higher rate of poor outcomes (adjusted odds ratio about 1.75, and the NHS page quotes 9 versus 5 per 1,000). Interventions were lower outside obstetric units, and transfers during labour were more common for first-time mothers.

whatToDo.action: Visit or tour the options and ask about transfer plans.
Confirm the chosen place still suits your risk level.

seeClinicianIf: Ask your midwife or doctor early if you have twins, a prior caesarean, high blood pressure or diabetes, as options narrow.
evidenceNote: One large national cohort plus NHS advice; risk figures are for England and depend on parity and system.

sources.title: Where to give birth: the options (NHS)
Perinatal and maternal outcomes by planned place of birth for healthy women with low risk pregnancies: the Birthplace in England study (BMJ 2011, via Europe PMC)

title: Chores by age
parentQuestions: What chores can a 6 year old do?
How do I get my child to help?
whatToKnow: The AAP lists chores by age: 5 to 7 make the bed, set the table, put toys away; 8 to 10 add vacuuming, help cooking and walking the pet; 11 to 12 add cleaning the bathroom, doing laundry, and watching younger siblings when an adult is home. Praise effort; use consequences not scolding.

whatToDo.action: Pick 1 new task at a time.
Use a chart and regular family meetings.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent avoidance of responsibility at home and school.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Age-appropriate chores for children

title: Caring for the circumcised penis
parentQuestions: How do I clean it after circumcision?
What is normal during healing?
whatToKnow: The tip may look raw or yellowish at first, and healing usually takes about 7 to 10 days. If a bandage is used, apply petroleum jelly so it does not stick; a plastic ring falls off in about 5 to 8 days. Follow the provider's instructions for bathing and dressings.

whatToDo.action: Check for bleeding and apply petroleum jelly if advised.
Redness and yellow film should fade rather than spread.

seeClinicianIf: Contact the doctor for bleeding, no urine in 6 to 12 hours, fever of 38 C or more, increasing redness after 3 to 5 days, or greenish or foul discharge.
evidenceNote: AAP and CPS give consistent aftercare advice.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: Circumcision
Caring for Kids (Canadian Paediatric Society): Circumcision

title: Circumcision benefits and risks: the numbers
parentQuestions: How common are complications?
Does it prevent infections?
Does it change sexual sensation?
whatToKnow: AAP lists lower risk of urinary tract infection in the first year, lower HIV and some STI risk in adulthood, and lower penile cancer risk (which is already very rare). WHO cites about 60% lower HIV acquisition in heterosexual men in African trials, an adult setting. RACP reports complication rates between 0.4% and 16% depending on definition, median about 1.5% in one review, bleeding about 0.8%, and notes the quality of published studies is low.

whatToDo.action: Ask the provider for their own complication rate and how bleeding or infection is handled.

seeClinicianIf: Call at once for bleeding that does not stop, no urine within 6 to 8 hours, fever, or spreading redness.
evidenceNote: Benefit studies are mostly observational or from adult African trials; complication rates vary with the operator and setting.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: Circumcision
RACP: Circumcision of Infant Males position statement (December 2022)
WHO: Voluntary medical male circumcision for HIV prevention

title: Circumcision: the decision overall
parentQuestions: Should we circumcise our son?
What do doctors recommend?
What happens if we decide later?
We cannot agree, what should we do?
Will our son be teased?
Will he resent us either way?
whatToKnow: Circumcision is the removal of the foreskin. Major medical bodies describe it as a family decision rather than a medical necessity for most boys. Some give a weak preference (AAP says health benefits outweigh risks), some do not recommend routine circumcision (RACP, Canadian Paediatric Society), and some recommend deferring to the boy himself (Nordic ombudsmen, KNMG).

whatToDo.action: Talk it through as a couple and with the pediatrician; write down what matters to you.
Ask who does it, which method, what pain relief, and what happens if there are complications.
Each parent writes their top three reasons and top three fears; compare.
Book a talk with the pediatrician and, if relevant, a religious leader or older relative.

seeClinicianIf: A medical reason (for example a repeatedly infected foreskin or scarring) is a clinician decision at any age.
evidenceNote: Experts disagree: benefits are real but small for the average boy in low-risk settings, risks are low when done by trained staff, and ethics views differ by body and country.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: Circumcision
Caring for Kids (Canadian Paediatric Society): Circumcision
RACP: Circumcision of Infant Males position statement (December 2022)
Nordic Ombudsmen for Children and pediatric experts: Let the boys decide on circumcision (30 Sept 2013)

title: Circumcision and pain control
parentQuestions: Is circumcision painful for newborns?
What pain relief works?
whatToKnow: AAP says circumcision is painful but pain can be reduced with numbing cream and with a local injection at the base of the penis, which blocks pain more fully. RACP says doing the procedure without anaesthesia and analgesia is unacceptable, and that sucrose and topical cream alone do not control the pain adequately. The Canadian Paediatric Society lists local anaesthetic, sugar solution, numbing cream and acetaminophen.

whatToDo.action: Ask exactly which pain relief is used and who gives it.
Hold, feed and comfort the baby; give pain medicine as the clinician advises.

evidenceNote: Bodies agree pain control is needed; they differ on which methods are enough.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: Circumcision
RACP: Circumcision of Infant Males position statement (December 2022)
Caring for Kids (Canadian Paediatric Society): Circumcision

title: What other bodies say about infant circumcision
parentQuestions: Do European doctors recommend it?
What do Dutch, Nordic, Australian and Canadian bodies say?
whatToKnow: RACP (2022) says disease frequency, protection and complication rates do not justify routine infant circumcision, yet parental choice should be respected and it must be done with proper pain control by trained staff. The Nordic ombudsmen and pediatric experts (2013) argue it conflicts with children's rights and ask that boys decide for themselves. The KNMG (2010) urged parents not to circumcise without medical reason but opposed a legal ban.

whatToDo.action: Notice which bodies speak about infant routine practice and which about adult HIV prevention; they are different questions.

evidenceNote: Statements differ in purpose (clinical benefit, ethics, public health) and are partly political; I could not open BMA or CDC infant-specific statements. WHO's circumcision page covers HIV prevention in boys aged 15 and older and men, not infants (see benefits topic).

sources.title: RACP: Circumcision of Infant Males position statement (December 2022)
Nordic Ombudsmen for Children and pediatric experts: Let the boys decide on circumcision (30 Sept 2013)
