title: Circumcision rates: US trend and worldwide
parentQuestions: How common is circumcision?
Is it declining in the US?
whatToKnow: In US hospitals, newborn circumcision recorded at birth fell from 64.5% in 1979 to 58.3% in 2010, with a low of 55.4% in 2007, and the West fell furthest (63.9% to 40.2%). These figures miss ritual and later procedures so are not full prevalence. Globally about 30% of males were estimated circumcised in 2007.

whatToDo.action: Check whether a rate means hospital newborn procedures or all men.

evidenceNote: The CDC trend data ended in 2010; I found no opened source for the 2010s.

sources.title: CDC NCHS: Trends in Circumcision for Male Newborns in U.S. Hospitals, 1979 to 2010
WHO and UNAIDS: Male circumcision: global trends and determinants of prevalence, safety and acceptability (2007)

title: How many colds per year is normal for a child?
parentQuestions: My child is sick all the time, is that normal?
How many colds do kids get per year?
Is a weak immune system the reason?
whatToKnow: CDC says children often get more colds than the two to three a year that adults have on average. The page does not give an exact number for children. Colds usually last less than a week per CDC, though NHS says symptoms can take 1 to 2 weeks and last longer in young children. Complications CDC lists include ear infections, sinus infections, asthma attacks, bronchitis and pneumonia.

whatToDo.when: When illnesses feel back to back
whatToDo.action: Keep a simple log of dates, temperature, and how your child ate and slept, so you can show a pattern to the doctor instead of relying on memory.
Handwashing and not sharing cups reduce spread (see handwashing-and-stomach-bugs).

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if illnesses come with poor weight gain, trouble breathing, a cough or wheeze that keeps returning, or any illness that is much more severe than the usual cold.
evidenceNote: CDC states children get more colds than adults but gives no exact count. We did not find an opened page with a specific number, so none is stated here.

sources.title: CDC: About common cold
NHS: Common cold

title: Colic and the Period of PURPLE Crying
parentQuestions: Why does my baby cry for hours in the evening?
Is it colic?
Does gripe water work?
When does crying get better?
whatToKnow: Many healthy babies cry more from about 2 weeks old, peaking in the afternoon and evening, and settling around 3 to 4 months. NHS describes colic as crying for more than 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for a week in an otherwise healthy baby. There is no cure; cuddling, upright feeding, winding, motion and white noise can help, and anti-colic drops and spinal manipulation are not recommended.

whatToDo.action: Check hunger, nappy, wind and temperature, then try holding, rocking, a warm bath, gentle white noise.
Put the baby safely in the cot and take a break if you feel overwhelmed; ask for help.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician for a weak or high pitched cry, a cry that sounds different from usual, fever, not feeding, poor weight gain, or if you cannot cope.
evidenceNote: NHS describes the typical pattern and says the cause is unknown; the PURPLE page frames crying in healthy infants as normal. Evidence for remedies is weak.

sources.title: NHS: Colic
NHS: Soothing a crying baby
National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome: Period of PURPLE Crying

title: Colds in children: what is normal and what helps
parentQuestions: My child has a runny nose and cough, what do I do?
How long does a cold last in a child?
Do cold medicines work for kids?
whatToKnow: A cold is caused by a virus and usually comes on over 2 to 3 days. NHS says people usually feel better in 1 to 2 weeks, and symptoms can last longer in young children, who may also be irritable, feed and sleep badly, breathe through the mouth and vomit after coughing. Antibiotics do not help a cold because it is viral. Cold medicines do not shorten it.

whatToDo.action: Offer plenty of fluids and rest. Small children often lose their appetite for a few days, which is common.
Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease aches or a high temperature. Check the label or ask a pharmacist, and see the weight-based dosing page rather than guessing (fever-medicine-by-weight).
Do not give aspirin under 16. Do not let a child breathe steam from a bowl of hot water (scald risk). Decongestants are not for children under 6 per NHS. Do not give honey under 12 months.
Wash hands, use tissues once and bin them, do not share cups or towels.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says to see a GP for a high temperature lasting more than 3 days, symptoms that get worse, shortness of breath or chest pain, a cold that has not improved after 10 days, or any time you are worried about your child. Call your local emergency number or go to the ER for blue or grey lips or severe breathing difficulty.
evidenceNote: NHS and CDC pages describe the same course and say antibiotics do not treat colds. NHS says little evidence supports vitamin C, echinacea or garlic.

sources.title: CDC: About common cold
NHS: Common cold

title: Constipation and stool withholding
parentQuestions: My toddler holds in poop
whatToKnow: Withholding stool because of fear or power struggle is the commonest cause of recurrent constipation in toddlers. Treat constipation, add fibre and fluids, keep toilet positive, and sometimes pause training.

whatToDo.action: Fibre, water, regular sit after meals; no punishment.

seeClinicianIf: Blood in stool, severe pain, belly swelling, vomiting, or constipation lasting over 2 weeks.
evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance: withholding is a main cause of functional constipation in children 2 to 5; do not push toilet training; treatment plans go through the pediatrician.

sources.title: Constipation in Children (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
AAFP American Family Physician: Toilet Training (2008)

title: Contraception while breastfeeding: LAM, IUD and the mini-pill
parentQuestions: Can I get pregnant while breastfeeding?
Does breastfeeding work as birth control?
Which contraception is safe while breastfeeding?
whatToKnow: NHS says you can get pregnant as early as 3 weeks after birth, even while breastfeeding and before periods return. The lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) works only while all conditions hold: baby under 6 months, breastfeeding fully or nearly fully with only breast milk, and no periods since birth. NHS lists the progestogen-only pill, implant, injection, condoms and IUD or IUS as options that can be started straight after birth, including while breastfeeding.

whatToDo.when: Before leaving hospital or at the early check
whatToDo.action: Choose a method with your midwife, doctor or family planning clinic, since fertility can return before the first period.

Switch to another method as soon as baby is over 6 months, gets formula, solids or a dummy, periods return (even light spotting), night feeds stop, or feeds get further apart. NHS notes expressing may make LAM less reliable.

whatToDo.when: If you want an IUD or IUS
whatToDo.action: NHS says if it is not fitted within 48 hours of birth, it is usually recommended to wait until 4 weeks after the birth. CDC describes the hormonal and copper IUD and the progestin-only pill but gives no postpartum timing.

whatToDo.when: If you want the combined pill, ring or patch
whatToDo.action: NHS says if breastfeeding you are usually advised to wait until at least 6 weeks after birth; discuss it with a clinician.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a clinician before choosing hormonal methods, and for personal advice on timing, especially after a cesarean, with blood clot risk factors, or if your period returns while relying on LAM.
evidenceNote: NHS and CDC agree on the LAM conditions. Timing for IUD and combined methods comes from NHS only; the ACOG page we tried returned a payment error and was not read.

sources.title: CDC: About contraception
NHS: Sex and contraception after birth

title: Cord blood banking: public donation or private storage
parentQuestions: Is it worth paying to store cord blood?
Can we donate it?
Does collecting it affect the birth?
whatToKnow: The AAP encourages donating to a public bank, which is free and does not interfere with the birth, and says private banks only make sense for a family with a known child who may need a sibling transplant. Most families never use privately stored blood, and public banks report cord blood used far more often than private units. Private storage costs roughly 1,350 to 2,300 US dollars to enrol plus yearly fees (US figures).

whatToDo.action: Check whether any public bank collects at your hospital; registration is usually needed before labor.
Ask what happens to the sample if the company closes, and what it is accredited for.

evidenceNote: AAP and similar bodies favour public banking; the main disagreement is marketing claims from private banks, not between medical societies.

sources.title: AAP Encourages Use of Public Cord Blood Banks (HealthyChildren.org)

title: Corrected age: judging a preemie's milestones
parentQuestions: How do I work out my premature baby's corrected age?
Is my preemie behind?
Until what age do we use corrected age?
whatToKnow: AAP says corrected (adjusted) age subtracts the weeks a baby was born early from the actual age, and recommends using it for milestones until about age 2. Example from AAP: a baby born at 32 weeks is 8 weeks early, so at 4 months she has the skills of a 2-month-old. AAP notes that by age 2 most preemies have caught up to the usual range, and that relatives judging by actual age may wrongly think a baby is delayed.

whatToDo.action: Tell the pediatrician your baby's due date as well as birth date so they use corrected age.
Compare milestones with the corrected age, and look for steady forward progress rather than one skill on one day.
Write it down and ask at the next visit, including whether early intervention would help.

seeClinicianIf: Raise it with the pediatrician if progress stalls, skills are lost, or you are worried at any age. Ask about early intervention if a milestone looks late even for the corrected age.
evidenceNote: AAP pages give the method and the two-year guide. Milestone checklists themselves are not used the same way in every country.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Corrected Age For Preemies
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Preemie Milestones

title: Coughs in children: honey, syrups and when to worry
parentQuestions: How long should a cough last?
Can I give cough syrup to my child?
Is honey safe for a cough?
whatToKnow: NHS says a cough usually clears up within 3 to 4 weeks, and most coughs come from a cold or flu. Hot lemon and honey may have a similar effect to cough syrup, but the evidence is limited, and honey is not for babies under 1 year. NHS adds that some cough medicines should not be given to children under 12 and that decongestants and codeine medicines will not stop a cough.

whatToDo.action: Rest, fluids, and keep the child home if they have a high temperature or feel too unwell for normal activity.
For a child over 1 year, a warm (not hot) drink with a little honey is the home option NHS names. Do not give hot drinks to small children.
Ask a pharmacist about age limits. Do not combine cough and cold products with paracetamol or ibuprofen, you can double up on ingredients.
Note how long it has gone on and whether it is worse at night or with running or cold air, and mention it at the next visit.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says to ask for an urgent appointment or call for help if the cough is very bad or quickly worsening, the child seems very unwell, finds it hard to breathe, has chest pain or coughs up blood. See a GP for a cough lasting more than 3 weeks. For severe breathing difficulty or blue or grey lips, call your local emergency number or go to the ER and open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS gives these steps and states the evidence for honey and herbal products is limited. The honey age limit comes from NHS wording (under 1 year).

sources.title: NHS: Cough
NHS: Common cold

title: Keeping the couple relationship
parentQuestions: We never talk any more
How do we stay a team?
whatToKnow: AAP self-esteem advice says to shield children from adult stress such as family conflict when possible, and divorce guidance says conflict hurts children most. Regular communication and backing each other's authority help.

whatToDo.action: A short check-in without kids.
Argue away from children.

seeClinicianIf: Ongoing conflict, fear or violence: get support.
evidenceNote: Thin; AAP pages opened.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Signs of low self-esteem in children and teens
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How to support children after parents separate or divorce

title: The couple relationship after a baby
parentQuestions: Why are we arguing so much?
How do we share the load?
whatToKnow: NHS says a baby strains relationships regardless of how good they were, mainly from tiredness and lost time. Listening, saying what you need, and sharing housework and childcare help. Parents may disagree on discipline, so settle it privately.

whatToDo.action: Ten minutes to talk about what each needs.
Do not disagree about parenting in front of the child.

seeClinicianIf: Seek couple counselling if conflict or low mood persists.
evidenceNote: NHS general advice.

sources.title: NHS: Relationships after having a baby

title: Cow's milk at 12 months
parentQuestions: Can I give cow's milk at 1?
Goat milk or plant milk?
whatToKnow: Cow's milk as a main drink is advised from 12 months; small amounts in cooking from about 6 months are fine. Limit to about 16 to 24 oz a day to protect iron intake. Plant drinks are not equivalent nutritionally; NHS advises against rice drinks under 5.

whatToDo.action: Switch to whole milk gradually; offer water with meals.
Check milk intake does not crowd out solid foods.

seeClinicianIf: Pale, tired, poor eating, or blood in stool.
evidenceNote: NHS opened for before-1 and rice drink; milk quantity limit from general AAP advice not opened.

sources.title: NHS: Your baby's first solid foods

title: Crib safety standards
parentQuestions: What should I look for in a crib?
Is a drop side crib OK?
Can I use a bumper?
whatToKnow: US rules since 2011 ban traditional drop side cribs, and AAP advises keeping bumpers, pillows and soft toys out. NHS lists a firm mattress that fits snugly, bars no more than 6.5 cm apart, and a cot marked to a recognised standard.

whatToDo.action: Check standards and mattress fit.
Check recalls and hardware.

seeClinicianIf: Remove the baby from any crib that is damaged or has missing parts.
evidenceNote: AAP and NHS cover the key points; standards differ between countries.

sources.title: AAP HealthyChildren: New crib standards, what parents need to know
NHS: What you'll need for your baby

title: The 'crisis of 1 year' (Vygotsky and Russian tradition)
parentQuestions: What is the crisis of 1 year?
whatToKnow: In the Russian developmental psychology tradition (Vygotsky, Elkonin) a crisis around 1 year marks the shift from infancy to early childhood: walking, first words, wishes and early protest. Western research does not use this label but describes the same changes: walking, first words, separation and strong attachment.

whatToDo.action: Offer safe independence; be consistent.

evidenceNote: Vygotsky names a crisis at age one tied to walking and first words; it is a theoretical period, not a measured stage. AAP guidance treats tantrums from age 1 as common and normal.

sources.title: Top Tips for Surviving Tantrums (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
L. S. Vygotsky, The Problem of Age (1932 to 1934), Collected Works vol. 5, marxists.org

title: The 'crisis of 3 years' (Vygotsky) vs the terrible twos
parentQuestions: What is the crisis of 3 years?
Is my toddler going through the crisis?
whatToKnow: Vygotsky described a crisis at about 3 with negativism, stubbornness, self-will and 'I myself'; he said crises are not inevitable and vary widely. The Western equivalents are the terrible twos or threenager, and research on autonomy and tantrums finds peak at 18 to 36 months. One Russian kindergarten study found marked symptoms in about 59 percent of children, often tied to adult handling.

whatToDo.action: Give limited choices, let child do tasks themselves, keep routines.
Hold the limit calmly and avoid power struggles.

seeClinicianIf: Aggression, extreme defiance daily, or difficulties lasting past 4 years.
evidenceNote: Vygotsky texts via search summaries; limited empirical research. Sullivan and Lewis opened for tantrum data.

sources.title: Sullivan and Lewis 2012, Infancy: Early goal blockage response and subsequent tantrum behavior (PMC3293480)

title: The 'crisis of 7 years'
parentQuestions: Is the crisis of 7 years real?
My 6 or 7 year old became moody and defiant before school, is that the crisis?
What is the 7 year crisis in Russian psychology?
whatToKnow: Lev Vygotsky described a transition around age 7 between the preschool and school periods. He wrote that the child becomes harder to teach, shows unsteady mood and will, and also becomes more independent. He thought it comes from the child's own development breaking up the old social situation, not from outside pressure. It is a theoretical concept from the 1930s, not a measured diagnosis.

whatToDo.action: If moods and defiance rise around school entry, treat it as a normal change in routines and expectations: keep sleep and meals steady, give small real responsibilities, and explain rules instead of only issuing them.
Do not treat the label as a reason to wait out serious problems; use it only as one possible reading of a transition.

seeClinicianIf: Lasting low mood, school avoidance, loss of interest, strong anxiety, or aggression that does not ease within a few weeks of settling in are worth raising with the pediatrician or school psychologist.
evidenceNote: Vygotsky's age periodization is a historical framework. The page we opened (his 1934 text) states the ideas but gives no measurement; we found no modern study here that confirms a universal crisis at 7. What research does support is that school entry is a stress point where behavior and sleep often wobble.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Back-to-school tips for families
Vygotsky, The Problem of Age (1934), Marxists Internet Archive
Elkonin, On the problem of stages in the mental development of the child (1971), Marxists Internet Archive

title: Croup: barking cough and noisy breathing
parentQuestions: My child has a barking seal cough at night, is it croup?
What do I do for croup?
When is croup an emergency?
whatToKnow: NHS describes croup as a common illness of babies' and young children's airways that is usually mild. It causes a barking cough like a seal, a hoarse voice, and sometimes a high-pitched rasping sound when breathing in, often after a few cold days and worse at night. NHS says to call your doctor or local health advice line if you think it is croup, because the child may need treatment. Mild croup usually gets better on its own within 48 hours.

whatToDo.when: When you think it is croup
whatToDo.action: Call your doctor or health line the same day for a check, as NHS advises.
Keep your child upright and calm, give fluids, and check on them regularly, including at night. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort.
NHS says do not put your child in a steamy room or have them inhale steam.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says call your local emergency number (911 in the US) or go to the ER if the child is struggling to breathe (grunting, tummy sucking in under the ribs), has blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin or lips, is very sleepy or hard to wake, is limp or floppy, is very upset and cannot be calmed, or is drooling and finding it hard to swallow. Open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS gives symptoms, home care and the emergency list. It also says a doctor may give medicine to shorten the illness.

sources.title: NHS: Croup
NHS: Bronchiolitis

title: When the crying is too much: put baby down safely, walk away, brief every caregiver
parentQuestions: What do I do when my baby will not stop crying and I am losing it?
How do I tell the babysitter or grandparents about crying and shaking?
Is it okay to leave a crying baby in the crib for a few minutes?
whatToKnow: Feeling upset or angry at a crying baby is normal; keeping control of your behavior is what matters. The practical rule from NHS and AAP: if you are stressed and nobody can take over, put the baby down safely in the cot or crib, leave the room and calm down. Shaking a baby can cause brain damage, blindness or death, and no soothing method works every time, which is the point of the Period of PURPLE Crying program.

whatToDo.action: Agree a plan with your partner: who takes over, which friend or relative to call, and the rule that nobody shakes, throws, hits or jerks the baby. Keep the NHS Cry-sis line or your local helpline handy.

Put baby on their back in the crib or cot (nothing soft in it), leave the room, and breathe. NHS suggests about 10 minutes before going back; AAP suggests 10 to 15 minutes and not picking the baby up until you feel calm. Music, a call to someone, or a simple chore can help.
Return and try soothing again, and rule out a cause: hunger, diaper, temperature, spit-up, illness. Call the doctor if you suspect a medical problem.

whatToDo.when: Before anyone else cares for baby
whatToDo.action: Brief babysitters, grandparents and partners: crying peaks in the early weeks and is normal, soothing may not work, if they feel overwhelmed they put baby down safely and step away or call you, and they never shake. AAP says to make sure partners and babysitters know this too.

seeClinicianIf: If a baby has been shaken or you fear it may have been, or baby is limp, hard to wake, has a fit, blue or pale skin, or trouble breathing, call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the ER, and use the app's fixed Urgent help screen. For a baby who seems unwell with a high temperature or not feeding, contact the doctor (your doctor or local health advice line). If you are afraid you may hurt your baby, put baby down safely, call someone to come, and tell your doctor.
evidenceNote: AAP and NHS give the same put-down-and-step-away advice; PURPLE is an established prevention program. We did not open a CDC page (they returned 404), and the PURPLE page we opened does not list the specific steps.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Responding to Your Baby's Cries
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How to Calm a Fussy Baby
NHS: Soothing a crying baby
Period of PURPLE Crying (National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome)

title: Curiosity about bodies and 'playing doctor'
parentQuestions: My 4 year old touches her genitals
My kids showed each other their bodies
Is this normal?
whatToKnow: The AAP says at 4 to 5 children may touch their own genitals or show interest in other children's bodies; this is normal interest, not adult sexual behavior, but limits are needed. Teach private parts, that no one should look at or touch them without permission, and asking before touching others.

whatToDo.action: Stay calm; say it is private and for private places.
Teach what is and is not okay, no shaming.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent or aggressive sexual behavior, explicit knowledge beyond age, or imitating adult acts.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened). Freudian framing of this age is covered separately as theory.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Talking to your young child about sex
AAP: 10 tips for parents to teach children about body safety and boundaries

title: Cuts and bleeding wounds
parentQuestions: How do I stop my child's cut from bleeding?
Does my child need stitches?
When is a cut an emergency?
whatToKnow: For a bleeding cut, press firmly with a clean cloth or bandage, raise a hand or arm above the head, and add more cloth on top if blood soaks through. If something is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out and do not press on it: press on both sides to bring the edges together. Once bleeding stops, rinse with tap or bottled water and cover with a clean dressing. Check that a bandage is not too tight by pressing the skin beyond it for 5 seconds and seeing colour return within 2 seconds.

whatToDo.action: Wash hands or put on gloves if you have them, press firmly with a clean cloth, raise the limb, and keep pressing.
Rinse with water, pat dry, cover with a plaster or dressing, and keep it clean and dry.
NHS notes some wounds need a tetanus injection. Ask the child's doctor if you are unsure about vaccines.

seeClinicianIf: Go to the ER or call your local emergency number if bleeding cannot be stopped, blood spurts out bright red, the wound is very large or deep, something is stuck in it, there is numbness or trouble moving the area, or it is a bad cut on the face or palm (NHS). Ask for same day advice for a dirty wound, a bite from a stray or wild animal, a cut over about 5 cm, signs of infection, or a child who feels unwell. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen for emergencies.
evidenceNote: NHS gives the steps and thresholds. The 5 cm and 10 minute check values come from the NHS page.

sources.title: NHS: Cuts and grazes

title: Death and grief
parentQuestions: How do I explain death to a child?
Should my child go to the funeral?
whatToKnow: The AAP says children under 5 need simple concrete language; preschoolers often see death as temporary, so avoid 'went to sleep'. School-age children usually understand death by 5 to 7 but accepting a personal loss is hard. Be honest, listen, expect repeats, and make funeral attendance optional with explanation.

whatToDo.action: Say plainly that the person died.
Expect questions to return; keep routines.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent problems with sleep, school, eating or friends, or talk of self-harm.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How children understand death and what you should say

title: Dehydration signs in a sick or feverish child
parentQuestions: How do I know my child is dehydrated?
My child has a fever and won't drink, what now?
How many wet nappies should there be?
whatToKnow: NHS says babies, children and older adults are at more risk of dehydration, and a high temperature is one cause alongside vomiting and diarrhea. In babies it may show as a sunken soft spot, sunken eyes, few or no tears, fewer wet nappies, drowsiness or irritability. In older children it can look like dark strong-smelling pee, peeing less, dry mouth and lips, tiredness or dizziness.

whatToDo.action: Offer fluids in small, frequent sips. Carry on breastfeeding or formula, and give the usual diet to small children.
Count wet nappies or toilet trips, check for tears and a moist mouth, and note drowsiness.
Look for dehydration at each check, NHS fever advice lists it as a reason to call.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says call for urgent advice for unusual tiredness or drowsiness, few wet nappies, dark yellow pee, fast breathing, no tears, or a sunken soft spot. Call your local emergency number or go to the ER if there is blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, cold skin, fast or difficult breathing, confusion, or a child who is very sleepy or hard to wake, since these can signal shock. Open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS dehydration and fever pages agree on these signs. The pages we opened do not give a rehydration schedule by weight.

sources.title: NHS: Dehydration
NHS: High temperature (fever) in children
NHS: Diarrhoea and vomiting

title: Delayed cord clamping: how long to wait
parentQuestions: Should we wait before the cord is cut?
Does waiting raise the jaundice risk?
What if the baby needs help breathing?
whatToKnow: WHO advises waiting at least one minute before clamping the cord, for babies who do not need immediate help with breathing. Waiting lets blood keep moving from the placenta to the baby and helps iron stores for the first months. A FIGO review suggests about 30 seconds to 3 minutes at term, and notes that a little more jaundice is expected to be outweighed by the benefits where phototherapy is available.

whatToDo.when: In the birth plan, by week 34
whatToDo.action: Ask the maternity team how long they usually wait and whether they wait for babies born by cesarean.
Skin-to-skin can happen while the cord is still attached if the baby is well.

seeClinicianIf: Ask your midwife or obstetrician early if you want a specific plan, because a baby who needs resuscitation or a mother with bleeding may change it on the day.
evidenceNote: WHO recommends at least one minute; FIGO gives a range and says optimal duration is still researched. Evidence for long-term development benefit is promising but limited.

sources.title: FIGO good practice recommendations on delayed umbilical cord clamping (PMC)
WHO ELENA: Optimal timing of cord clamping for the prevention of iron deficiency anaemia in infants

title: Delaying school ('redshirting')
parentQuestions: Will holding my summer-born child back help?
Does waiting a year give an advantage?
whatToKnow: Some parents delay children with birthdays near the cutoff hoping for an advantage. The AAP says this is not necessarily helpful, early gaps often fade by third or fourth grade, and being older than classmates has been linked to more behavior problems in adolescence.

whatToDo.action: Ask what the extra year would contain; a year of poor care is worse than school.
Choose a rich preschool or home plan for the year.

evidenceNote: Based on AAP parent guidance; researchers do not fully agree on long-term effects and results differ by country.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Is your preschooler ready for kindergarten?

title: Dental sealants
parentQuestions: Should my child get sealants?
Are sealants safe?
whatToKnow: The AAPD/ADA guideline gives a strong recommendation for sealants on baby and permanent molars with sound or early decay. Sealants work better than none and no clear difference from fluoride varnish was shown. The evidence does not support risk from the small amounts of BPA in some sealants.

whatToDo.action: Ask the dentist about sealing new permanent molars.
Check retention at dental visits.

evidenceNote: AAPD/ADA guideline (opened).

sources.title: AAPD/ADA: Evidence-based clinical practice guideline for pit-and-fissure sealants

title: Diaper changes and diaper rash
parentQuestions: How often should I change the diaper?
What to do for diaper rash?
Should I use powder?
whatToKnow: Young babies may need 10 to 12 changes a day. Change wet or dirty nappies promptly, clean with water or fragrance free wipes, dry well and allow nappy-free time. Avoid soaps, lotions, talc and antiseptic creams on the rash; a pharmacist can suggest a barrier cream.

whatToDo.action: Clean front to back for girls, no need to pull back a boy's foreskin, and pat dry.
Change more often, leave the nappy off when possible, and use a thin barrier cream.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician if the rash gets worse or spreads, does not clear, causes distress, or comes with a fever.
evidenceNote: NHS guidance.

sources.title: NHS: How to change your baby's nappy
NHS: Nappy rash

title: Dill water, fennel tea and herbal remedies for newborns
parentQuestions: Can I give dill water for gas?
Is fennel tea safe?
whatToKnow: NHS says remedies for colic such as drops, herbal or probiotic supplements are not recommended and have no evidence. WHO says breastfed babies should have no other food or drink, even water, unless medically necessary in the first 6 months.

whatToDo.action: Try holding upright, winding, rocking and white noise.
Check with the pediatrician before giving any liquid or supplement.

seeClinicianIf: Contact a clinician if the baby has vomiting, fever or poor feeding.
evidenceNote: NHS and WHO; dill water specifically is not named in these pages.

sources.title: NHS: Colic
WHO: Infant and young child feeding fact sheet

title: Discipline and consequences
parentQuestions: How do I discipline without yelling?
Are time outs OK?
What consequences work?
whatToKnow: The AAP advises modeling, clear consistent rules, calm consequences with follow-through, lots of praise for good behavior, ignoring minor misbehavior when safe, redirecting, and brief time outs (about one minute per year of age). It says not to spank or hit; research links it to more aggression, and yelling or shaming is also harmful.

whatToDo.action: Catch good behavior; keep rules few and clear.
Make them related, short and consistent.

seeClinicianIf: Extreme or dangerous behavior, or when you feel out of control.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened). The corporal punishment ban is a firm AAP position; the research base we did not re-open.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): What's the best way to discipline my child?

title: Divorce or separation
parentQuestions: How will divorce affect my child?
What do I tell my kids?
whatToKnow: The AAP says children cope better when parents fight less and shield them from conflict, keep both safe parents involved, coordinate rules, preserve routines, and back each other's authority. Many children recover within 2 to 3 years but some have lasting difficulties. Parents' own adjustment matters.

whatToDo.action: Keep routines and avoid conflict in front of children.
Coordinate rules across homes; use mediation if needed.

seeClinicianIf: Ongoing anxiety, school decline, aggression or sadness.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How to support children after parents separate or divorce

title: Drowning: rescue, CPR and why a rescued child still needs a doctor
parentQuestions: What do I do if my child is pulled from the water?
Does my child need a doctor if they seem fine?
What does drowning look like?
whatToKnow: St John Ambulance says drowning may not look like the loud call for help seen on TV, and a person can go unnoticed even with people nearby. Do not put yourself in danger. Once the child is out of the water, check response and breathing, call for emergency help, and start CPR if they are unresponsive and not breathing. AAP says young children can drown in an inch or two of water, quickly and silently, and that being ready to respond with rescue and CPR is one layer of protection.

whatToDo.action: Reach or throw something first, and do not endanger yourself.
Call for help (speaker phone) and start CPR. See the CPR topic.
Put in the recovery position, cover with warm clothes and blankets, and replace wet clothes if possible.
Always get medical advice, even if the child seems well.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number for any child pulled from water who is unresponsive, not breathing, coughing hard, or struggling to breathe. St John Ambulance says people who have been rescued, with or without resuscitation, may need to be observed in hospital, so seek medical advice even if they appear well. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: The rescue steps are St John Ambulance. AAP supports the layered protection approach. See swimming-and-drowning for prevention.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Drowning prevention for curious toddlers
St John Ambulance: Drowning

title: Dyslexia and reading difficulty: early signs
parentQuestions: How do I know if my child has dyslexia?
My child reverses letters, is it dyslexia?
When to test for dyslexia?
whatToKnow: NHS lists signs such as late speech, little interest in language play or the alphabet, reading below age level or slowly and hesitantly, spelling errors, trouble with sequences like days of the week, and frustration or withdrawal. A GP cannot diagnose dyslexia but can check hearing and vision; the school special needs coordinator can arrange screening, and formal assessment is by an educational psychologist or specialist teacher. Some letter reversal is common in early writing.

whatToDo.action: Talk to the teacher or school coordinator first; ask for support while waiting.
Have vision and hearing checked.

seeClinicianIf: Reading well below peers by age 6 to 7, or marked frustration with reading, after a term of support.
evidenceNote: NHS and AAO pages (opened). The International Dyslexia Association page was blocked, so no IDA source is cited.

sources.title: NHS: Dyslexia
American Academy of Ophthalmology: Vision screening for infants and children (2022 joint statement)

title: Ear infections
parentQuestions: How do I know my toddler has an ear infection?
Does my baby need antibiotics?
whatToKnow: Ear infections are common under 3. Most settle within about 3 days, up to a week, with pain relief. NHS says see a GP for under 12 months, pain beyond 3 days, or repeats; antibiotics are not always needed. Pacifier use in the second half of the first year is linked to more infections.

whatToDo.action: Give age-appropriate paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain; keep water out of the ear; do not insert anything.
Seek help the same day for under 12 months.

seeClinicianIf: Under 12 months with ear pain, swelling behind the ear, discharge, new hearing loss, very high fever, or repeated infections.
evidenceNote: NHS opened; AAP watchful waiting protocol not opened.

sources.title: NHS: Ear infections
AAPD: Policy on Pacifiers (2024 revision, Reference Manual 2026)

title: Early academics and prep courses
parentQuestions: Should my 5 year old learn to read before school?
Are preparatory courses necessary?
Is it bad to push academics early?
whatToKnow: The AAP highlights play as central for preschool-age learning and notes that social and emotional skills matter as much as academics for school success. It records that structured, academic activity has crowded out play in many settings. We found no source we opened showing that early drilling gives a lasting advantage.

whatToDo.action: Read together daily, count and talk during daily life, and keep most time for play.
Pick a playful one, limit hours, and watch the child's mood and sleep.

evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance on play and readiness is our evidence; long-term trial data on prep courses was not found or opened.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): The power of play
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Is your preschooler ready for kindergarten?
Elkonin, On the problem of stages in the mental development of the child (1971), Marxists Internet Archive

title: Cavities in baby teeth and night feeding
parentQuestions: Do baby teeth cavities matter?
Can breastfeeding at night cause cavities?
whatToKnow: Decay depends on how often and how long teeth meet sugar, not only how much. Sweet drinks in a bottle, juice and sticky snacks are the main risk; at night give only milk or water. Baby teeth cavities spread and hurt, and baby teeth are not 'going to fall out anyway'.

whatToDo.action: Brush with fluoride toothpaste; no sugary drinks in bottles.
Offer water from a free-flowing cup with meals.
Check hidden sugars in baby snacks and drinks.

seeClinicianIf: Dark spots, chalky white lines at the gumline, swelling, or pain when eating.
evidenceNote: NHS opened; AAPD/ADA caries guidance not opened.

sources.title: NHS: Looking after your baby's teeth

title: Early puberty (precocious puberty)
parentQuestions: My 7 year old has breast buds
Is early puberty dangerous?
whatToKnow: KidsHealth describes early puberty as before about 7 to 8 in girls and before 9 in boys; NHS says puberty before 8 may be early. Signs include breast development, rapid growth, pubic or underarm hair, acne, or enlarged testes. Doctors may use blood tests and bone X-rays. Usually there is no serious cause but check.

whatToDo.action: Write down what you notice and when.
Ask the pediatrician; early evaluation helps.

seeClinicianIf: Any puberty signs before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys.
evidenceNote: KidsHealth (a hospital page) and NHS (opened); wording differs between 7 and 8 for girls.

sources.title: KidsHealth (Lurie Children's): Precocious puberty
NHS: Puberty

title: Electric shock
parentQuestions: My child got an electric shock, what do I do?
Is it safe to touch them?
Should I call an ambulance if they seem fine?
whatToKnow: St John Ambulance says do not touch the person while they are still in contact with the electrical source, because you can be shocked. Turn off the power, or move them away with something dry that does not conduct, then check them and treat injuries such as burns. Shock can cause a burn or cardiac arrest. Wet hands and frayed flexes are common causes.

whatToDo.action: Switch off the electricity if you can. Do not touch the child until contact is broken.
Check response and breathing, start CPR if needed, and cool any burn under running water (see burns topic).
Call for emergency help.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number for any electric shock per St John Ambulance. NHS also lists a burn caused by electricity as an emergency. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen. We did not open a page about chewing on cords, so that detail is not included.
evidenceNote: St John Ambulance for the steps and NHS for the burn rule. Not enough opened sources for prevention.

sources.title: St John Ambulance: Electric shock
NHS: Burns and scalds

title: Play first, study later: Elkonin's leading activity
parentQuestions: Why do Russian kindergartens stress play-based learning before school?
Is role play important before school?
whatToKnow: Elkonin (a Vygotsky student) proposed that role play is the main activity of the preschool period and that it prepares the child for school, where formal learning becomes the main activity. The AAP likewise says play supports planning, self-control, social skills, language and math. The two views agree on the practical point even though Elkonin's scheme is a theory.

whatToDo.action: Protect daily time for pretend play with other children and with you, and let the child lead the story.
Practice school routines in play (a doll goes to school) rather than drilling worksheets.

evidenceNote: Elkonin's stages are a theoretical model. The AAP play page supports the benefit of play, but it is parent guidance, not a trial of Elkonin's claim.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): The power of play
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Emotional development in preschoolers
Elkonin, On the problem of stages in the mental development of the child (1971), Marxists Internet Archive

title: Emotional intelligence and emotion coaching
parentQuestions: How do I teach my child to handle feelings?
My child melts down after school
whatToKnow: The AAP's four building blocks: safe family relationships, open communication, understanding and managing emotions, and social relationships. Emotion coaching means acknowledging and naming feelings, then addressing the need. For stress use regulate, relate, reason, with slow breathing and side-by-side activities.

whatToDo.action: Name the feeling, validate it, then solve it.
Calm yourself first, then comfort, then talk.

seeClinicianIf: Frequent explosive behavior, persistent sadness, or self-harm.
evidenceNote: AAP pages (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Healthy mental and emotional development, 4 key building blocks
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Why kids act out, tips to help your child cope with stress

title: The EPDS: the 10-question mood check after birth
parentQuestions: What is the Edinburgh scale my midwife gave me?
What score on the EPDS is worrying?
Does a high score mean I have postnatal depression?
whatToKnow: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item self-report questionnaire developed in 1987 to screen for postnatal depression in the community. It takes about 5 minutes and has a simple scoring method. It is a screening tool: it flags who should be talked to, and the original validation study compared it with a clinical interview. We could not open a guideline page that states the cutoff scores, so none are given here; the clinician who scores it applies the local cutoff.

whatToDo.when: At the postnatal check or a visit in the first months
whatToDo.action: Ask whether the scale is offered and answer how you have felt over the past week, not how you think you should feel.

whatToDo.when: After a high score or any day you feel unsafe
whatToDo.action: Talk to the clinician the same day; a score starts a conversation and does not give a diagnosis.

seeClinicianIf: Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, or feeling unable to cope: call your local emergency number or go to the ER and use the app's fixed Urgent help screen. Low mood, anxiety or loss of interest lasting more than two weeks: contact your midwife, doctor or pediatrician.
evidenceNote: Source is the original 1987 development paper abstract (Cox, Holden, Sagovsky) via Europe PMC. Cutoffs and fathers' versions were not confirmed from an official body page in this pass; ACOG, CDC and NICE pages could not be opened.

sources.title: Cox et al. 1987: Detection of postnatal depression, development of the 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (Europe PMC)

title: Erikson's industry vs inferiority (school age)
parentQuestions: Why does my 8 year old give up when something is hard?
How do I build confidence at school age?
whatToKnow: Erikson saw the school years as a time when children want to finish real tasks and measure themselves against others; praise builds confidence and repeated failure or ridicule can build a sense of inferiority. The age range given varies (Wikipedia: 7 to 10). AAP self-esteem guidance matches the practical side: success experiences, listening, and unconditional love.

whatToDo.action: Find tasks the child can finish and be proud of (a model, a recipe, a sport, a chore).
Notice giving up, blaming, or pulling back from friends and talk with the teacher.

seeClinicianIf: Falling grades, withdrawal from friends, persistent sadness, or school avoidance deserve a pediatric or school counselor visit.
evidenceNote: Theory with limited empirical testing for these ages (Wikipedia). AAP self-esteem signs page is parent guidance.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Signs of low self-esteem in children and teens

title: Erikson's initiative vs guilt (about 3 to 6)
parentQuestions: My preschooler is bossy and wants to do everything, is that normal?
Will criticism make my child feel guilty?
whatToKnow: Erikson described preschoolers as testing planning and starting their own activities; if efforts are mocked or punished harshly they may feel guilt. His stage ages vary by source (Wikipedia lists 3 to 6). The practical message, that children this age need room to try things and gentle correction, fits AAP guidance on offering simple choices and giving responsibilities.

whatToDo.action: Offer two or three real choices, give small jobs, and praise effort and the attempt.
Correct the behavior, not the child, and help them redo it.

evidenceNote: Erikson's stages are a theory; Wikipedia notes a lack of evidence for the proposed stages and ages. CDC parenting tips support the practical advice only loosely.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Emotional development in preschoolers
CDC: Positive parenting tips, preschoolers 3 to 5 years

title: Erikson's stages: trust, autonomy, initiative, industry
parentQuestions: What does 'trust vs mistrust' mean for my baby?
Is saying no to everything part of autonomy?
How do I build my 7-year-old's confidence at school?
Стадии развития по Эриксону: что важно в каждом возрасте?
whatToKnow: Erik Erikson described eight life stages; four cover childhood: trust vs mistrust (birth to about 18 months), autonomy vs shame and doubt (to about 3), initiative vs guilt (3 to 5) and industry vs inferiority (5 to 12). Each is a theme, not a test a child passes or fails. Critics point out vague mechanisms, a Western and middle-class sample, and that children vary in timing. The practical themes (reliable care, room for 'I do it myself', encouragement of ideas, credit for effort) are consistent with other research on warm, supportive parenting.

whatToDo.action: Respond to cries and needs fairly consistently; predictable routines matter more than perfect responses.
Offer two acceptable choices (which shirt, which cup), allow extra time for 'I do it', keep limits clear and calm.
Welcome questions and pretend play, let the child plan small things (what we build, what we draw), avoid mocking big ideas.
Give real jobs (set the table, pack the bag), praise effort and strategy, break hard tasks into steps, notice comparison with peers and talk about it.

evidenceNote: Erikson's stages are a descriptive framework, not tested as a causal model. Age bands vary by child and culture.

sources.title: Top Tips for Surviving Tantrums (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
Erik Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development (Simply Psychology)

title: Erythromycin eye ointment for newborns
parentQuestions: Why do they put ointment in my baby's eyes?
Can we refuse it?
whatToKnow: Erythromycin 0.5% ointment is used to prevent eye infection from gonorrhea and, less reliably, chlamydia picked up during birth. The 2025 AAO and AAPOS statement notes that US mandates are being reassessed and that it is most useful where gonorrhea is common and prenatal screening cannot be assured. It does not treat an infection already present.

whatToDo.action: Make sure you had the routine infection tests; treated infections lower the risk for the baby.
Ask whether it is given and whether it can wait until after the first hour of skin-to-skin.

seeClinicianIf: Report eye redness, swelling or discharge in the first weeks to the pediatrician the same day.
evidenceNote: USPSTF and CDC recommend it; AAP has said universal mandates should be re-evaluated. Policy varies by country.

sources.title: AAO and AAPOS: Use of Erythromycin in the Prevention of Ophthalmia Neonatorum (2025)

title: Executive function: working memory, self-control, flexibility
parentQuestions: Why does my 4-year-old have such a hard time waiting and following instructions?
How can I help my child's self-control?
Is my preschooler ready for school?
Что такое исполнительные функции у детей?
whatToKnow: Executive function is the set of skills that help us focus, hold information in mind, filter distractions and switch tasks (working memory, inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility). Harvard's Center on the Developing Child says children are not born with these skills but with the potential to build them through interaction and practice, and that growth is fast between ages 3 and 5, so adults should adjust support and then reduce it. A 2015 review argues self-regulation is a unifying framework for school readiness. Evidence for specific training games is weaker than for supportive relationships and play.

whatToDo.action: Use simple routines, songs and games with rules (peekaboo, 'stop and go' with music).
Do pretend play with roles and rules, make a play plan before playing, tell stories together, play sorting games and change the rule, Simon Says, Freeze Dance.
Try card and board games with turns, short memory games and a visual routine chart; reduce your reminders as the child manages.
Help the child plan homework steps, use checklists and review how it went.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent, severe difficulty with attention, impulse control or following simple instructions across settings, or loss of skills; ask the pediatrician, who can assess instead of the app or a checklist.
evidenceNote: Executive function is an established research field. Skills grow with age and experience, but the benefits of 'brain training' games beyond the trained task are debated, so the app promotes play and routines rather than apps.

title: Exercise in pregnancy
parentQuestions: Is exercise safe while pregnant?
How much exercise?
What should I avoid?
whatToKnow: The NHS says exercise is safe and recommends about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle strengthening twice. The Canadian guideline found moderate benefit and no identified harms for active healthy women. The NHS advises not to scuba dive and not to exercise on an empty stomach. If you are new to exercise, start gently.

whatToDo.action: Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity, e.g. walking or swimming.
Stop if you feel dizzy, short of breath or have pain or bleeding.

seeClinicianIf: Ask before exercising if you have bleeding, a low placenta, high blood pressure or a history of preterm birth.
evidenceNote: NHS and Canadian guideline agree; individual limits depend on conditions.

title: Extracurriculars and overscheduling
parentQuestions: How many clubs are too many?
Does my child need so many activities?
whatToKnow: The AAP says play supports development and notes time for free play has declined with tightly structured schedules. It encourages unstructured time and some boredom. We did not open a specific cutoff. Watch your child's mood, sleep and free time.

whatToDo.action: Keep daily time for free play and family.
Let the child help choose; drop what they dread.

seeClinicianIf: Anxiety, fatigue, sleep loss or school decline.

title: Eye injuries in children
parentQuestions: Something got in my child's eye, what do I do?
Chemical splash in the eye?
Do I remove an object stuck in the eye?
whatToKnow: For a chemical splash, NHS and St John Ambulance say to rinse the eye with lots of clean, not hot, water for at least 20 minutes and take the container with you. Do not rub the eye. Do not remove an object that has pierced or is stuck in the eye: cover the eye and get help. NHS says to ask for medical advice for a child with an eye injury if you are worried.

whatToDo.action: Hold the eye open and run gentle water over it for at least 20 minutes, keep splash away from the other eye, bring the container.
Do not rub. Rinse with clean water. Remove contact lenses if the child can.
Do not touch it. Cover the eye lightly and go for emergency care.

seeClinicianIf: Go to the ER or call your local emergency number for a strong chemical, a sharp object piercing the eye, a high speed impact, any change in vision, severe pain, light sensitivity with headache, nausea or vomiting, an eye that cannot move or open, or blood or pus (NHS). Ask for urgent advice if the injury does not improve in 24 hours. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS and St John Ambulance agree.

title: Falling asleep while feeding: the AAP safer plan
parentQuestions: What if I fall asleep while breastfeeding my baby?
Is it safer to feed in bed or on the sofa at night?
What should I do if I might fall asleep with my baby?
whatToKnow: AAP advises against bed-sharing in all circumstances and says the risk of sleep-related infant death is up to 67 times higher when a baby sleeps with someone on a couch, soft armchair or cushion. It adds that bed-sharing is especially risky after alcohol, marijuana or sedating medicine, if anyone smokes or vapes, or if baby is under 4 months, small or preterm. AAP's practical point is to plan for dozing off before it happens.

whatToDo.action: If you might doze, do not feed on a sofa or armchair, clear away bedding and pillows, and have someone sit with you. Set repeating phone alarms and keep your mind busy with a low-key podcast or article; eat a light snack and drink water.
Return baby to their own sleep space before you fall asleep. If you might sleep in bed, remove pillows, blankets and anything that could cover baby's face, head or neck or cause overheating.
Move baby to a crib or bassinet, on the back, as soon as you wake.
Back to sleep on a firm flat surface with a fitted sheet only, room-share for at least 6 months, and dress baby in about one layer more than you wear.

seeClinicianIf: Ask your pediatrician or midwife for help with night feeding plans if you are exhausted, or are on medicines or substances that make you hard to wake.
evidenceNote: AAP policy explainers; NHS gives similar advice against sofas and armchairs and lists conditions where bed sharing is more risky. AAP gives a harm-reduction plan but still recommends not bed-sharing.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe, AAP Policy Explained
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Safe Sleep Tips for Sleep-Deprived New Parents

title: Falls from furniture, stairs and playgrounds
parentQuestions: My baby rolled off the bed, what now?
My child fell down the stairs, do we go to the ER?
What if my child fell from a height and says their neck hurts?
whatToKnow: Most falls only cause bruises, but a fall can injure the head, neck and bones. NHS lists a fall from more than 1 metre or 5 stairs among the reasons to call emergency services after a head injury. St John Ambulance describes possible spinal injury after a fall from a height and says not to move the person or ask them to move unless in immediate danger.

whatToDo.action: Check the child is alert and responding, look for bleeding, swelling, a limb at an odd angle, or head or neck pain.

whatToDo.when: If a neck or back injury is possible
whatToDo.action: Do not move the child, support the head and neck in line and call for help.
Cold compress for swelling, watch for 24 hours, and use the head bump and broken bone topics for the warning signs.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number if the child has a head injury with the warning signs, cannot move limbs, has weakness, numbness or tingling, neck or back pain, trouble breathing, loss of bladder or bowel control, or fell from more than 1 metre or 5 stairs (NHS). Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS gives the height and stairs threshold for head injury. St John Ambulance lists spinal signs. No opened page gave playground or furniture specific prevention advice, so none is written here.

title: Family rituals and routines
parentQuestions: How to build family traditions?
Does family dinner matter?
whatToKnow: The AAP's building blocks say predictable routines like family meals, bedtime rituals, and homework and chore schedules help children feel secure. Eat meals together and model healthy foods (CDC).

whatToDo.action: Shared meals and a bedtime routine.
One family activity.

evidenceNote: AAP and CDC (opened).

title: Fears and anxiety
parentQuestions: My child is afraid of everything
How do I know if worry is anxiety?
whatToKnow: NHS says anxiety shows as irritability, clinginess, sleep trouble, bedwetting in younger children, and avoidance or concentration problems in older ones. Listen, problem-solve, keep routines, teach slow breathing, use a worry box, and do not push into a stressful situation before talking. See a GP if severe, long lasting or affecting daily life.

whatToDo.action: Name the worry, make a small plan, practice breathing.
Tell the teacher if it affects school.

seeClinicianIf: Severe or prolonged worry affecting school, sleep or friendships.
evidenceNote: NHS (opened).

title: Febrile seizures
parentQuestions: My child had a febrile seizure, will it happen again?
Does it cause brain damage?
whatToKnow: Febrile seizures usually occur between 6 months and 5 years with a peak near 18 months; simple ones last under 15 minutes. Recurrence in the first two years is roughly 15 to 70 percent; epilepsy risk after a simple one is about 2 percent. They do not usually affect intellect, and giving fever medicine does not prevent recurrence.

whatToDo.action: Lay the child on their side, time it, do not put anything in the mouth, stay beside them.
See a clinician the same day for a first seizure.

seeClinicianIf: Seizure over 5 minutes, repeated seizures, one-sided or after head injury, child not waking, or any first seizure: call emergency services.
evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance: affects 3 to 4 in 100 children between 6 months and 5 years, usually harmless; call emergency services if a seizure lasts over 5 minutes.

sources.title: Febrile Seizures in Children (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
AAFP American Family Physician: Febrile Seizures, Risks, Evaluation, and Prognosis (2012)

title: Feed on demand or on a schedule?
parentQuestions: Should I feed every 3 hours?
Will feeding on demand spoil the baby?
What about a regimen?
whatToKnow: WHO and NHS recommend responsive, baby led feeding for breastfed babies, day and night, and say you cannot spoil a baby by feeding when hungry or needing comfort. Strict clock schedules are not part of current guidance for newborns.

whatToDo.action: Feed when the baby shows cues.
A pattern develops by itself; discuss routines with a health visitor.

seeClinicianIf: Check with a clinician if the baby is not gaining weight or rarely wakes to feed.
evidenceNote: WHO and NHS; schedule evidence in newborns is limited.

sources.title: WHO: Infant and young child feeding fact sheet
NHS: Your breastfeeding questions answered

title: Fever medicine: where to find the right amount
parentQuestions: How much paracetamol or ibuprofen can I give?
Can I give both?
Is it safe to give aspirin?
whatToKnow: The American Academy of Pediatrics says to use your child's weight to choose the amount of acetaminophen (paracetamol) or ibuprofen, and the age if the weight is unknown, and to confirm with your doctor. It warns that giving the wrong amount is one of the biggest mistakes parents make. This topic gives no numbers: use the official dosing tables.

whatToDo.action: Weigh your child recently, open the AAP acetaminophen or ibuprofen table, and measure with an oral syringe.
Pick a single ingredient product. AAP says it is best not to give multi-ingredient medicines under 6 years.

NHS says no aspirin under 16, no paracetamol under 2 months, and no ibuprofen under 3 months, under 5 kg, with chickenpox, when dehydrated, or with asthma unless a doctor advises. AAP says ibuprofen should not be used under 6 months unless a doctor says so. The pages differ, so ask your own doctor.
NHS says do not alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor or nurse tells you to.

seeClinicianIf: A fever in the first 12 weeks needs medical attention at once (AAP). Ask the doctor or pharmacist before giving any medicine to a baby under 2 years. Call your local emergency number or go to the ER if a child has a stiff neck, non-fading rash, breathing difficulty or is hard to wake.
evidenceNote: AAP tables and NHS fever advice differ on the youngest ages for ibuprofen. We state both and give no numbers.

HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Ibuprofen dosing table for fever and pain

title: Fever: red flags by age and when to call
parentQuestions: At what temperature should I call?
What fever signs are an emergency?
My baby has a fever, what age matters?
whatToKnow: NHS says a high temperature is 38C or more and usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days. The age rules in NHS advice: call for urgent help if the child is under 3 months with 38C or more, or 3 to 6 months with 39C or more, or has a fever for 5 days or more. A fever with a rash, poor feeding or dehydration also needs a call. NHS says do not sponge or undress a child to cool them.

whatToDo.action: Take the temperature (see taking-a-baby-temperature) and note the time, other symptoms, and how much your child drinks.
Fluids, light clothing, rest, medicine only if distressed (see fever-medicine-by-weight).
Check for signs of dehydration and for the glass test rash.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says call your local emergency number (911 in the US) or go to the ER for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, bothered by light, a first fit, unusually cold hands and feet, blue, grey or blotchy skin, drowsy and hard to wake, extreme agitation or confusion, breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, or not responding as usual. Open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: This topic only adds a red-flag angle. Detailed toddler fever advice and the under 3 months page already exist in the atlas.

sources.title: NHS: High temperature (fever) in children
NHS: Sepsis
NHS: Meningitis symptoms

title: Fever in babies and toddlers
parentQuestions: When should I worry about a fever?
Should I give medicine for fever?
whatToKnow: Fever is a symptom, most often from a viral infection. Under 3 months any fever is an emergency. Fever medicines treat comfort, not seizure risk. Warm room, light clothes and fluids; do not overdress a feverish child.

whatToDo.action: Dress lightly, offer fluids, give weight-based paracetamol or ibuprofen only if uncomfortable.
Note temperature, how the child drinks, plays and wets nappies.

seeClinicianIf: Under 3 months with 38C or more; fever over 5 days; stiff neck, rash that does not fade under a glass, trouble breathing, blue lips, very sleepy or inconsolable, dehydration, or a seizure.
evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance: call right away at 38.0 C or higher under 3 months, fever over 24 hours under age 2 or over 3 days from age 2, or a child who looks very ill; sponging and ice packs are no longer advised.

sources.title: Fever Without Fear: Information for Parents (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
AAFP American Family Physician: Febrile Seizures, Risks, Evaluation, and Prognosis (2012)

title: Fever in a baby under 3 months: same day care
parentQuestions: My newborn feels warm, is it a fever?
What temperature is dangerous?
Can I give paracetamol first?
whatToKnow: A temperature of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher in a baby under 3 months needs urgent medical assessment, not waiting. Both NHS and AAP give this threshold. Do not wait for other symptoms; young babies can be seriously ill with few signs.

whatToDo.when: As soon as you measure 38 C or higher
whatToDo.action: Call the pediatrician or emergency service the same day, or go to emergency care.
Do not wait to see whether it passes.

seeClinicianIf: This whole topic is the red flag: any temperature of 38 C or higher in a baby under 3 months, or a low temperature under 36 C, should be assessed immediately.
evidenceNote: NHS and AAP agree on the threshold. Method differs: NHS recommends the armpit for under 5s, while US practice often uses rectal; ask your clinician which they want.

title: First dental visit by age 1
parentQuestions: When is the first dentist visit?
Does a baby need a dentist?
whatToKnow: AAPD and ADA advise a dental home by the first birthday or within 6 months of the first tooth. The visit checks teeth, discusses feeding, fluoride and habits, and gets the child used to the dentist. The AAPD pacifier policy I opened also encourages a dental home by 12 months.

whatToDo.action: Book a first dental visit.
Ask the dentist about fluoride varnish and bite development.

seeClinicianIf: Brown or white lines on upper front teeth, pain, swelling, or a knocked tooth: see a dentist promptly.
evidenceNote: The 12 month recommendation comes from AAPD (opened, in its pacifier policy) and ADA/AAPD summaries seen in search.

title: First feeding and starting breastfeeding
parentQuestions: When should the first feed be?
Should I give water or formula in the hospital?
How do I know the baby is feeding enough?
whatToKnow: WHO and UNICEF advise starting breastfeeding within the first hour, feeding only breast milk for six months and not giving water or other fluids unless there is a medical reason. Newborns usually feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. The AAP suggests a first checkup within 48 hours of discharge to confirm feeding is going well.

whatToDo.action: Offer the breast during skin-to-skin and let the baby find it.
Count feeds and wet and dirty nappies; ask for a lactation check before leaving.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the same day if the baby feeds fewer than 8 times in 24 hours, is hard to wake for feeds, has very few wet nappies or looks yellow.
evidenceNote: WHO and AAP agree on breastfeeding start; individual feeding choices (formula, mixed) are the parent's decision and should be supported.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: How to Tell if Your Breastfed Baby is Getting Enough Milk
WHO: Infant and young child feeding fact sheet

title: First pediatrician visit and what is checked
parentQuestions: When is the first checkup?
What should I bring?
What should I ask?
whatToKnow: The AAP suggests the first visit at 3 to 5 days, and no more than 48 hours after discharge. The pediatrician weighs and measures the baby, examines them, reviews hearing and blood screening results, and may give a hepatitis B dose if not given in hospital. They also ask about feeding, sleep and how the parents are coping.

whatToDo.action: Bring hospital papers and discharge weight; write your questions.
Ask about nappy counts, cord and circumcision healing, fever plan.

seeClinicianIf: Call before the visit for worries listed under jaundice, feeding or breathing; do not wait.
evidenceNote: AAP visit schedule is a guideline; other countries use home visits by midwives or nurses.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: 1st Week Checkup Checklist, 3 to 5 days old

title: When to give a first phone
parentQuestions: At what age should my child get a phone?
Is 8 too young for a phone?
whatToKnow: The AAP says to delay personal tablets and think carefully before a first phone, considering maturity and how the child handles social situations. It gives no single age. Keep phones out of bedrooms and meals and use parental controls.

whatToDo.action: Ask: can they follow rules, handle conflict, and tell me when something is wrong?
Start with limited functions and review together.

seeClinicianIf: Secrecy, mood change, sleep loss or contact with strangers.
evidenceNote: The AAP says no fixed age; surveys and some authors push for later ages. We did not open those.

title: The 12-week and 20-week ultrasound scans
parentQuestions: What is the nuchal translucency scan?
What does the anatomy scan check?
Can the scan miss something?
whatToKnow: In the NHS programme the 12-week scan and the combined test (usually 11 to 14 weeks) screen for Down, Edwards and Patau syndromes using the scan and blood; a quadruple blood test at about 14 to 20 weeks is the fallback if the combined test is not possible. The 20-week anomaly scan, usually done at 18 to 21 weeks, looks for 11 specific conditions and checks growth, placenta and blood flow. The NHS notes some conditions are seen more clearly than others and the scan may not find everything. WHO recommends at least one scan before 24 weeks.

whatToDo.action: Book the 12-week scan and the combined test if you want screening.
Book the anatomy scan; decide in advance whether you want to know the baby's sex.

seeClinicianIf: Ask for a clear explanation if a scan shows anything unexpected, and for a referral to a fetal medicine specialist if suggested.
evidenceNote: NHS and WHO are official; scans are screening, not guarantees.

title: Fish in pregnancy: how much and which kinds
parentQuestions: Can I eat fish when pregnant?
Which fish contain mercury?
Is sushi safe?
whatToKnow: The FDA advises 2 to 3 servings a week of lower-mercury 'best choices' fish in pregnancy (a serving is 4 ounces) and says to avoid shark, swordfish, king mackerel, Gulf tilefish, bigeye tuna, marlin and orange roughy. The NHS says no more than 2 portions of oily fish a week and limits tuna to 4 cans or 2 steaks. The NHS lists sushi made with cooked fish as safe.

whatToDo.action: Choose fish such as salmon, sardines or cod in measured portions.
Cook fish thoroughly and avoid the high-mercury list.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a clinician if you ate a lot of a high-mercury fish.
evidenceNote: FDA and NHS agree on limits, with different numbers.

title: Flat head (positional plagiocephaly) versus craniosynostosis
parentQuestions: My baby's head is flat on one side
Does it need a helmet?
How do I tell craniosynostosis?
whatToKnow: Positional plagiocephaly is a flattening of the soft skull from lying in one position. GOSH describes it as cosmetic, not affecting brain development, and often improving by about a year. Prevention is more tummy time while awake, varying head position and limiting time in car seats and buggies. Craniosynostosis is a rarer early fusion of skull plates that typically needs surgery.

whatToDo.action: Tummy time awake, vary which way the baby faces in the cot.
Show it to the pediatrician at the next visit.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the clinician if the head shape worries you or looks unusual, or if the baby turns the head more easily to one side; a clinician may arrange scans to rule out other problems.
evidenceNote: GOSH. A clinician decides on any scans.

sources.title: Great Ormond Street Hospital: Positional plagiocephaly
NHS Best Start in Life: Baby moves

title: Flu in children
parentQuestions: Is it a cold or the flu?
Should my child get the flu vaccine?
When is flu serious in a child?
whatToKnow: NHS says flu symptoms come on quickly (a sudden high temperature, aches, tiredness, dry cough), while colds appear gradually and mainly affect the nose and throat. Children may also have ear pain, sore eyes, swollen glands and seem less active. CDC says children under 5, especially under 2, and those with conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease are at higher risk, and recommends a yearly flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older. Prescription antivirals can be used in children.

whatToDo.action: Rest, fluids, and paracetamol or ibuprofen if distressed (see fever-medicine-by-weight).
Ask about the yearly vaccine. CDC says some children aged 6 months to 8 years need two doses at least 4 weeks apart.
Keep home with a high temperature and wash hands.

seeClinicianIf: CDC lists complications such as pneumonia and dehydration. Call the doctor early for a child at higher risk or one who is not drinking or is getting worse. Call your local emergency number or go to the ER for breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, a stiff neck, or a child who is hard to wake. Open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: CDC and NHS pages opened. The CDC page we read does not list emergency warning signs, so the emergency lines come from NHS fever and sepsis pages.

title: Flu vaccine in pregnancy
parentQuestions: Is the flu shot safe while pregnant?
When should I get it?
What about COVID vaccine?
whatToKnow: The NHS says pregnant women are eligible for the flu vaccine at any stage of pregnancy. The NHS lists it among the routine pregnancy vaccines with whooping cough and RSV. The pages I opened do not cover COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy, so ask your clinic about the current local recommendation.

whatToDo.action: Get the flu vaccine before the season peaks, in any trimester.
Ask your clinician about the current local recommendation.

seeClinicianIf: Seek care for fever, shortness of breath or flu symptoms in pregnancy rather than waiting.

title: Tooth brushing and fluoride toothpaste
parentQuestions: When should I start brushing?
How much toothpaste for a toddler?
Is fluoride safe for babies?
How much toothpaste should I use?
Should I supervise brushing?
whatToKnow: Brush from the first tooth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste: a smear (rice grain) under 3 years, a pea-sized amount from 3 to 6. Spit but do not rinse, so fluoride stays on the teeth. Children need help brushing until about age 7. ADA and AAPD recommend the same smear amount from the first tooth; I opened only the NHS page, not ADA text.

whatToDo.action: Brush morning and just before bed with a smear of fluoride toothpaste.
Move to a pea-sized amount; supervise spitting.
Parent finishes the brushing.
Brush morning and night; you finish until they can do it well.
Dentist check.

seeClinicianIf: White or brown spots on teeth, visible holes, or a child who refuses brushing for weeks. Raise with the dentist.
evidenceNote: NHS opened for amounts. ADA/AAPD wording (smear from first tooth) was seen only in search summaries, so cite NHS until ADA is opened.

title: Folic acid before you conceive
parentQuestions: Do I need folic acid before I am pregnant?
How much folic acid and for how long?
Who needs the higher dose?
whatToKnow: Folic acid lowers the chance of neural tube defects, serious conditions of the brain and spine that form in the first weeks, often before a pregnancy is known. CDC advises 400 micrograms daily for anyone who could become pregnant, starting at least a month before trying. The NHS advises starting about three months before and continuing to week 12. A higher 5 mg prescription dose is used for some groups, such as a previous neural tube defect, diabetes, certain blood conditions, or some epilepsy or HIV medicines.

whatToDo.action: Start 400 micrograms a day of folic acid, ideally 1 to 3 months before conception.

whatToDo.when: If you have diabetes, epilepsy, a blood condition or a past neural tube defect
whatToDo.action: Ask the doctor about the 5 mg dose before you stop contraception.
Keep taking it; the NHS also advises vitamin D from October to March and avoiding vitamin A supplements.

seeClinicianIf: Ask your doctor before stopping or changing any regular medicine, and if you may need the 5 mg dose.
evidenceNote: CDC and the NHS agree on 400 micrograms and differ slightly on how early to start (1 month versus about 3 months). Strong evidence for neural tube defect prevention.

sources.title: About Folic Acid (CDC)
Pregnancy vitamins and supplements (NHS)

title: Introducing allergenic foods
parentQuestions: When can my baby have peanut butter?
Should I avoid egg?
whatToKnow: Delaying egg and peanut does not prevent allergy; early introduction of peanut may prevent it in high-risk infants (LEAP trial). Introduce after a few low-risk foods, one at a time, in safe forms like thinned peanut butter, never whole nuts. Babies with severe eczema or egg allergy need a clinician first.

whatToDo.action: Offer small tastes of cooked egg and peanut butter in safe forms.
Talk to the pediatrician or allergist first.

seeClinicianIf: Hives, vomiting, swelling, wheeze or pale floppy child soon after a food: emergency.
evidenceNote: AAP HealthyChildren opened.

sources.title: AAP HealthyChildren: When to introduce egg, peanut butter and other allergens

title: Food allergy: signs and what to do
parentQuestions: How do I know if my baby is allergic?
whatToKnow: Immediate reactions (within minutes to 2 hours) include hives, swelling, vomiting, wheeze and floppiness. These can be emergencies. Many milk and egg allergies are outgrown; peanut allergy often persists.

whatToDo.action: Stop the food, note what was eaten, and contact the pediatrician.
Call emergency services.

seeClinicianIf: Any breathing difficulty, swelling of lips or tongue, repeated vomiting after food, or blood in stools.
evidenceNote: Signs listed in AAP page I opened (rash, diarrhea, vomiting).

sources.title: AAP HealthyChildren: When to introduce egg, peanut butter and other allergens

title: Food safety: listeria, toxoplasma, eggs and the 'eating for two' idea
parentQuestions: What foods should I avoid?
Which cheese is safe?
Do I really eat for two?
whatToKnow: CDC advises avoiding raw milk products, deli meats unless reheated, refrigerated pâté, raw sprouts and some soft cheeses unless heated to steaming. For toxoplasma, cook meat thoroughly, wash produce and have someone else change cat litter or use gloves. The NHS lists foods to avoid and limits. One NHS trust page says pregnancy needs only about 200 extra calories a day, and only in the last three months, so 'eating for two' is a myth.

whatToDo.action: Choose pasteurised dairy and cook meat through.
Wear gloves or avoid cat litter, and wash hands.

seeClinicianIf: Call a clinician for fever, chills or flu-like illness after risky food, as listeria can be serious.
evidenceNote: Official lists are consistent. The calorie figure comes from an NHS trust leaflet, not national policy.
