title: Formula feeding: safe preparation
parentQuestions: How do I make formula safely?
Do I need to boil water?
How much formula?
whatToKnow: NHS says to boil fresh tap water, let it cool for no more than 30 minutes so it stays at least 70 C, put the water in the bottle first, then add the powder per the label. Wash hands, clean surfaces, and sterilise bottles. Newborns take small amounts and feed little and often.

whatToDo.action: Follow the 70 C rule and measure carefully.
Wash and sterilise equipment.

seeClinicianIf: Contact the clinician for refusal of feeds, vomiting, blood in stool, or signs of dehydration.
evidenceNote: NHS; local water safety may differ, so follow the can and local advice.

title: Foster care: a child's health in the first months
parentQuestions: What health checks does a foster child need?
Can a foster child get early intervention?
How do I help a child who has been through trauma?
whatToKnow: AAP says up to 200,000 US babies and children enter foster care each year, more than half under 5. Ages 0 to 5 are key for brain development, and AAP says children in foster care are at especially high risk of developmental delays, yet only 10 to 26 percent of those who need services get them. Foster parents can help by arranging well-child visits, vaccines and follow-up, making sure the pediatrician has the health history, and learning about trauma. AAP says children in foster care should automatically qualify for early intervention services.

whatToDo.action: Take the child to a pediatrician soon, share the health history you have, and ask about developmental screening.
Ask the pediatrician about early intervention and trauma-informed care.
Keep routines predictable and safe; AAP names stable relationships and predictable routines as what young brains need.

seeClinicianIf: Raise delays, behaviour changes, sleep or feeding problems, or signs of distress with the pediatrician, who can screen for developmental issues, trauma exposure and prenatal risks.

title: Freud's anal stage (1 to 3 years) and toilet learning
parentQuestions: Will early potty training harm my child?
whatToKnow: Freud said toilet training around age 2 sets traits like orderliness or messiness. Current science finds the stages are not fixed and do not reliably determine adult personality. What matters in practice: readiness, no shaming, and treating constipation.

whatToDo.action: Follow readiness and keep a positive tone; never punish accidents.

evidenceNote: Wikipedia overview opened.

title: Freud's latency stage (6 to puberty)
parentQuestions: Do children go through a quiet sexuality phase at school age?
What is the latency period?
whatToKnow: Freud proposed that from about 6 until puberty sexual drives lie dormant and energy goes into school, friends and hobbies. Modern evidence does not support a dormant phase: children keep curiosity about bodies and relationships, and puberty can begin as early as 8 in girls. School-age children really do shift focus to skills, rules and same-sex friendships.

whatToDo.action: Keep answering questions on bodies, babies and relationships honestly at the child's level; do not assume the topic has gone away.
Start explaining puberty before it begins.

evidenceNote: Theory only; the Wikipedia summary we opened describes the claim and notes the wider criticism. The puberty age range comes from NHS.

title: Freud's oral stage (0 to 1 year)
parentQuestions: What is the oral stage?
whatToKnow: Freud claimed the mouth is the main source of pleasure in the first year and that weaning shapes personality. It is widely considered unscientific, but it is true that feeding is a central experience; modern advice focuses on responsive feeding and not forcing weaning.

whatToDo.action: Feed responsively; wean gradually without shame.

evidenceNote: APA defines the oral stage as Freud's first psychosexual phase, about the first year, with sucking and biting sub-phases and fixation thought to shape personality. The entry describes the theory only; its scientific status was not assessed in the page opened.

title: Freud's phallic stage and the Oedipus complex
parentQuestions: Is my 4 year old in love with me? Is that the Oedipus complex?
Do I need to worry that my son wants to marry me?
What does Freud say about ages 3 to 6?
whatToKnow: Freud placed a phallic stage at about 3 to 6, with the Oedipus complex as the boy's rivalry with his father for his mother, resolved by identifying with the father. Modern science regards the theory as untestable and poorly supported; studies of children's attitudes did not show the shifts it predicts, and anthropologists such as Malinowski disputed that it is universal. What children of this age actually show is real curiosity about bodies and families, strong attachment, and the wish to 'marry' a parent as a way of saying they love them.

whatToDo.action: Answer 'I'll marry you' warmly and plainly: you love them, you are married to the other parent, and they will have their own life later.
Keep answers short and calm; no teasing or shaming.

seeClinicianIf: Sexualized behavior beyond curiosity (imitating adult sexual acts, persistent explicit talk) is a reason to talk with the pediatrician, because it can have causes such as exposure to adult content.
evidenceNote: Freud's stages are historical psychoanalytic theory. Wikipedia's summaries (opened) record criticism: weak empirical support, Malinowski, and testability problems. Wikipedia is a secondary source; no primary study was opened.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Talking to your young child about sex

title: Freud's oral, anal and phallic stages: what to make of them
parentQuestions: Is my child stuck in the oral stage because of the pacifier?
Does early or strict potty training cause an anal personality?
My 4-year-old touches her genitals, is that normal?
Что такое оральная и анальная стадии по Фрейду и это правда?
whatToKnow: Freud proposed that children pass through oral (birth to about 1 to 1.5 years), anal (1 to 3), phallic (3 to 6), latency (6 to puberty) and genital stages, and that too little or too much satisfaction at a stage shapes adult personality. It is a historical theory built on case studies and Freud's own self-analysis, and critics note it lacks systematic, testable evidence. Parents should not read a child's thumb sucking or potty-training pace as a sign of a personality flaw. What is useful today is the plain pediatric knowledge about the same ages: sucking is a normal need, toilet training works best when the child shows readiness, and touching genitals at ages 3 to 6 is common curiosity.

whatToDo.action: Treat sucking (breast, bottle, pacifier, fingers) as normal self-soothing; talk to the pediatrician about pacifier weaning timing rather than worrying about 'fixation'.

Wait for readiness signs before toilet training: dry for about two hours or after naps, shows cues before peeing or pooping, follows simple instructions, can walk to the bathroom and help undress, asks for the potty or underwear. No shaming for accidents.
If your child touches or looks at genitals, stay calm, redirect, and say that touching private parts is for a private place. Teach correct names for body parts and that bodies are private.
Keep answering questions about bodies and babies briefly and honestly; do not wait for a 'talk'.

seeClinicianIf: Sexual behavior that disrupts daily activities, takes over other play and cannot be redirected, causes pain or injury, involves force or aggression, imitates adult sexual acts, or involves a much older child. Also raise any concern about toilet training that is painful or involves withholding stool.
evidenceNote: Psychosexual stages are a historical psychoanalytic framework with no solid experimental support and several recognised criticisms. The pediatric facts about the same ages come from AAP guidance and are separate from the theory.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
Sexual Behaviors in Young Children: What's Normal, What's Not? (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
Psychosexual Stages of Development (Simply Psychology)

Cross-gender play is common and does not necessarily predict identity. By about 6 most children mostly play with same-sex peers. Offer diverse toys and avoid pressuring conformity.

Watch for teasing.

Ask the pediatrician about local support.
Use correct simple words; follow the child's interests without labels.

title: Genetic carrier screening before or early in pregnancy
parentQuestions: Should we be tested for genetic conditions before having a baby?
What is carrier screening?
Do both partners need to be tested?
whatToKnow: Carrier screening checks whether a parent carries a gene for a recessive or X-linked condition that could affect a child, even when the parent is healthy. Panels range from a few conditions to hundreds, and professional genetics bodies describe a tiered approach rather than one right panel. The NHS offers sickle cell and thalassaemia screening early in pregnancy, usually before 10 weeks. It is your choice whether to test, and results help you discuss options with a clinician.

whatToDo.when: Before conception or at the first visit
whatToDo.action: Ask whether your family background or local programme suggests a carrier panel.
If sickle cell and thalassaemia screening is offered, do it early.
Ask for genetic counselling before deciding anything.

seeClinicianIf: Raise it early if you or your partner have a family history of an inherited condition, a relative with a genetic disease, or parents who are blood relatives.
evidenceNote: The NHS programme is official but covers specific conditions; broad panels are recommended by genetics societies as an option, not a universal duty. Panel choice is debated.

title: Gentle or respectful parenting: what it is and what the research says
parentQuestions: Is gentle parenting the same as not setting limits?
Does gentle parenting actually work, or does it raise spoiled kids?
I am exhausted trying to stay calm all the time, am I doing it wrong?
Что такое мягкое воспитание и не избалуется ли ребёнок без наказаний?
whatToKnow: Gentle or respectful parenting is a popular label, not a tested program. It usually means staying calm, naming feelings, avoiding punishment and shaming, and still holding limits. That core overlaps heavily with what researchers call authoritative parenting (warm and firm), which has the best-supported track record. Warmth without limits is the permissive style, which is linked to somewhat more behavior problems, so the limits are the part that matters.

whatToDo.action: Hold the limit and be kind about it: 'I won't let you hit. You can hit the pillow.' Move the child or the object rather than arguing.
Name the feeling, keep the boundary ('You are angry, and we still hold hands to cross the road'). Offer two acceptable choices instead of open questions.
Agree rules and consequences in advance, in calm moments, and follow through the same way each time. Repair afterwards: a short talk once everyone is calm.
If you lose your temper, apologize briefly and move on. Perfect calm is not the goal and not required.
Protect your own rest and support. A tired parent finds limits harder, whatever the approach.

seeClinicianIf: Raise with the pediatrician or a family counselor if you feel constantly overwhelmed, dread time with your child, fear you may hurt them, or if aggression or defiance is frequent, severe, or at several places (home, kindergarten, school).
evidenceNote: The branded 'gentle parenting' has not been tested as a whole. Its ingredients (warmth, responsiveness, clear limits, no harsh punishment) match research on authoritative parenting and the AAP position on discipline. Disagreement is about how it is practiced: critics say it can drift into permissiveness or exhaust parents, which the cited sources do not test directly.

parentQuestions: Do I need a glucose tolerance test?

Will it go away after birth?
whatToKnow: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that first appears in pregnancy and usually goes away after birth. Testing usually happens between 24 and 28 weeks, earlier for people at higher risk such as a previous case or a family history of type 2 diabetes. Management centres on food, activity and blood sugar monitoring, and medicine or insulin if needed. Dieting to lose weight is not advised in pregnancy.

whatToDo.action: Do the glucose test; fasting is usually required, so plan the morning.
Follow the dietitian's plan and check sugars as advised.

seeClinicianIf: Report extreme thirst, frequent urination or very high readings, and attend all visits.

title: Going home with a preemie
parentQuestions: When will my preterm baby be allowed home?
How should my preemie sleep at home?
What follow-up will we need?
whatToKnow: AAP says the pediatrician approves discharge when the baby breathes on her own, holds her body temperature, feeds by breast or bottle and gains weight steadily. Some babies go home with monitors or oxygen, and caregivers are trained. Healthy infants should be put on their backs to sleep; AAP notes that some preemies with lung problems may need another position, so ask. Pediatricians check development at each well-child visit, and early intervention may start in the NICU or later through the state system.

whatToDo.action: Ask what to watch for, when to call the office, and the schedule of follow-up visits; learn infant CPR if the team offers it.
Back to sleep, bare crib, no smoking at home, keep every check-up.
Go to all well-child visits and bring up feeding, growth and development questions.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician before discharge what signs mean calling the office or going to hospital; AAP says it does not list them on its page. In an emergency go to the ER or call your local emergency number.

title: Group B strep (GBS) test and antibiotics in labour
parentQuestions: Do I need a GBS swab?
What if I test positive for GBS?
Does GBS harm the baby?
whatToKnow: Group B strep is a common bacterium that many healthy women carry and that can pass to the baby at birth. CDC advises universal screening at 35 to 37 weeks in the US, and antibiotics during labour for carriers lower the risk of infection in the newborn. The NHS describes antibiotics through a vein during labour and about 12 hours of baby monitoring after birth for carriers. The NHS page says GBS is not routinely tested for in the UK, so policy differs between countries.

whatToDo.action: If screening is used in your country, do the swab.
Tell staff you carry GBS as soon as labour starts or waters break.

seeClinicianIf: Call the maternity unit early if waters break, you have a fever in labour, or a previous baby had GBS infection.

title: Growth mindset and praise: what the research shows
parentQuestions: Should I praise my child's effort instead of being smart?
Does growth mindset improve school results?
What do I say when my child says 'I can't do it'?
Как правильно хвалить ребёнка, чтобы не вырастить неуверенного?
whatToKnow: Dweck's idea is that believing abilities can grow helps motivation and learning. A 2018 meta-analysis (Sisk, 365,915 students, then 43 interventions) found overall effects were weak, with some benefit for low-income or academically at-risk students. A large pre-registered US national study (Yeager 2019, Nature) found a short online course improved grades among lower-achieving secondary students and raised advanced math enrollment, depending on school peer norms. Praising effort and strategy is reasonable but is not a proven way to raise grades.

whatToDo.action: Describe what the child did ('you tried three ways') rather than saying 'you are so smart'.
When they say 'I can't', add 'yet' and break the task into one next step.
Let them struggle a little before helping; praise returning to a hard task.
Show your own mistakes and what you did next.

seeClinicianIf: If a child is very distressed about school, refuses to attend, or shows a sudden fall in learning or mood, speak to the teacher and the pediatrician; it is not a mindset problem to fix at home alone.
evidenceNote: Reviews disagree on size: Sisk 2018 reports weak average effects, Yeager 2019 reports effects in specific subgroups and contexts; some authors of the Nature study disclosed ties to an institute that offers free mindset programs. Studies are mostly with adolescents; parent praise for young children is less tested.

title: Hand, foot and mouth disease
parentQuestions: My child has blisters on hands and sores in the mouth, what is it?
Is hand foot and mouth contagious?
Can my child go to daycare?
whatToKnow: NHS says hand, foot and mouth disease is a common childhood illness that usually gets better in 7 to 10 days. It often starts with a sore throat, a high temperature and not wanting to eat, then mouth ulcers and a rash of spots on the hands and feet that can blister. Antibiotics do not cure it. It spreads in coughs, sneezes, poo and blister fluid, mostly in the first 5 days.

whatToDo.action: Offer cool fluids and soft foods, avoid acidic drinks like fruit juice and hot, salty or spicy food. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease a sore mouth. A pharmacist can suggest mouth gels for children.
Watch peeing and drinking, because mouth pain can lead to dehydration.
NHS says to keep your child home only while too unwell, and they can return once feeling better without waiting for blisters to heal. Check your own daycare's rule too.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says to ask for urgent advice if there is a very high temperature or the child feels hot, cold or shivery, if they are peeing less than usual, or if you are worried. See a doctor if symptoms last beyond 7 to 10 days, and tell a doctor or midwife if a pregnant person has been in contact.
evidenceNote: NHS gives symptoms, course and school guidance. Other bodies may set different exclusion rules for settings, so ask the daycare.

title: Handwashing and stopping stomach bugs spreading
parentQuestions: How should my child wash their hands?
How do I stop the stomach bug spreading in the family?
Is hand sanitizer enough?

Soap and water is best, and if unavailable use a sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol. NHS adds for stomach bugs: wash soiled clothes and bedding hot, clean toilet seats, flush handles and taps daily, do not share towels, and stay home until 2 days after the last symptoms.

whatToDo.action: Before eating and cooking, after the toilet or changing a diaper, after coughing or blowing the nose, after touching animals.
Soap and water (not only sanitizer), daily cleaning of shared surfaces, separate towels.
Make the 20 seconds a song or a count.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the doctor if illness keeps spreading through the household, or if a child shows dehydration or blood in the stool (see vomiting-and-diarrhea-children).

title: Head bumps: minor or ER?
parentQuestions: My toddler hit their head, when do I go to the ER?
Can my child sleep after a head bump?
How long do I watch a child after a head injury?
whatToKnow: Most head bumps are minor. AAP says a child who is alert, responds to you and cries for no more than about 10 minutes after the bump usually needs no scan, but a bump that is more than light is worth a call to the child's doctor. The AAP page is not meant for children under 2, so for babies use the NHS and St John pages and call the doctor early. NHS lists a bruise, swelling or large cut on the head of a baby under 1 year as an emergency.

whatToDo.action: Comfort the child, hold a cold compress wrapped in cloth on the area, and watch how they act and respond. Note when and how it happened for the doctor.
Keep an adult with the child. AAP says sleep is fine, and the doctor may suggest checking every 2 to 3 hours that the child moves normally, wakes enough to know you and responds.
AAP says to give only acetaminophen for pain unless the doctor says otherwise. Use the official dosing table by current weight.

seeClinicianIf: Lost consciousness, or a seizure, or cannot be woken or kept awake. AAP says call 911 if a child loses consciousness. NHS also lists a fall from more than 1 metre or 5 stairs, clear fluid or blood from the ears or nose, bruising behind the ears, weakness, trouble walking or speaking, vision or hearing problems, a dent or foreign object in the head wound, a changed or very irritable mood, and any swelling or large cut on the head of a baby under 1 year. Also call the doctor or go to the ER for repeated vomiting (more than 2 or 3 times), a worsening headache, unequal pupils, or a child who is more and more sleepy. Call your local emergency number (911 in the US) and open the app's fixed Urgent help screen for any of these.
evidenceNote: AAP, NHS and St John Ambulance agree on the warning signs. Exact lists differ a little between countries, so the app shows the AAP and NHS lists side by side and defers to the child's doctor.

title: Heat illness and heatstroke in children
parentQuestions: My child is very hot and drowsy, is it heatstroke?
How do I cool a child down?
When is heat an emergency?
whatToKnow: NHS says heat exhaustion (tiredness, headache, sweating, pale clammy skin, thirst, irritability) should improve within about 30 minutes if the child is cooled and given fluids. Heatstroke is an emergency: very high temperature, hot skin with no sweating, fast breathing and heartbeat, confusion, a seizure or loss of consciousness. The opened pages do not talk about children left in parked cars, so this topic does not cover that.

whatToDo.action: Move to a cool place, remove unnecessary clothing, give plenty of water or oral rehydration, and cool the skin with cool water and fanning.
Call emergency services, wrap in a cool wet sheet or sponge with cold water, and put in recovery position if unconscious.
NHS suggests light loose clothing, more cold drinks and avoiding the sun between 11am and 3pm.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number if the child is still unwell after 30 minutes of cooling and fluids, or shows signs of heatstroke (NHS lists confusion, hot dry skin, a fast heartbeat, seizure or loss of consciousness). Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS and St John Ambulance agree. The hot car angle was not supported by an opened page and is omitted; a CDC or AAP page should be added.

title: Hepatitis B vaccine at birth
parentQuestions: Why vaccinate against hepatitis B on day one?
What if the mother is hepatitis B positive?
whatToKnow: WHO recommends the first dose within 24 hours of birth, because most chronic hepatitis B comes from mother-to-child or early childhood infection. The AAP still recommends a first dose within 24 hours for all medically stable newborns (its page was updated 5 December 2025 and calls the federal change dangerous). On 16 December 2025 the CDC adopted individual-based decision-making for babies of mothers who test negative: parents and clinician decide, and a skipped birth dose would start no earlier than 2 months. Babies of mothers who test positive or whose status is unknown still get the vaccine plus immune globulin at birth, with no change.

whatToDo.action: Ask that your hepatitis B test result is in your records and shared with the maternity unit.
Ask the maternity unit which schedule it follows and talk it through with the pediatrician; if you skip the birth dose, ask when the series will start.
Confirm what was given and have it written into the vaccination record.

seeClinicianIf: Tell the pediatrician if the baby did not get the dose in hospital so it can be given at the first visit.
evidenceNote: The official bodies now differ: WHO and AAP recommend the dose for all newborns, while the US CDC (December 2025) recommends individual decisions when the mother tests negative. Both pages were opened on 2026-11-14. Nothing changes for babies of positive or unknown-status mothers. Which schedule applies depends on the country; Kazakhstan's calendar is covered in its own topic.

title: Hip dysplasia: newborn check and what parents can notice
parentQuestions: What is hip dysplasia?
Why do doctors check the hips so often?
Is a clicking hip normal?
whatToKnow: Developmental dysplasia of the hip means the hip joint is loose and can move out of position. It is usually painless, so it is often found at the newborn examination, and treatment started early usually works well. Parents may notice clicking, one leg moving differently, unequal leg length, or later dragging a leg or limping.

whatToDo.when: At birth and the 6 to 8 week check
whatToDo.action: Make sure the hips are examined and ask about any family history.
Avoid forcing the legs straight in wraps and carriers; let the hips bend and spread.

seeClinicianIf: Raise with the pediatrician any hip clicking, asymmetry in leg movement or length, or a baby who dislikes a leg being moved. These are not diagnoses; a clinician decides if imaging is needed.
evidenceNote: NHS describes detection through the newborn physical exam; local screening policies (ultrasound for risk factors) differ between countries.

sources.title: NHS: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
NHS: Your 6-week postnatal check

title: Hip-healthy swaddling and the hip joint
parentQuestions: Does swaddling hurt my baby's hips?
How should the legs sit in a swaddle?
What is a hip-healthy sleep sack?
whatToKnow: The baby's hips are best held slightly bent and spread, with the knees slightly bent, which is the natural curled position. Forcing the legs straight and together for long periods is linked by IHDI and AAP to hip dysplasia. A snug upper body with a loose pouch for the legs is the practical rule.

whatToDo.action: Wrap snug at chest and arms but leave room for the knees to bend and the legs to move.
Choose swaddle sacks with a roomy leg pouch and do not tighten them around the thighs.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if one leg moves differently, a hip clicks, or the legs look unequal in length.
evidenceNote: IHDI position statement plus AAP page; the product list is an IHDI judgement, so treat brand claims cautiously.

title: Hiring a nanny or sitter: references, trial, tax basics
parentQuestions: How do I vet a nanny?
Do I have to pay taxes for a nanny?
Should we do a trial day?
whatToKnow: The AAP says in-home care gives more individual attention but good providers are hard to find, and recommends frequent unannounced visits plus clear rules on discipline, TV, activities and outings. For vetting it advises asking for references and checking them, interviewing about past roles and children's ages, and paying for a trial hour while you are home so the caregiver meets your child. In the US, IRS Topic 756 treats a nanny you direct as a household employee; for 2026 it says that cash wages of $3,000 or more to one household employee generally mean withholding Social Security and Medicare, with other taxes and forms in IRS Publication 926.

whatToDo.action: Ask about past positions, children's ages, and how they would handle common situations; write down your rules on media, smoking or drinking, outings and housework.
Pay for a trial visit while you are home, then ask your child about the person and take it seriously.
Check IRS Publication 926 or a payroll service; we did not open pages on background checks or the Department of Labor household rules, so check those separately.
Leave emergency contacts, your pediatrician and the poison control number where the caregiver can see them.

evidenceNote: Vetting advice is from AAP pages; tax facts are from the IRS page and can change yearly. We found no official page on background checks or contracts that opened, so the app should not claim a legal standard.

title: Staying home alone
parentQuestions: At what age can my child stay home alone?
whatToKnow: The AAP says around 11 or 12 is a reasonable age for a few hours, most children are not ready for regular solo time until 10 or 11, and some mature 8 or 9 year olds can manage half an hour now and then. Consider maturity, judgment, comfort, emergency knowledge, and local rules.

whatToDo.action: Practice emergency steps and phone use.
Short and easy time of day.

evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Is your child ready to stay home alone?

title: Home safety: falls, burns, poisoning, tip-overs
parentQuestions: How do I baby-proof?
whatToKnow: Injuries are the main preventable danger. Key steps: stair gates, window locks, anchor furniture and TVs, hot water under 49C, medicines and detergents locked, cords out of reach, and supervision around water.

whatToDo.action: Anchor furniture, add gates, move chemicals and medicines up and away.
Walk through the house at child height.

seeClinicianIf: Any ingestion of medicine, detergent pod or batteries: call poison control or emergency immediately.
evidenceNote: CDC drowning page opened; the rest is general injury prevention, and CPSC and AAP pages failed to open.

sources.title: CDC: Drowning prevention

title: Homework help and routine
parentQuestions: How much should I help with homework?
My child fights me over homework
How long should homework take?
whatToKnow: The AAP advises a consistent time and a designated spot, with electronics off, staying nearby to answer questions, and talking with the teacher if a subject is a struggle. Parents are helpers, not answer keys. We did not find an AAP minute-per-grade rule.

whatToDo.action: Same time and place; start after a snack and rest.
Ask guiding questions, then contact the teacher rather than doing the work.

seeClinicianIf: Hours of tears nightly, avoidance, or physical complaints around homework suggest an underlying problem to raise with the teacher or pediatrician.
evidenceNote: AAP guidance (opened); homework research is mixed and was not reviewed.

title: Hospital bag checklist: what to pack and when
parentQuestions: What do I need in my hospital bag?
When should I pack?
What should my partner bring?
What does the baby need?
What should I pack in the hospital bag?
When should the bag be ready?
Is it bad luck to buy baby things early?
whatToKnow: The NHS says only 1 in 20 babies arrives on the due date and suggests packing at least 3 weeks before. The list covers documents, loose clothes, nightwear, nursing bras, maternity pads, toiletries, snacks, a water bottle, phone charger, a car seat for the trip home, and baby clothes, nappies and a blanket. ACOG adds keeping the bag in a handy place, planning child care and pets, and having a car seat installed properly. Packing is practical rather than clinical: your hospital may have its own list.

whatToDo.action: Ask the maternity unit for its own list of what to bring and what it supplies.
Pack the bag, keep documents and notes on top, and put it by the door.
Install the car seat and do a practice drive; pack the partner's bag.
Pack the bag and keep documents together.
Install the car seat and plan the route.

evidenceNote: NHS gives the checklist and ACOG gives planning tips; neither is a clinical rule. Hospitals differ in what they supply.

title: Hospital stay length and going home
parentQuestions: How long will we stay?
Is early discharge safe?
What do we need before we leave?
whatToKnow: WHO recommends that healthy mothers and babies stay in the facility at least 24 hours after birth, with postnatal contacts on day 1, day 3, days 7 to 14 and at 6 weeks. WHO says discharge is acceptable once the mother's bleeding is controlled, neither has signs of infection or other disease, and the baby is breastfeeding well.

whatToDo.action: Ask for a feeding check, screening results, discharge weight and written follow-up.
Ask when the first postnatal contact will happen and who to call.

seeClinicianIf: Ask to stay longer if feeding is not going well, the baby looks yellow, or you feel unwell.
evidenceNote: WHO sets a minimum of 24 hours; stay length otherwise depends on local policy and birth type.

title: How often and how much a newborn eats
parentQuestions: How often should a newborn eat?
Do I wake the baby to feed?
How much formula per feed?
whatToKnow: Breastfed babies feed at least 8 times in 24 hours in the first weeks; the jaundice guidance suggests 8 to 12 times. Formula feeds start small and rise as the baby grows, following cues. The NHS jaundice page suggests encouraging sleepy babies to feed; ask the midwife how long a gap between feeds is acceptable.

whatToDo.action: Respond to hunger cues such as rooting and hand to mouth.
Ask your midwife whether to wake for feeds.

seeClinicianIf: Seek help for refusing feeds, very few wet nappies, extreme sleepiness, or weight loss.
evidenceNote: Numbers are rough guides; the pattern varies.

title: Imaginary friends
parentQuestions: Is an imaginary friend normal?
My child talks to someone who is not there
whatToKnow: The AAP says imaginary friends are usually normal, help social skills and empathy, and fade with time; children can usually make them go away. Talk to the pediatrician if it never goes away, is always talking, threatens or encourages violence, or comes with other developmental concerns or sudden changes.

whatToDo.action: Be curious and play along without taking over.
Note content and control.

seeClinicianIf: Companion that threatens violence, never goes away, or sudden social, speech or hygiene changes.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

title: Independence and walking to school
parentQuestions: When can my child walk to school alone?
How do I teach road safety?
whatToKnow: No official age for walking to school was found in sources we opened. CDC says teach preschoolers to stay out of traffic and use sidewalks. The AAP home-alone page says readiness depends on maturity, judgment, comfort and knowing emergency steps and that some mature 8 or 9 year olds can manage short periods. Start with a practice route and a buddy.

whatToDo.action: Walk the route together and practice crossing.
Start with short distances and check in.

evidenceNote: Extrapolated from AAP and CDC safety advice; local rules vary.

title: Induction of labour and the ARRIVE trial
parentQuestions: Should I be induced at 39 weeks?
When is induction offered?
Does induction raise caesarean risk?
whatToKnow: The ARRIVE trial in the US randomised 6,106 low-risk first-time mothers to induction at 39 weeks or waiting. The main composite outcome did not differ significantly (4.3 versus 5.4 percent), but caesarean delivery was lower with induction (18.6 versus 22.2 percent). The NHS offers induction by 41 weeks and a membrane sweep from 39 weeks, and notes induced labour is often more painful and more likely to need forceps or ventouse.

whatToDo.action: Ask your doctor about a sweep or planned induction.
Discuss induction offers and monitoring if you decline.

evidenceNote: ARRIVE is randomised but US-based and the main outcome narrowly missed significance; the NHS policy is later (41 weeks). Experts weigh benefits against hospital stay and preference.

title: Infant and child CPR: the basics
parentQuestions: How do I do CPR on a baby?
Do I give breaths to a child?
What do I do if I am alone?
whatToKnow: St John Ambulance says cardiac arrest in children is likely caused by a breathing problem, so rescue breaths are part of child and baby CPR. Check for a response, call for help, open the airway and look for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If the child is unresponsive and not breathing normally, give five rescue breaths, then 30 chest compressions pressing down about a third of the chest depth at 100 to 120 per minute, then two breaths, repeating 30 to 2. Their page gives about 4 cm for a baby and 5 cm for a child This does not replace a certified course.

whatToDo.action: Shout and shake gently. If no response, shout for help and call, speaker phone on.
Give five rescue breaths and one minute of CPR, then take the child with you to call.
Baby: encircle the chest with both hands and use thumbs on the centre of the chest. Child: heel of one hand in the centre of the chest.
AAP recommends a certified CPR and first aid course (American Red Cross or American Heart Association).

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number first for any unresponsive child and follow the call handler. If the child is not breathing normally start CPR at once. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: One detailed source (St John Ambulance, UK; reviewed September 2026) plus AAP's advice to take a class. Practices may differ slightly in other countries, so check the local course.

title: Pregnancy after IVF: what is known
parentQuestions: Is an IVF pregnancy riskier?
Are IVF babies healthy?
Is it normal to be anxious after IVF?
whatToKnow: HFEA says fertility treatment is generally very safe and most people have no problems. The main risk is a multiple pregnancy; HFEA says freezing spare embryos is normally best practice because putting two embryos back raises the chance of twins or triplets. HFEA also lists a slightly increased risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, high blood pressure and possible birth defects, noting these are rare and research is ongoing. NHS says IVF can strain you emotionally and recommends counselling before, during and after treatment. The pages we opened give no data on later health of children conceived by IVF, so we make no claim.

whatToDo.action: Ask your clinic how many embryos will be transferred and what that means for the chance of twins.
Tell your ob-gyn that you conceived by IVF so monitoring can match.
Use the clinic's counselling or a support group if worry or low mood is heavy.

seeClinicianIf: After egg collection or transfer: contact your clinic or local health line for belly pain, vaginal bleeding or feeling faint, and call your local emergency number or go to the ER for severe pain, trouble breathing or chest pain, as NHS says. Use the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: HFEA and NHS are official; CDC's page we opened only defines ART and gives no outcome data. Long-term child outcomes are not covered by these pages.

title: Kangaroo care for a preterm baby
parentQuestions: What is kangaroo care?
Can dad do skin-to-skin too?
Does skin-to-skin help premature babies?
whatToKnow: Kangaroo care means holding your baby bare-chested against your skin. AAP lists warmth, steadier heartbeat and breathing, more deep sleep and quiet alert time, less crying, better weight gain and improved breastfeeding, and says these can show up even with a few minutes a day. Either parent can do it. WHO's 2022 guidance for preterm babies includes kangaroo mother care immediately after birth among the simple steps that can substantially cut deaths in preterm and low birth weight babies.

whatToDo.action: Ask the nurse when your baby is stable enough to be held skin-to-skin, and how to set it up.
Keep doing it at calm times such as first thing in the morning or after a bath, in open-front clothing.

seeClinicianIf: Check with the baby's care team before starting if the baby is premature or in intensive care, as AAP advises.
evidenceNote: AAP and WHO both recommend it. WHO's mortality figures come from settings with limited neonatal care, and the effect size in high-income units is different.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Skin-to-Skin Contact, Kangaroo Care
WHO: Preterm birth fact sheet

title: When to keep a child home from daycare or school
parentQuestions: Can my child go to school with a cold?
How long after vomiting should they stay home?
Which illnesses need time off?
whatToKnow: NHS says a child with a high temperature should stay home until it goes away. A slight cough or common cold symptoms are fine for school if the child is otherwise well. Keep them home for vomiting or diarrhea until 2 days after the last episode, for chickenpox until spots have crusted over (about 5 days), and for scarlet fever until 24 hours on antibiotics. NHS says no exclusion is needed for conjunctivitis unless very unwell, hand, foot and mouth if they feel well enough, head lice, threadworms, or slapped cheek.

whatToDo.action: Check temperature and how your child feels and behaves.
Phone the school or nursery on day one and give the reason.
Your daycare may have stricter rules, so ask.

seeClinicianIf: Call a doctor if a child with a high temperature gets worse or has any red flag from the fever topic, or if an infection like measles is suspected (NHS says call the surgery first and keep home for at least 4 days from the start of the rash).
evidenceNote: These are NHS rules for England, which refers to government health protection guidance. We did not find an opened Kazakhstan or CDC exclusion page, so local rules may differ.

sources.title: NHS: Is my child too ill for school?
NHS: Diarrhoea and vomiting

title: Starting school: the first weeks
parentQuestions: How do I help my child settle into first grade?
My child cries before school
How to prepare for the first day?
whatToKnow: The AAP suggests visiting the school before the first day, rehearsing the walk in, arranging a buddy, and moving bedtime earlier a week or two before term. Ask what worries them and solve it together. Sleep is linked to better school performance and fewer absences.

whatToDo.action: Shift bedtime earlier and practice the morning routine.
Arrive early, keep the goodbye short and warm.
Keep after-school time free for rest.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent refusal to go, stomachaches or headaches that clear on weekends, or marked behavior change after several weeks.
evidenceNote: AAP back-to-school guidance, practical but not trial-based.

title: The 5-1-1 rule and its variations (4-1-1, 3-1-1)
parentQuestions: When should I leave for the hospital, 5-1-1?
Do I leave earlier for a second baby?
We live far from the hospital, when do we go?
whatToKnow: 5-1-1 is a popular rule of thumb: contractions about every 5 minutes, lasting about 1 minute, for about an hour. Official sources word it differently. The NHS says to call when contractions come every 5 minutes or more often, and ACOG gives no number but says to call if you think you are in labor or are unsure and to agree the right time to call with your provider beforehand. Quebec's public health institute says first-time parents go in at regular contractions 5 minutes apart for an hour, later-baby parents at 5 minutes apart, and anyone living over 30 minutes away at about 10 minutes apart.

whatToDo.action: Ask your clinician which threshold they use for you (5-1-1, 4-1-1 or 3-1-1) and write it on the fridge.
Do a practice drive at rush hour and note the time; if over 30 minutes, ask whether to leave earlier.

whatToDo.when: If this is not your first baby
whatToDo.action: Expect labor to often be shorter and plan to call earlier than you did last time.

whatToDo.when: If GBS positive or you had a previous cesarean
whatToDo.action: Ask whether your unit wants a call or arrival earlier than the standard rule, and note the answer in your plan.
Call the unit to talk it through even if you are not yet at the threshold.

seeClinicianIf: Always call right away, whatever the timing, if waters break, you bleed, the baby moves less, pain is constant and severe, or you are under 37 weeks.
evidenceNote: The 5-1-1 numbers come from handouts and hospital advice, not from a trial, and 4-1-1 or 3-1-1 are local variants without a primary guideline source. Services differ, so your own unit's number wins.

sources.title: ACOG: How to Tell When Labor Begins

title: Bloody show and the mucus plug
parentQuestions: I lost my mucus plug, is labor starting?
Pink mucus at 38 weeks, is that normal?
How much blood is too much?
whatToKnow: A thick plug of mucus seals the cervix in pregnancy and can come away in one piece or several, sometimes days before labor or in early labor. The NHS calls the sticky pink or slightly bloody mucus a show and says labor may follow quickly or take a few days; some people have none. A show alone is not an emergency, but bright red bleeding like a period needs a call straight away.

whatToDo.action: Learn the difference between a pink show and fresh red bleeding.
Rest, keep eating and drinking, and watch for contractions; no need to rush.
Call the unit immediately and note how much, using a pad to judge.

seeClinicianIf: Fresh red bleeding, a show with constant pain, less baby movement, or any bloody discharge before 37 weeks.
evidenceNote: NHS and ACOG describe it similarly; timing of labor after a show varies widely and no study predicts it.

sources.title: ACOG: How to Tell When Labor Begins
NHS: Signs that labour has begun

title: Breathing and relaxation techniques for labor (Lamaze and similar)
parentQuestions: Does breathing really help with labor pain?
Which breathing technique should we learn?
Do yoga or music help in labor?
whatToKnow: Relaxation methods such as paced breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, yoga, music and mindfulness are low risk and many women like them. A Cochrane review of 19 trials found low to very low quality evidence that relaxation, yoga and music may reduce pain or raise satisfaction with pain relief, and too little evidence on mindfulness. NICE says to support a woman who chooses breathing and relaxation and to support music of her choice. WHO recommends relaxation techniques for women who ask for pain relief.

whatToDo.action: Pick one simple method (for example slow breathing with a long exhale) and practice 5 to 10 minutes a day.
Practice together with your partner during timed 60 second 'contractions', for example holding an ice cube.
Make a music playlist and test it; pack headphones or a speaker.
Start the breathing early in the contraction and keep it slow; change technique if it stops helping.

evidenceNote: Evidence for pain relief is low to very low quality, with no sign of harm. NICE and WHO both support using these methods by choice.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Relaxation techniques for pain management in labour (2018)

title: Early (latent) labor at home: eat, drink, rest, bath
parentQuestions: Should I go to the hospital at 2 cm?
Can I eat during early labor?
Can I take a bath in early labor?
They sent me home, is that normal?
whatToKnow: The latent phase can take many hours or even days and is usually the longest part of labor. NHS and NICE advise staying at home if all is well: eat lightly, drink when thirsty, sleep if it starts at night, stay upright and gently active in the day, and use a bath, shower or breathing exercises; the NHS says paracetamol is safe in labor. WHO also recommends oral fluids and food for low-risk women. Being sent home before labor is established is common and not a sign something is wrong.

whatToDo.action: Stock easy snacks, isotonic drinks, a heat pack and playlists; practice breathing with your partner.
Eat something light, drink, empty your bladder, and rest or sleep; use a bath or shower for comfort.
Walk, sway or use a ball; avoid lying flat on your back.
Call the unit when your threshold is reached or if you are worried; agree on the next call time.

seeClinicianIf: Any red-flag sign, no baby movement, pain that does not ease between contractions, or you feel unable to cope.
evidenceNote: NHS and NICE give the same advice; WHO recommends fluids and food for low-risk labor. Evidence for individual comfort measures is low quality, but harm is not shown.

sources.title: NHS: The stages of labour and birth
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations

title: Fear of childbirth (tokophobia) and where to get support
parentQuestions: I am terrified of giving birth, is that normal?
Can I request a cesarean because of fear?
Who can I talk to about my fear?
whatToKnow: A 2026 meta-analysis of 67 studies found severe fear of childbirth in about 1 in 6 women (16.5 percent) worldwide, more often in first pregnancies, after a traumatic birth, and with anxiety. NICE says that if someone with tokophobia or severe anxiety asks for a cesarean, the team should explore the reasons, discuss alternatives such as continuity of midwifery care and pain relief, and offer referral to perinatal mental health support. Fear is a medical topic you can raise at any visit.

whatToDo.when: As soon as you notice it
whatToDo.action: Tell your midwife or doctor; fear is a medical topic you can raise at any visit.
Ask about a counselling or birth-reflection appointment; join a class and visit the unit.
Share the fear with your partner and decide what reassurance helps (for example info, a tour, a clear plan).

seeClinicianIf: Panic, trouble sleeping or eating, intrusive thoughts, avoiding pregnancy care, or low mood: contact your clinician, who can refer to perinatal mental health care. In crisis, use your local emergency number.
evidenceNote: NICE sets the pathway; prevalence data come from very heterogeneous studies.

title: Hypnobirthing and hypnosis for labor
parentQuestions: Is hypnobirthing worth it?
Does hypnosis reduce the need for an epidural?
Can I do hypnobirthing with a cesarean?
whatToKnow: Hypnobirthing combines deep relaxation, breathing, visualisation and self-hypnosis. The NHS says it can help you feel calm and in control but cannot guarantee a birth without interventions. A Cochrane review of 9 trials (2954 women) found women in hypnosis groups were somewhat less likely to use drugs for pain relief (very low quality evidence) but no clear difference in coping, spontaneous vaginal birth or satisfaction with pain relief. NICE says not to offer hypnosis in labor but to support a woman who wants it.

whatToDo.action: If you want it, choose a course early, since most run over several weeks and need daily practice.
Practice a 10 to 15 minute audio session; partner learns the cues.
Treat it as one tool alongside others; pain relief remains available any time.

evidenceNote: Cochrane finds a modest, low-certainty drop in drug use; NICE does not recommend offering it but supports choice; NHS lists it as an option. Courses vary a lot in quality and cost.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Hypnosis for pain management during labour and childbirth (2016)

title: Massage, acupressure, TENS and sterile water injections
parentQuestions: Does massage help labor pain?
Is TENS worth it?
What are sterile water injections for back pain?
Does acupuncture work in labor?
whatToKnow: Cochrane finds low quality evidence that massage lowers pain in the first stage of labor. For acupuncture, one review found little or no difference in pain compared with sham needling but possibly higher satisfaction and less drug use, with low certainty. NICE supports massage taught to birth companions and TENS by choice (very little evidence it works in established labor, no evidence of harm), suggests considering sterile water injections for back pain, and says not to offer acupuncture or acupressure but to support a woman who wants them.

whatToDo.action: Ask your partner to learn two or three massage strokes (lower back, shoulders) and practice them.
If you want TENS, rent or buy it and test it before labor; the NHS does not supply one.
If back pain is severe, ask the midwife whether sterile water injections are offered.

evidenceNote: Quality ratings are low or very low and trials are small. These are choice-based comfort measures, not replacements for effective drugs.
