Cochrane review: Acupuncture or acupressure for pain management during labour (2020)
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations

title: The partner's role: support, counter-pressure, advocacy, and whether to attend
parentQuestions: What should my partner do during labor?
Should my husband be at the birth?
Can a doula or relative come instead?
whatToKnow: A Cochrane review of 27 trials found continuous support in labor increases spontaneous vaginal birth and shortens labor slightly, while lowering cesarean, instrumental birth, pain medication use and negative birth experiences. The NHS suggests partners know the birth plan, attend classes, plan the route, offer drinks and snacks, breathe with her, give physical support, speak up for her wishes and look after themselves. Whether the partner attends is a choice.

whatToDo.action: Decide together who will be the companion and tell the maternity unit; ask about rules and costs.
Partner reads the birth plan, learns the signs, and does a drive and parking check.
Practice massage, breathing together, and a phone script for calling the unit; pack the partner's bag.
Offer water and snacks, change positions with her, keep the room calm, and ask the staff to explain choices.

evidenceNote: Continuous support has the strongest evidence of the comfort measures; it can be a partner, relative, doula or midwife. Cultural preferences about who attends differ and are valid.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Continuous support for women during childbirth (2017)
Bakhta and Lee 2010 (Int J Gynaecol Obstet): Survey of Russian women on a companion during labor
NHS Best Start in Life: Tips for your birthing partner

title: Perineal massage in late pregnancy
parentQuestions: Should I do perineal massage before birth?
From which week do I start?
Does it prevent tearing?
whatToKnow: Cochrane (4 trials, 2497 women) found antenatal digital perineal massage lowers the chance of trauma needing stitches and of episiotomy, mostly in women without a previous vaginal birth. It lowered perineal pain at 3 months in women who had given birth before. It did not clearly change first or second degree tears, severe tears, or instrumental births. The NHS says it is done in the last few weeks of pregnancy and that the most benefit was seen in women who did it every day.

whatToDo.when: In the last few weeks (often taught from about 34 to 35 weeks)
whatToDo.action: Ask your midwife to show you the technique and how often to do it.
Follow the routine your midwife teaches and stop if there is pain or bleeding.
Tell your midwife in advance if you want perineal support such as warm compresses.

seeClinicianIf: Pain, burning, unusual discharge or bleeding: stop and ask your midwife.
evidenceNote: Moderate to good quality trials with modest benefit (about 1 in 15 avoids stitches). The exact week to start varies by teacher; the sources say 'the last few weeks'.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Antenatal perineal massage for reducing perineal trauma (2013)
NHS: Episiotomy and perineal tears

title: Positions and moving in labor, including the birth ball
parentQuestions: What are the best positions for labor?
Should I stay in bed?
Does a birth ball help?
Can I move with an epidural?
whatToKnow: NICE says to encourage women to move and take whatever positions are comfortable, except lying flat on the back. A Cochrane review of 25 trials found the first stage was about 1 hour 22 minutes shorter for upright positions, with fewer cesareans and epidurals, though trial quality was variable; with an epidural there was no clear difference. A review of trials found birth balls lower labor pain in the first stage without changing mode of birth.

whatToDo.action: Practice upright positions at home: kneeling over a ball, leaning on a wall, hands and knees, side lying.
Keep moving and change position regularly.
Use an anti-burst ball that fits your height, and only if you practiced it in pregnancy and feel safe on it.
Ask about side lying or semi-upright positions and a peanut ball; change position regularly.

evidenceNote: NICE recommends free movement; Cochrane evidence is moderate to low quality. Birth ball evidence is about pain, not about shortening labor.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Maternal positions and mobility during first stage labour (2013)
AJOG 2023 review: Birthing balls and peanut balls, what is the evidence?
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations

title: Pushing: your own urge, directed pushing, and delayed pushing with an epidural
parentQuestions: Should I push on command?
How long can pushing last?
Should I wait to push with an epidural?
Do I have to hold my breath?
whatToKnow: NICE says that without an epidural spontaneous pushing may shorten the second stage compared with directed pushing, and with an epidural delaying pushing for 1 to 2 hours may shorten active pushing. Cochrane found no clear difference in the length of second stage between spontaneous and directed pushing, and a 2020 meta-analysis found delayed pushing shortened active pushing but lengthened the total second stage, with no gain in spontaneous birth and more chorioamnionitis. The NHS says pushing usually lasts up to 3 hours for a first baby and 2 hours after a previous birth.

whatToDo.action: Practice pelvic floor relaxation and open-mouth breathing out with your partner or midwife.
Ask your midwife if you can wait for your own urge; if you have an epidural, ask about waiting.
Try different positions, breathe out as you push, and rest between contractions.

seeClinicianIf: Pushing is ineffective after a long time, the baby's heartbeat is a concern, or you have severe pain or bleeding: the team will review options.
evidenceNote: Trials show similar birth outcomes between methods, so the choice is about comfort and monitoring.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Pushing/bearing down methods for the second stage of labour (2017)
Meta-analysis (AJOG 2020): Delayed versus immediate pushing with neuraxial analgesia
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations

title: Warm bath or birthing pool during labor
parentQuestions: Does a pool help with pain?
Is water birth safe?
Can I use the bath in early labor?
whatToKnow: NICE advises offering the chance to labor in water for pain relief, with the water kept at or below 37.5 C and checked hourly. The Cochrane review of 15 trials (3663 women) found immersion in the first stage probably makes little difference to the type of birth and may reduce use of epidural or spinal pain relief, with no evidence of more harm to mother or baby; evidence for birth in water is limited. NHS says a warm bath or shower can ease early labor.

whatToDo.action: Ask whether your unit has pools and the rules for using them.
Try a bath or shower at home when contractions are uncomfortable.
If a pool is available, ask when it is best to enter (many units advise established labor).

seeClinicianIf: Fever, bleeding, or concerns about the baby's heartbeat: the team will ask you to leave the pool.
evidenceNote: NICE recommends offering it; Cochrane evidence is moderate to low quality and none of the trials were in midwifery-led units.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Immersion in water during labour and birth (2018)
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations
NHS: The stages of labour and birth

title: Waters breaking: what to do, 24 hours, infection, GBS
parentQuestions: My water broke but no contractions, what now?
How long can I wait after my water breaks?
What color should the fluid be?
I am GBS positive, does that change things?
whatToKnow: About 60 percent of people with waters breaking at term start labor within 24 hours (NICE). Without fluid there is a small rise in infection risk for the baby, and NICE gives serious early infection as about 1 percent versus 0.5 percent with intact membranes. NHS and NICE advise calling the unit, noting the colour and smell, using a pad rather than a tampon, checking temperature every 4 hours while awake, and being offered induction if labor has not started by about 24 hours. A positive group B strep test is a reason to be seen promptly, and NICE advises immediate induction if waters break at term in that case.

whatToDo.action: Ask your midwife about GBS testing and what a positive result would change in your labor plan; tell the unit if you are positive when you call.
Note time, color and smell, put on a pad, and call the unit; expect a phone check and likely an invitation to be seen.
Take your temperature every 4 hours when awake and note baby movements; a shower or bath is fine, sex is not advised.
If labor has not started, discuss induction as offered.

seeClinicianIf: Green, brown, bloody or smelly fluid, fever or feeling unwell, less movement, GBS positive, or leaking before 37 weeks.
evidenceNote: NHS and NICE agree on calling promptly; NICE allows up to 24 hours of expectant management by choice. Cochrane finds planned early birth lowers infection without a clear rise in cesareans, but the evidence is low quality.

sources.title: Cochrane review: Planned early birth vs expectant management for prelabour rupture of membranes at term (2017)
NHS: Signs that labour has begun
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations

title: When to call or go to the maternity unit right away
parentQuestions: What are the emergency signs in late pregnancy?
Should I go if my baby is moving less?
Waters broke and they are green, what now?
Contractions before 37 weeks
whatToKnow: Some signs mean calling the maternity unit immediately at any hour, not waiting for a contraction pattern. The NHS lists waters breaking, vaginal bleeding, less baby movement, contractions before 37 weeks, a contraction over 2 minutes, or 6 or more in 10 minutes. ACOG lists waters broken without contractions, heavy bleeding, constant severe pain with no relief between contractions, and less fetal movement. The NHS adds that smelly or coloured waters need urgent attention and a strong urge to push means calling emergency services.

whatToDo.action: Learn your baby's usual movement pattern and who to call if it changes.
Put the unit's 24 hour number and the emergency number on your phone's favorites and in your bag.
Call straight away, say your gestation, and ask whether to come in; do not wait until morning.

whatToDo.when: If your baby seems to be coming now
whatToDo.action: Call the emergency number and follow the instructions you are given.

seeClinicianIf: Waters breaking, any bleeding beyond a pink show, reduced movement, constant severe pain, fever, or contractions or fluid leak before 37 weeks.
evidenceNote: NHS, ACOG, and NICE agree on this core list. Thresholds for who should go in at once differ slightly by country.

sources.title: ACOG: How to Tell When Labor Begins
NHS: Signs that labour has begun
NICE NG235: Intrapartum care, recommendations

title: Language development by age
parentQuestions: How many words should my 2 year old say?
whatToKnow: By 12 months babies understand some words and say one or two; between 1 and 2 years two-word combinations appear; by 2 to 3 years phrases are understood by family; by 3 to 4 sentences of 4 or more words.

whatToDo.action: Talk, name things, read, sing, respond to babbling.
Mention concerns if few or no words.

seeClinicianIf: No babbling by 9 months, no words by 16 months, no 2 word phrases by 24 months, any loss of speech, or no response to name or sounds.
evidenceNote: NIDCD opened.

sources.title: NIDCD: Speech and language developmental milestones

title: Late talkers
parentQuestions: My 2 year old barely talks
Should I wait?
whatToKnow: Late talkers are children with fewer words than peers but typical understanding and play. Many catch up, but some have developmental language disorder or hearing problems. A hearing test is part of any evaluation. Waiting is not harmless if comprehension is also delayed.

whatToDo.action: Ask for hearing and speech evaluation if words are few.
Narrate, expand child's words, reduce screens.

seeClinicianIf: Few words at 24 months, no gestures, not understanding simple instructions, regression.
evidenceNote: NIDCD opened for DLD and evaluation advice; 'wait and see' debate is not in this page.

sources.title: NIDCD: Speech and language developmental milestones

title: Lead exposure
parentQuestions: Should my toddler be tested for lead?
whatToKnow: CDC says there is no safe blood lead level in children; low levels still link to learning and behavior effects. Sources: old paint, pipes, soil, some imports and traditional remedies. Hand-to-mouth toddlers are most exposed; testing is by blood test.

whatToDo.action: Wash hands, damp-wipe dust, avoid peeling paint.
Ask the pediatrician about testing if the risk is present.

seeClinicianIf: Known exposure, pica, or developmental delay with possible exposure.
evidenceNote: CDC opened.

sources.title: CDC: About lead prevention

title: Other learning difficulties (math, writing, attention)
parentQuestions: My child is smart but struggles at school
Could it be a learning disability?
whatToKnow: AAP checkups at about 7 include discussion of school progress and following directions, with possible screening for ADHD or learning differences. NHS lists difficulty with numbers, messy writing, and planning schoolwork among dyslexia-related signs, but struggles can also come from vision, hearing, sleep, anxiety, or attention.

whatToDo.action: Ask the teacher which areas are behind and what helps.
Ask the pediatrician about vision, hearing, sleep and attention.

seeClinicianIf: No progress after extra help, or big gaps between ability and results.
evidenceNote: AAP checkup summary and NHS (both opened); parent-level advice.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Your checkup checklist, 7 years old
NHS: Dyslexia

title: Learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic): the myth
parentQuestions: Is my child a visual learner?
Should I teach my child in their learning style?
Is the VAK test useful?
Мой ребёнок аудиал или визуал, как с ним заниматься?
whatToKnow: Pashler and colleagues (2008) reviewed the evidence for the idea that teaching to a person's preferred style (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) improves learning. They found people do have preferences, but no adequate studies showing that matching instruction to style improves outcomes. A later school-based study (Rogowsky 2020) also found that learning-style-based instruction did not improve learning. Good teaching uses several modes for everyone, matched to the content.

whatToDo.action: Mix senses: songs, pictures, movement and real objects for every new idea, not one 'type'.
For letters, numbers and facts, use pictures and words together, retrieval practice (quiz yourself), and spaced review.
Let the child choose how they like to practice, but check by results, not by the label.
Skip paid 'learning style' tests; spend the time reading together.

seeClinicianIf: If a child struggles to learn letters, reading, or numbers, or has trouble hearing or seeing, ask the pediatrician or school about hearing, vision and learning assessment rather than a learning-style label.
evidenceNote: The meshing hypothesis (instruction must match style) lacks supporting evidence in the reviews cited. Preferences exist but do not predict better learning; stating this as 'myth' refers to the instructional claim only.

sources.title: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, Bjork 2008, Learning styles: concepts and evidence, Psychol Sci Public Interest, PubMed
Rogowsky, Calhoun, Tallal 2020, Providing instruction based on students' learning style preferences does not improve learning, Front Psychol, PubMed

title: Low supply worries and cluster feeding
parentQuestions: Am I making enough milk?
Why does the baby feed constantly in the evening?
Do I need to top up?
whatToKnow: NHS signs of enough milk include swallowing you can hear, relaxed feeds, and the baby coming off the breast on their own; frequent feeds are normal and a baby cannot be overfed or spoiled. Introducing bottles can reduce supply. Feeding at least 8 times in 24 hours in the first weeks is a rough guide.

whatToDo.action: Count wet and dirty nappies and watch for swallowing.
Ask a lactation specialist before adding formula.

seeClinicianIf: Seek advice if there are few wet nappies, poor weight gain, a very sleepy baby, or persistent pain.
evidenceNote: NHS; cluster feeding is described in common terms rather than a formal definition.

sources.title: NHS: Is my baby getting enough milk?
NHS: Your breastfeeding questions answered

title: Lying and imagination
parentQuestions: My 4 year old lies all the time
When do children know the difference between truth and fantasy?
whatToKnow: The AAP says under about 6 children often blur fantasy and reality; from about 6 they know when they lie. Reasons include fear of punishment and high expectations. Avoid harsh punishment, talk about honesty, and model it. Chronic lying should be seen by a counselor.

whatToDo.action: Treat tall tales as imagination; gently state the facts.
Respond calmly; reward truth-telling.

seeClinicianIf: Chronic lying or lying with stealing or aggression.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): When children lie
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Emotional development in preschoolers

title: The marshmallow test: waiting, self-control and what it predicts
parentQuestions: Can my 4 year old wait? Does it predict success?
Should I teach my child to delay gratification?
Is the marshmallow test debunked?
Что такое зефирный тест и нужно ли учить ребёнка ждать?
whatToKnow: Mischel's marshmallow studies suggested that preschoolers who waited longer did better as teens. A 2018 conceptual replication (Watts, Duncan, Quan) in a larger, more diverse sample found a correlation half as large as the original, and about one third as large once family background, early cognitive ability and home environment were controlled. Kidd (2013) showed that children wait less when they have learned an adult is unreliable. So waiting reflects both self-control and trust in the environment.

whatToDo.action: Keep small promises you make ('after your bath, a story') so waiting feels safe.
Teach tools for waiting: a sand timer, a distracting song, 'first then' charts.
Practice simple saving or planning goals (a sticker chart for a small toy) and talk about what helped.
Do not use waiting as a character test; if your child grabs now, check how reliable the day has felt.

seeClinicianIf: If a child seems extremely impulsive, cannot wait at all for most daily things, or has very short attention that affects home, kindergarten or school, mention it to the pediatrician. This is not a screening test.
evidenceNote: The replication reduced but did not erase the link; waiting more than 20 seconds mattered most. Reliability findings (Kidd 2013) come from a small experiment (28 children).

sources.title: Watts, Duncan, Quan 2018, Revisiting the marshmallow test: a conceptual replication, Psychol Sci, PubMed
Kidd, Palmeri, Aslin 2013, Rational snacking: wait-times moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability, Cognition, PubMed

title: Math at home
parentQuestions: How do I teach my child math?
My child says 'I hate math'
whatToKnow: AAP tips suggest using daily moments like cooking to practice counting, measuring and following directions. Early math concepts are part of readiness. Relaxed practice and praise for effort help avoid math anxiety.

whatToDo.action: Count steps, set the table, measure ingredients, play board and card games.
Ask them to explain how they got an answer.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent trouble with numbers, time or sequences beyond peers may relate to learning difficulties; ask the teacher.
evidenceNote: Thin: AAP parent tips only.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Ten tips for your child's success in school
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Is your preschooler ready for kindergarten?

title: Meconium and the first stools
parentQuestions: Why is the first poop black and sticky?
What colour changes are normal?
whatToKnow: Meconium is the thick black or dark green first stool, usually passed in the first few days. Stools then turn greenish to yellow in breastfed babies, with at least 2 by days 3 to 4 and 3 to 4 daily by days 5 to 7. Formula-fed stools are tan or yellow and firmer; green is common.

whatToDo.action: Note colour and number of stools.
Expect yellow stools.

seeClinicianIf: Contact a clinician for blood, large amounts of mucus or water in the stool, diarrhea with fever in a baby under 3 months, or a baby who simply seems sick.
evidenceNote: Consistent AAP guidance.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org: Baby's First Days, Bowel Movements and Urination

title: Montessori: what the evidence says
parentQuestions: Is Montessori better than a regular kindergarten?
Does Montessori work for every child?
How do I know a Montessori school is genuine?
Монтессори школа: стоит ли отдавать ребенка?
whatToKnow: The Montessori method, from Maria Montessori in the early 1900s, uses mixed-age classrooms, long uninterrupted work periods, child-chosen activities and special materials. The best evidence comes from a lottery-based study in Hartford (141 children, 2017) and a 2023 Campbell systematic review of 32 studies, which found small to moderate advantages for Montessori in academic and non-academic outcomes (academic composite about 0.24, non-academic about 0.33). Limits: the lottery study was not a true randomized trial, only high-fidelity schools were studied, and the review found some evidence of publication bias and noted that not all studies described how faithfully Montessori was implemented. The name 'Montessori' is not legally protected in many countries, so program quality varies.

whatToDo.action: Visit, watch a work period, check teacher training and accreditation, and ask how long children work without interruption.
Offer a low shelf, a few toys at a time, child-sized tools, and let the child do real tasks (pour, wipe, dress).
Provide choice and long play periods; avoid constant correction.
Do not judge the child's progress against a school brand; ask the teacher for observations of focus, independence and social play.

evidenceNote: Meta-analytic evidence is positive but based mostly on non-randomized studies, with GRADE quality varying by outcome (high for general academic, maths and language; lower for science and some non-academic outcomes).

sources.title: Randolph et al. 2023, Montessori education's impact on academic and nonacademic outcomes: a systematic review, Campbell Systematic Reviews (PMC)
Montessori education's impact on academic and nonacademic outcomes: A systematic review (RePEc record of the Campbell review)
Lillard et al. 2017, Montessori Preschool Elevates and Equalizes Child Outcomes: A Longitudinal Study, Frontiers in Psychology

title: Motor milestones and late walking
parentQuestions: When should a baby walk?
My baby isn't crawling
whatToKnow: Most babies roll by about 6 months, sit by 9, crawl or cruise around 9 to 12, and walk between 9 and 18 months. Walking by 18 months is the usual benchmark. CDC milestones list what most children do by each checkpoint.

whatToDo.action: Use the CDC milestone checklist and share concerns.
Give supervised floor time and tummy time.

seeClinicianIf: Not walking by 18 months, losing a skill, very stiff or floppy, or asymmetry. Ask the pediatrician.
evidenceNote: CDC milestone checkpoints opened; exact walking ages from general knowledge.

sources.title: CDC: Developmental milestones

title: Mouthguards for sports
parentQuestions: Does my child need a mouthguard?
whatToKnow: ADA recommends a properly fitted mouthguard for activities with significant risk of dental or facial injury; users had less than half the injury risk in a 2019 review. Custom, boil-and-bite and stock types exist; the best is the one worn.

whatToDo.action: Wear for contact and collision sports.
Check after growth spurts or tooth loss.

seeClinicianIf: Knocked out tooth or mouth injury: go to a dentist immediately.
evidenceNote: ADA page (opened).

sources.title: ADA: Athletic mouth protectors (mouthguards)

title: Moving house or changing school
parentQuestions: How do I help my child after we move?
Changing schools mid-year
whatToKnow: NHS anxiety advice says prepare children for changes such as moving house and keep routines. AAP friendship advice suggests helping children keep friendships going after a move. Visiting the new school ahead helps.

whatToDo.action: Visit the school and talk about what will stay the same.
Rebuild routines and arrange playdates.

seeClinicianIf: Prolonged withdrawal or school refusal.
evidenceNote: NHS and AAP (opened); thin on moving-specific data.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): What parents can do to support friendships
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Back-to-school tips for families
NHS: Anxiety in children

title: The Mozart effect: does music make babies smarter?
parentQuestions: Does playing Mozart make my baby smarter?
Should I play classical music in pregnancy?
Does music help brain development?
Музыка Моцарта для малышей развивает интеллект?
whatToKnow: In 1993 Rauscher and colleagues reported a short-lived boost in spatial reasoning in college students after listening to a Mozart sonata. The original study used college students, not babies. A 2010 meta-analysis (Pietschnig and colleagues, about 40 studies and over 3,000 participants) found no support for gains specifically from Mozart. A later experiment suggests any brief arousal effect, if it exists, is about sound properties and not Mozart himself. Music is still worthwhile for enjoyment and bonding.

whatToDo.action: Sing, hum and play music you enjoy; babies like voices and rhythm. Keep volume moderate.
Dance, clap, play simple instruments and do action songs together.
If you want lessons, choose for fun and commitment, not as an IQ plan.
Spend 'smart baby' money on books, talking and play instead of special CDs.

evidenceNote: The original finding was small, short-lived and in adults; the 2010 meta-analysis found no Mozart-specific effect. The claim that music or Mozart raises infant intelligence is a popular belief.

sources.title: Rauscher, Shaw, Ky 1993, Music and spatial task performance, Nature (PubMed record, no abstract)
Padulo et al 2020, The effects of music on spatial reasoning, Psychol Res, PubMed

Pietschnig, Voracek, Formann 2010, Mozart effect-Shmozart effect: a meta-analysis, Intelligence (publisher abstract paywalled; findings read from the University of Vienna press release summary on ScienceDaily)

title: Myopia (short-sightedness) and outdoor time
parentQuestions: Will glasses make my child's eyes worse?
How to prevent myopia?
How much time outside is enough?
whatToKnow: NHS says myopia usually starts between 6 and 13 and often runs in families; signs are trouble seeing the board, sitting close to screens, headaches and eye rubbing. NHS recommends outdoor time, which may help stop it worsening. Specially designed lenses may slow progression but are not available on the NHS.

whatToDo.action: Encourage outdoor time, ideally daily.
Get an optician test; free for under 16 in the UK.

seeClinicianIf: Trouble seeing the board, squinting, headaches, or a family history with school-age symptoms.
evidenceNote: NHS says outdoor time may help. Trial reviews (Cochrane 2024) were surfaced in search but the page was blocked, so we did not verify them and do not cite them. Effect size and dose are uncertain.

sources.title: NHS: Short-sightedness (myopia)

title: Morning sickness and severe vomiting
parentQuestions: Is nausea normal and when does it end?
What helps morning sickness?
When is it hyperemesis?
whatToKnow: Nausea and vomiting are very common early on. The NHS suggests small frequent meals, sips of fluid, ginger and acupressure bands, noting limited evidence. A severe form, hyperemesis gravidarum, can lead to dehydration and poor nutrition and may need hospital treatment. Urine infections can also cause nausea.

whatToDo.action: Eat little and often, sip fluid, rest and avoid triggers.

whatToDo.when: If you cannot keep fluids down
whatToDo.action: Contact the midwife or GP the same day.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician if you cannot keep fluids down, are losing weight, have very dark urine, or feel dizzy or faint.
evidenceNote: The NHS gives ginger and acupressure as 'some evidence'; severity warnings are standard.

sources.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms (CDC Hear Her)
Vomiting and morning sickness (NHS)

title: Newborn appearance: milia, baby acne, birthmarks
parentQuestions: Why does my baby have white spots?
Are Mongolian spots a problem?
Why is my baby peeling?
whatToKnow: Milia are tiny white bumps that fade without treatment. Baby acne starts around 2 to 3 weeks and clears within a few weeks. Erythema toxicum is a harmless rash in the first week. Blue-gray Mongolian spots on the lower back usually fade by age 2 to 5, and stork bites fade within about 18 months. Peeling in the first week is normal as the vernix wears off.

whatToDo.action: Skip creams and oils on the spots; wash with water.
Ask the pediatrician to look at birthmarks, especially large moles.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician to check any mole present at birth, and call for fever of 38 C or more or redness, pus or a foul smell at the cord.
evidenceNote: Consistent across medical sources.

sources.title: MedlinePlus: Skin findings in newborns
Caring for Kids (Canadian Paediatric Society): Your baby's skin

title: Bathing a newborn: how often, sponge bath or tub
parentQuestions: How often should I bathe my newborn?
Can I bathe the baby before the cord falls off?
Do I need to boil the water?
Is a daily bath bad for the skin?
whatToKnow: A newborn does not need a bath every day. Washing the face, neck, hands and bottom (topping and tailing) is enough, and a bath a few times a week or daily if the baby enjoys it is also fine. Water should be warm, not hot, checked with wrist or elbow, and the baby is never left alone in it, not even for a second.

whatToDo.action: Top and tail with warm water and cotton wool, using a fresh piece for each eye and wiping from the nose outward. Dry the skin folds well.
Run cold water first, then hot, mix it, test with wrist or elbow, keep the head clear of the water, and empty the bath right after.
Avoid bathing right after a feed or when the baby is hungry or tired. Keep the room warm and have towels and a clean nappy within reach.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician or nurse if the skin is cracked, weeping or very dry after baths, or if the cord stump looks red, smells or oozes.
evidenceNote: NHS guidance. Bath frequency is a comfort and skin question, not a safety one; there is no evidence that daily bathing is needed for health.

sources.title: NHS: Washing and bathing your baby
NHS: Nappy rash

title: Newborn blood spot (heel prick) screening
parentQuestions: What does the heel prick test for?
When do we get results?
What if the test is repeated?
whatToKnow: A few drops of blood from the heel are collected on a card, usually at about day 5 in the UK, to look for rare but serious conditions such as cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, hypothyroidism and some metabolic diseases. A normal result usually arrives by about 6 weeks. A repeat sample is common and often unrelated to any problem.

whatToDo.action: Attend or request the test; hold and feed the baby during it.
If you have heard nothing, contact the midwife or doctor.

seeClinicianIf: Return promptly if you are called back for a repeat sample or a specialist visit.
evidenceNote: National programmes differ in which conditions are included.

sources.title: NHS: Newborn blood spot test

title: Newborn hearing screening
parentQuestions: Does my baby need a hearing test?
What does a 'refer' result mean?
whatToKnow: A hearing screen is offered to all babies, usually before 4 weeks and up to 3 months, using a soft earpiece and gentle clicks while the baby is calm or asleep. A clear result makes hearing loss unlikely but does not exclude later loss. If the result is not clear, an audiology appointment is arranged, ideally within about 4 weeks.

whatToDo.action: Have the screen done.
Mention any hearing worries even after a pass.

seeClinicianIf: Raise it if the baby does not react to loud sounds, or if there is family history of childhood deafness.
evidenceNote: UK NHS programme described; schedules differ by country.

sources.title: NHS: Newborn hearing test

title: Newborn jaundice: normal and when to worry
parentQuestions: My baby looks yellow, is that normal?
How long does jaundice last?
Should I put the baby in the sun?
Why is my baby yellow?
When is jaundice dangerous?
whatToKnow: Newborn jaundice is common and usually harmless. It is most visible around day 3 and usually clears in about 2 weeks. Feeding 8 to 12 times a day helps. Call for same day review if yellow after 24 hours, getting worse, or dark pee or pale poo.

whatToDo.action: Check skin and eyes in daylight and keep feeding often.
Contact the midwife or pediatrician the same day.
Check skin and eyes in daylight; feed 8 to 12 times a day.
Ask whether bilirubin was checked.

seeClinicianIf: Emergency care if jaundice comes with sleepiness, not feeding, floppiness, fever, no wet nappies or breathing trouble, or in a baby under 24 hours old.
evidenceNote: NHS guidance. Sun exposure is not a proven treatment.

sources.title: NHS: Jaundice in babies

title: Trimming a newborn's nails
parentQuestions: How do I cut my newborn's nails without hurting them?
How often do newborn nails need cutting?
Can I bite my baby's nails off?
whatToKnow: Newborn fingernails grow fast and are sharp enough to scratch the face. Toenails grow slowly and are soft, so they can look ingrown without being a problem. AAP advises against biting the nails off because it can cause a skin infection.

whatToDo.action: Trim after a bath, when baby is calm, or while asleep. Push the skin at the fingertip back and away from the nail first, and keep nails short and smooth. In the first weeks this may be about twice a week.
Use a soft emery board, baby nail clippers, or blunt-nosed scissors, and take extra care with clippers and scissors. Do not bite the nails.
Toenails need less often: once or twice a month is usually enough, and they do not need to be cut as short as fingernails.

seeClinicianIf: Call the pediatrician if the skin beside a nail becomes red, swollen or hard, or if there is pus. The AAP page does not say what to do for a nick that bleeds, so ask your pediatrician about that.
evidenceNote: One AAP HealthyChildren page; practical advice, no trial evidence. The NHS page we opened on newborn care did not cover nails.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How to Cut Your Baby's Nails Safely

title: Newborn red flags: when to get help now
parentQuestions: When should I call the doctor right away?
Is my baby breathing too fast?
What are danger signs in a newborn?
whatToKnow: NHS lists signs needing immediate help: fast or hard breathing (grunting, sucking in tummy), blue, grey or mottled skin, cold clammy skin, a rash that does not fade when pressed, a weak, high pitched or continuous cry, being hard to wake, a seizure, or no wet nappy for 12 hours. Fever of 38 C or higher under 3 months is also an urgent sign.

whatToDo.action: Call emergency services or go to emergency care now.
A baby not interested in feeds, floppy or very sleepy needs same day evaluation.

seeClinicianIf: This is the red flag list itself; trust your instinct and seek care.
evidenceNote: NHS guidance; local emergency numbers differ.

title: Newborn reflexes
parentQuestions: Why does my baby startle?
When do reflexes disappear?
whatToKnow: Rooting fades by about 4 months, Moro startle by about 2 months, stepping by about 2 months, palmar grasp around 5 to 6 months and plantar grasp at 9 to 12 months. Timing varies by baby.

whatToDo.action: Mention anything that looks different on one side.
Gentle handling; swaddling is a choice and is covered elsewhere.

seeClinicianIf: Tell the pediatrician if the Moro or tonic neck reflex looks different on one side or one side moves better than the other.
evidenceNote: AAP gives consistent timelines.

title: What newborns can see and hear
parentQuestions: How well can my newborn see?
Does my baby recognise my voice?
whatToKnow: Newborns see best at about 20 to 30 cm, color vision develops around 4 to 6 months, and by 2 months babies follow moving objects and prefer faces. Hearing is fully developed at birth and newborns prefer human voices.

whatToDo.action: Hold the baby at face distance and talk and sing.
Ask about vision and hearing.

seeClinicianIf: Mention any worry about vision or hearing at checkups.
evidenceNote: MedlinePlus summary; no controversy.

title: Newborn skin: cradle cap, eczema, dry skin
parentQuestions: What is cradle cap?
Is this eczema?
Should I moisturize every day?
whatToKnow: Cradle cap is a harmless greasy, scaly scalp rash common in babies that usually clears on its own. Atopic eczema often starts in babies and young children with dry, itchy patches, commonly on the face in young infants. Flare-ups come and go.

whatToDo.action: Wash gently and soften scales with a baby-safe oil if you wish; do not pick.
Keep skin moisturized with a fragrance free emollient and ask a clinician about itchy patches.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician if the rash is weeping, crusted, spreading, painful, or the baby is unwell or has a fever.
evidenceNote: NHS pages describe both conditions; details on treatment belong with the clinician.

NHS: Atopic eczema

title: Newborn sleep patterns and night and day
parentQuestions: How much should a newborn sleep?
Why is my baby awake all night?
When will she sleep through?
whatToKnow: Newborns often sleep about 18 hours a day in short stretches, waking to feed. Helping the baby learn day from night means bright and normal noise by day and dim, quiet, minimal talking at night. By 3 to 6 months some sleep 5 to 8 hours at night, but not all.

whatToDo.action: Open curtains and do not mute the house.
Keep lights low and handling brief.

seeClinicianIf: Contact the pediatrician for very hard to wake, poor feeding or fever.
evidenceNote: NHS; individual variation is large.

sources.title: NHS: Helping your baby to sleep

title: Newborn weight loss and regaining birth weight
parentQuestions: Is it normal for my baby to lose weight?
When should birth weight be regained?
whatToKnow: A well-fed newborn may lose up to about 8 to 10% of birth weight in the first few days, then gain; the AAP page does not say by which day birth weight should return, so ask your pediatrician. By day 5 to 7 expect at least 6 wet nappies and yellow stools.

whatToDo.action: Count wet and dirty nappies and feeds.
Have a weight check.

seeClinicianIf: Call if the baby is losing steadily, is very sleepy or has few wet nappies.
evidenceNote: The AAP page gives the 8 to 10% figure; some UK guidelines suggest earlier review.

title: NICU stay: your role and your feelings
parentQuestions: What can I do for my baby in the NICU?
I feel guilty and angry, is that normal?
Can I be present during procedures?
whatToKnow: AAP says parents commonly feel fear, anger, guilt, loss, powerlessness and sometimes feel on display in a shared room. These feelings can come back for years. Parents can learn care tasks such as diapering, taking a temperature and bathing, and AAP says that sometimes taking part is simply being there. Many NICUs let parents attend some procedures, and in teaching hospitals you may be asked to step out during complex ones.

whatToDo.action: Tell the nurse when you are ready to start hands-on care, and ask about feeding times and when your baby is most awake.
Talk with your partner, the NICU team, and other NICU parents; ask what parent support the unit offers.

whatToDo.when: If you want to attend a procedure
whatToDo.action: Tell the staff in advance and say if you feel faint or upset.

seeClinicianIf: If low mood, panic, or intrusive fear lasts or gets in the way of eating, sleeping, or caring for your baby, tell the NICU team or your own clinician. See the postpartum depression topic.
evidenceNote: The AAP pages describe common reactions and advice; they are professional guidance and not a measured trial. Visiting rules differ by hospital, and we opened no page on visiting hours.

HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How You Can Participate in the Care of Your Baby in the NICU

title: Night terrors and nightmares
parentQuestions: My child screams at night but is asleep
What is the difference between nightmares and night terrors?
whatToKnow: NHS says night terrors are most common between about 3 and 8. During one, stay nearby and let it pass; do not wake or restrain unless unsafe. Waking the child about 15 minutes before the usual time for 2 weeks may help. See a GP if nightmares continue after 6, if terrors start after 5 or continue after 12.

whatToDo.action: Stay calm and keep the child safe.
Keep consistent bedtimes and reduce stress.

seeClinicianIf: Nightmares after 6 years, terrors starting after 5, or after 12, or when they harm daytime life.
evidenceNote: NHS (opened).

sources.title: NHS: Night terrors and nightmares

title: NIPT: the blood test for Down syndrome and other conditions
parentQuestions: What is NIPT and how accurate is it?
Is NIPT a diagnosis?
Should I do NIPT or the combined test?
whatToKnow: NIPT, or cell-free DNA testing, analyses fetal DNA fragments in the mother's blood from early in the second trimester onward (the large US laboratory series averaged 15 weeks). A meta-analysis found detection of Down syndrome around 99.7 percent with a false positive rate of about 0.04 percent in the studied groups. Large laboratory data show high positive predictive value for trisomy 21 but lower for trisomy 13 and sex chromosome results. It is a screening test: a positive result needs confirmation by a diagnostic test such as amniocentesis.

whatToDo.action: Ask what the test covers and whether it is free or paid in your area.
Ask for a diagnostic test and genetic counselling before any decision.

seeClinicianIf: Ask promptly for follow up if a result is positive, unclear or could not be reported.
evidenceNote: Strong performance data for trisomy 21; predictive value depends on how common the condition is. Offered as a first line or follow up depending on country, so access varies.

title: Nosebleeds in children
parentQuestions: How do I stop my child's nosebleed?
Should my child lean back?
When is a nosebleed serious?
whatToKnow: Nosebleeds are common in children and usually not serious. NHS says to sit down, lean forward with the mouth open, pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils for 10 to 15 minutes, and breathe through the mouth. Common causes are picking, blowing hard and dry air. For 24 hours afterwards avoid blowing or picking the nose, hot drinks and strenuous play.

whatToDo.action: Sit upright, lean forward, pinch for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to check, breathe through the mouth.
Avoid nose blowing, picking, hot drinks and rough play for 24 hours.
Mention frequent nosebleeds to the doctor.

seeClinicianIf: Go to the ER or call your local emergency number if bleeding lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes, seems excessive, started after a blow to the head, the child swallows so much blood that they vomit, is weak or dizzy, or has trouble breathing (NHS). See a doctor for any nosebleed in a child under 2, or for regular nosebleeds. Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen for the emergency signs.
evidenceNote: Single official page (NHS, last reviewed December 2023). NHS notes the evidence for an ice pack is not strong.

sources.title: NHS: Nosebleed

title: Nutrition at school and packed lunches
parentQuestions: What should my child eat at school?
How much sugar is too much?
whatToKnow: The AAP says serve a variety from the five food groups, include fiber, choose lean protein, limit sugary foods and drinks and salt, and favor unsaturated fats. The AAP checkup list asks about school meals, packed lunches and water.

whatToDo.action: Breakfast, a vegetable or fruit at every meal, water.
Plan snacks to avoid sweets replacing fruit.

seeClinicianIf: Picky eating with weight loss, constant hunger, or food refusal.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Your checkup checklist, 7 years old

title: Preparing an older child for a new baby, and jealousy in the first weeks
parentQuestions: How do I prepare my toddler for a new baby?
My older child is jealous and acting like a baby again, is that normal?
How do I keep my first child from feeling pushed out after the birth?
whatToKnow: Jealousy and some backsliding (toileting accidents, asking for a bottle, baby talk) are common after a sibling arrives; AAP says children do it to check they still have your attention. Children who are included in the preparation tend to feel less left out, and even school-aged children can resent the attention the baby gets. Honest, simple explanations work better than promises that the baby will be fun right away.

whatToDo.action: Talk about the baby early and often, read picture books about new siblings, let a preschooler help shop or care for a doll, and say plainly that babies cry and need a lot of care. Explain the hospital stay in simple terms, including when you will be back.
If you can, avoid big changes such as potty training or moving to a bed right around the due date.

Give the older child a real job (helping at bath or feeding time), let them snuggle beside you during feeds, and ask visitors to spend time with them. Let your partner or another relative take them out one-on-one.
Set aside a short daily one-on-one time for reading, play or talk. If they backslide, answer with patience instead of 'act your age' and praise grown-up behavior when it appears.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if regression or distress is intense, lasts for many weeks, or comes with aggression toward the baby that you cannot keep safe, or with sleep, eating or mood changes that do not settle.
evidenceNote: The AAP HealthyChildren page gives this practical advice; it is expert guidance rather than trial evidence.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Preparing Your Family for a New Baby

title: Online gaming and online safety
parentQuestions: Is Roblox safe?
Who is my child talking to online?
How do I talk about online strangers?
whatToKnow: The AAP advises talking before they play (who they can play with, no personal info, how to block and tell you), using parental controls, disabling voice or text chat when needed, keeping devices in shared rooms, playing with them, and setting time limits. Choosing games with limited communication helps for younger children.

whatToDo.action: Set rules and settings together.
Ask what they played and who with.

seeClinicianIf: Secrecy, requests for money or photos, bullying, or sudden mood change after play.
evidenceNote: AAP online-games guidance (opened).

title: Open bite and crossbite: what they are
parentQuestions: What is an open bite?
Crossbite in a toddler: serious?
whatToKnow: Open bite means the front teeth do not meet; posterior crossbite means upper back teeth sit inside the lower ones. Prolonged pacifier or thumb sucking is a recognised cause; AAPD notes an anterior open bite from pacifier use often improves if it stops before age 3. Mouth breathing and tongue habits can contribute.

whatToDo.action: If a habit is present, stop or limit it, then recheck the bite.
Ask 'is the bite developing normally?'

seeClinicianIf: Teeth that do not meet at the front, jaw shifting sideways when closing, or persistent mouth breathing: ask the dentist for an orthodontic opinion.
evidenceNote: AAPD policy opened; treatment timing varies between orthodontists.

sources.title: AAPD: Policy on Pacifiers (2024 revision, Reference Manual 2026)

title: Orthodontic check by age 7
parentQuestions: When should my child see an orthodontist?
Do I need braces?
whatToKnow: The AAO recommends a first orthodontic check-up by age 7, when children have a mix of baby and permanent teeth and the orthodontist can advise whether and when to treat. If something looks off earlier do not wait. Treatment at 7 is not common.

whatToDo.action: Book an exam if there are crowding, bite or jaw concerns.
See sooner for crossbite or thumb sucking.
Ask the dentist to look at bite and habits.
Book an orthodontic screening, earlier if signs appear.

seeClinicianIf: Crowding, bite problems, early or late loss of teeth, mouth breathing, thumb sucking.
evidenceNote: AAO recommendation (opened). Whether routine early checks change outcomes is debated among clinicians, not examined here.

title: Pacifiers and SIDS, and breastfeeding
parentQuestions: Is a pacifier bad?
Will it hurt breastfeeding?
When can I offer one?
Does a pacifier ruin teeth?
When should my toddler stop the dummy?
whatToKnow: CDC advises offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime, and if breastfeeding you may wait until it is well established. NHS says some research suggests a dummy may lower SIDS risk. If the baby refuses, do not force it.

whatToDo.action: Offer one at naps and bedtime if you choose to.
Do not hang it around the neck.
Use at naps and bedtime if it helps; clean it and never dip it in sweet things.
Start limiting to sleep only.
Aim to stop; if still using it ask the dentist to check the bite.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a clinician about breastfeeding concerns before introducing it.
evidenceNote: The SIDS link is observational; breastfeeding effects differ between studies.

title: Pain relief options in labor: an overview
parentQuestions: What are my pain relief options?
Gas and air or epidural?
Do I have to decide in advance?
What are the side effects?
Should I have an epidural?
Is water birth safe?
What other pain relief exists?
whatToKnow: The NHS lists self-help (learning, breathing, movement, partner, bath, paracetamol), gas and air, pethidine or diamorphine injections, and epidural; options vary by place of birth. A Cochrane overview found epidural and inhaled analgesia effectively relieve pain but have side effects (epidural: more instrumental births; inhaled: nausea and dizziness), while most non-drug methods look safe but have unclear effectiveness. WHO recommends epidural and opioids for women who ask for pain relief, and relaxation and manual methods, depending on preferences. Detailed epidural evidence is not repeated here.

whatToDo.action: Read the options, ask which are available at your hospital and whether an anesthetist is always on site.
Write your first, second and third choices in your plan and share with your partner.
Reassess often; changing your mind is normal.
Learn the options and talk through your preferences.
Ask early if you want an epidural, since it takes time to set up.

seeClinicianIf: Pain feels out of control, you have a fever, or contractions are constant with no break: tell the midwife.
evidenceNote: Cochrane and WHO agree on the strength of drug methods and uncertainty for non-drug methods; choice depends on preference.

title: Parents' own wellbeing
parentQuestions: I am exhausted and angry
How do I look after myself?
whatToKnow: NHS notes that children pick up parents' anxiety and advises not becoming overprotective. The AAP says how parents adjust after divorce affects children and that modeling seeking support helps. We did not open a dedicated parental mental health page.

whatToDo.action: Plan rest, one outlet, and a person to talk to.
See a GP if low mood or anxiety lasts.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent low mood, anxiety, anger you cannot control, or thoughts of self-harm.
evidenceNote: Thin: NHS and AAP pages only (opened).

title: Parents as role models
parentQuestions: Do kids copy me?
How should I behave around my kids?
whatToKnow: The AAP says children copy how parents handle anger, and kids notice white lies. The family media plan page says make a plan for everyone, including adults, and put phones away at meals and bedtime.

whatToDo.action: Choose one habit to model (calm voice, phones away).
Repair after mistakes.

evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

title: Parenting styles: authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, neglectful
parentQuestions: Am I too strict or too soft?
What is authoritative parenting?
Is spanking ever okay according to doctors?
Какой стиль воспитания самый правильный: авторитарный или либеральный?
whatToKnow: Baumrind described authoritative, authoritarian and permissive styles; Maccoby and Martin crossed warmth (responsiveness) with control (demandingness) and added the neglectful or uninvolved style. A very large meta-analysis links authoritative parenting with fewer behavior problems and harsh control with more. Effects are small to moderate and these are associations, not proof of cause, because children's temperament also shapes parents. The AAP (2018) advises against spanking and harsh verbal discipline.

whatToDo.action: Use short, consistent rules with warmth: explain once, redirect, praise what went right. Avoid hitting and shouting as teaching tools.
Give reasons for rules in a sentence, allow small choices, and keep consequences predictable and brief.
Involve the child in setting family rules, listen to objections, and keep the final decision with you on safety and health.
Notice which style you slip into when tired, and plan the exact words you want to use next time.
If you were raised strictly and want to do differently, pick one situation (bedtime, screens) and rehearse a calmer response.

seeClinicianIf: Talk to the pediatrician or a counselor if discipline at home often becomes physical, if you fear harming your child, or if a child is aggressive, withdrawn or fearful in ways that worry you. If you or the child are in danger, call local emergency services.
evidenceNote: Meta-analyses (Pinquart 2017; Gershoff and Grogan-Kaylor 2016 on spanking) support the pattern, with small effects and mostly correlational designs. The AAP 2018 statement is a guideline against corporal punishment. Style labels fit some cultures poorly and effect sizes vary by culture.

title: Feelings about leaving your baby, and sharing the load
parentQuestions: Why do I feel so guilty going back to work?
Is it normal that drop-off is harder for me than for my baby?
How do we split childcare duties as a couple?
whatToKnow: The AAP says starting child care is often harder on the parents than on the child, and that babies up to about 7 months usually adjust well to good, consistent care. The AAP leave page links paid leave to fewer cases of postpartum depression and better relationships between spouses, and supports leave for both parents equally. We found no opened AAP, NHS or APA page on guilt or on how couples should divide the load, so this topic does not give figures or a formula.

whatToDo.action: Say out loud with your partner who does drop-off, pickup, sick days and night wakings, and revisit it after a few weeks.
Use a short goodbye routine; the AAP describes this as helping the child, and it gives parents something to do too.
Mention it to your own clinician; see the postpartum topics.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent low mood, anxiety or loss of interest should be raised with a clinician promptly. For thoughts of harming yourself or your child, call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the ER, and use the app's fixed Urgent help screen.

title: The partner's role during pregnancy
parentQuestions: How can I support my pregnant partner?
Can fathers get depressed too?
What should I do at visits?
whatToKnow: A meta-analysis of 43 studies found about 10 percent of fathers have depression between the first trimester and the first postpartum year, with a rise at 3 to 6 months after birth and a moderate link with the mother's depression. The NHS tells birthing partners to attend classes, learn the birth plan and keep their own energy up. Practical help, listening and attending visits are all useful roles.

whatToDo.action: Go to visits, classes and talk about fears and the plan.
Check in on your own mood and sleep too.

seeClinicianIf: Partners should talk to a doctor if low mood, anger or anxiety lasts more than 2 weeks.
evidenceNote: The meta-analysis is robust but shows wide variation in rates; NHS advice is practical and not trial based.

parentQuestions: Can dads get depression after the baby?
I feel detached, is that normal?
whatToKnow: NHS notes that fathers and partners can also have depression after the birth, and the same symptoms and the same routes to help apply.

whatToDo.action: Share duties and rest.
Speak to a GP.

title: Losing baby teeth and permanent teeth
parentQuestions: When do kids lose baby teeth?
Why is my child's adult tooth coming behind the baby tooth?
whatToKnow: The AAP says front teeth start to loosen at about age 6, molars are shed at 10 to 12, and most baby teeth are replaced by about 13. First permanent molars come in behind the baby molars at about age 6, which is commonly taught but not stated on the pages we opened. ADA says all 32 permanent teeth have usually erupted by 21.

whatToDo.action: Brush well around new molars.
Let them fall out on their own; call the dentist if not loosening.

seeClinicianIf: Toothache, swelling, baby tooth not loosening when the adult tooth appears, or late eruption.

parentQuestions: Can the dog stay?
Is the cat dangerous for the baby?
whatToKnow: CDC advises washing hands after touching pets or their supplies, supervising young children with animals, and keeping hands and objects away from mouths. Children under 5 and pregnant women are at higher risk of some animal diseases. The page does not give a newborn introduction plan.

whatToDo.action: Wash hands after pet contact.
Never leave a baby alone with an animal.

parentQuestions: How much exercise does my child need?
whatToKnow: CDC says ages 3 to 5 should be active throughout the day through play; ages 6 to 17 need at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily, with vigorous activity, muscle strengthening and bone strengthening on at least 3 days a week.

whatToDo.action: Outdoor play, walking to school, active games.
Include running, jumping and climbing.

title: Piaget's stages of thinking and what later research changed
parentQuestions: Why does my 4-year-old think the taller glass has more juice?
When does a baby understand that hidden things still exist?
Is my child 'behind' Piaget's stages?
Стадии развития мышления по Пиаже: что это значит для моего ребенка?
What can a 5 year old actually understand?
Why does my child not get that the amount stays the same?
Are Piaget's stages still used?
whatToKnow: Piaget described sensorimotor (birth to about 2), preoperational (2 to 7) and concrete operational (7 to 11) thinking. His observations of how children reason are still useful descriptions, for example that young children focus on one feature and struggle with conservation tasks. Later research revised him: infants show signs of expecting hidden objects to still exist well before the 8 to 9 months he reported, partly because his tasks required reaching, and task wording can hide what preschoolers understand. Stages are now seen as less rigid and more varied across domains and cultures.

whatToDo.action: Play peekaboo and hide a toy under a cloth; it is fun and practises the idea that things persist.
Offer hands-on play, pretend play and many 'why' conversations; do not expect logical conservation or another person's viewpoint yet.
Let children pour, measure and compare real things; ask 'how do you know?' and accept wrong answers as information.
Move from concrete to simple reasoning with games, sorting, early maths with objects, and short experiments.
Explain simply and concretely; expect strange logic (the moon follows us) and repeat explanations.
Use hands-on examples for math and science before abstract rules.

seeClinicianIf: Your child is losing skills they already had, or you have persistent concerns about language, understanding or play at any age; raise these with the pediatrician rather than comparing with stage charts.
evidenceNote: Piaget's stage model is a historical framework that shaped education; core observations are robust but the claimed ages, fixed order and universal stages have been revised. Infant looking-time studies are informative but their interpretation is still debated.

sources.title: CDC: Positive parenting tips, preschoolers 3 to 5 years
Piaget's Theory and Stages of Cognitive Development (Simply Psychology)
Margoni, Surian & Baillargeon 2024, The violation-of-expectation paradigm: a conceptual overview, Psychological Review

title: Picky eating and food refusal
parentQuestions: My toddler only eats pasta
Should I force vegetables?
whatToKnow: Food refusal is common and usually normal in toddlers and preschoolers. Repeated exposure (AAP says 10 or more tries), eating together, and no pressure work better than forcing or bribing. Growth tracks stay the key check.

whatToDo.action: Offer one safe food plus new ones, no pressure, eat together.
Keep to regular meal and snack times.

seeClinicianIf: Weight falling across percentiles, gagging with all textures, very restricted diet under 10 foods, or choking fears.
evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance recommends repeated exposure, no pressure, no bribes, one family meal, and calling the pediatrician if concerned about nutrition. This is guidance from an official body, not a formal clinical guideline, and I did not open trials behind it.

sources.title: 10 Tips for Parents of Picky Eaters (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)

title: Pink eye (conjunctivitis) in children
parentQuestions: My child's eye is red and sticky, is it pink eye?
Does pink eye need antibiotic drops?
Can my child go to school with pink eye?
whatToKnow: NHS says conjunctivitis is caused by infection or allergy and usually gets better in a couple of weeks without treatment. Eyes are red, gritty or itchy, and may water or produce sticky pus. Antibiotics are only prescribed if it is bacterial and do not work for viral or allergic types. For treatment of a child under 2 years old, NHS says a prescription from a GP is needed.

whatToDo.action: Gently wipe crusts from lashes with cooled boiled water and a clean cotton pad, one pad per eye. A cool flannel can soothe.
Wash hands, do not share towels or pillows, wash pillowcases and face cloths hot, and try not to rub the eyes.
NHS says no need to stay away unless the child feels very unwell.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says see a GP for red, sticky eyes in a baby, and get an urgent appointment if the baby is under 30 days old. Get urgent advice for eye pain, sensitivity to light, changes in vision or very red eyes. Ask for help if it has not cleared within 7 days.
evidenceNote: NHS gives this advice. A newborn with sticky eyes is treated as urgent on the same page.

sources.title: NHS: Conjunctivitis
NHS: Is my child too ill for school?

title: Play and toys
parentQuestions: What toys are best?
whatToKnow: Babies and toddlers learn best through play with caregivers; simple toys like blocks, balls, stacking cups and everyday objects work as well as expensive ones. Free play and being outside matter more than 'educational' devices.

whatToDo.action: Floor play, outdoor play, pretend play with you.
Choose few open-ended toys; rotate them.

evidenceNote: General developmental research; NHS play page opened but gave only links.

sources.title: NHS: Vitamins for children

title: Poisoning and medicines
parentQuestions: My child swallowed something
whatToKnow: Toddlers swallow whatever is within reach: medicines, cleaning products, laundry pods, button batteries, and cosmetics. Keep them locked and in original containers; save the poison control number.

whatToDo.action: Lock away and keep original packaging.
Call poison centre immediately; do not induce vomiting.

seeClinicianIf: Any suspected ingestion.
evidenceNote: AAP and CPSC recommend locked storage, original child-resistant containers, sealing laundry packets and keeping button batteries out of reach. AAP says do not induce vomiting. The US Poison Help number is 1-800-222-1222; Kazakhstan parents need the local poison center and emergency number instead.

sources.title: Childproofing Your Home for Poisons (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
Poison Prevention (CPSC)

title: Poisoning: what to do right now
parentQuestions: My child swallowed something, what do I do?
Should I make them vomit?
Who do I call for poisoning?
whatToKnow: Act quickly even if the child seems fine, because symptoms of poisoning may take hours or days to appear (NHS). Find out what was swallowed, when and how much, and keep the packaging. NHS and St John Ambulance both say do not make the child vomit and do not give anything to eat or drink. Poison Control (US) lists a poison center number, 1-800-222-1222, and an online tool.

whatToDo.action: Take the child away from the substance, check they are awake and breathing, and look for the container or packaging.
Call your local emergency number if the child is drowsy, has trouble breathing, has a seizure or is unresponsive. For other cases call your poison center or doctor.
Do not induce vomiting, give nothing to eat or drink, and if the child vomits save some in a container. Bring the packaging to the hospital.

seeClinicianIf: Call your local emergency number or go to the ER if the child is unconscious, has stopped breathing, has severe trouble breathing, has a seizure, or if you think a child has swallowed, touched or breathed in something harmful (NHS). Open the app's fixed Urgent help screen. In the US call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. We did not open a Kazakhstan poison line page, so the app must show a local number.
evidenceNote: NHS and St John Ambulance agree. The Poison Control number is taken from the opened Poison Control battery page.

sources.title: NHS: Poisoning
St John Ambulance: Poisoning
Poison Control (National Capital Poison Center): Swallowed a button battery?

title: Postpartum depression and anxiety
parentQuestions: Is this baby blues or depression?
Can I be anxious not sad?
How do I get help?
whatToKnow: NHS describes postnatal depression as common and treatable, with low mood, loss of enjoyment, hopelessness, guilt, anxiety, irritability and sleep problems. Baby blues usually go within 2 weeks, so lasting or worsening symptoms need help. The EPDS questionnaire is widely used by clinicians for screening, but a score is never a diagnosis.

whatToDo.action: Tell a partner, midwife or doctor how you feel.
Use the postnatal check to raise mood.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician if symptoms last past 2 weeks, worsen, or you have thoughts of harming yourself or the baby; seek urgent help immediately.
evidenceNote: NHS. I could not open a usable EPDS source, so EPDS cutoffs are intentionally left out.

sources.title: NHS: Postnatal depression

title: Postpartum physical recovery after vaginal birth or cesarean
parentQuestions: How long does recovery take?
Is the separation in my belly normal?
When can I drive after a cesarean?
whatToKnow: Recovery varies. After a caesarean most women go home in 1 to 2 days and may avoid driving until the 6 week check. The two stomach muscles often separate by about two finger widths and usually close by about 8 weeks. Pelvic floor exercises help a leaky bladder or heaviness, and back pain can be eased with exercises.

whatToDo.action: Rest, pelvic floor exercises, gentle activity.
Attend the postnatal check and list concerns.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician for leaking urine that persists, heaviness in the vagina, severe pain, heavy bleeding, fever, or wound problems.
evidenceNote: NHS pages; recovery times are ranges.

sources.title: NHS: Your post-pregnancy body
NHS: Caesarean section, recovery
NHS: Your 6-week postnatal check

title: Postpartum psychosis: a medical emergency
parentQuestions: What is postpartum psychosis?
Is it the baby blues?
whatToKnow: NHS says postpartum psychosis is a serious illness affecting about 1 in 1,000 mothers soon after birth, very different from baby blues, and a medical emergency.

whatToDo.action: Seek emergency help if confusion, hallucinations or extreme mood changes appear.

seeClinicianIf: Seek emergency help immediately.
evidenceNote: NHS.

sources.title: NHS: Postpartum psychosis

title: Postpartum warning signs: urgent maternal symptoms
parentQuestions: What bleeding is too much?
Is a headache after birth dangerous?
When should I go to emergency?
whatToKnow: CDC Hear Her lists urgent warning signs that apply during pregnancy and up to a year after birth: severe or persistent headache, vision changes, fever of 38 C or higher, chest pain, trouble breathing, heavy bleeding or large clots, foul smelling discharge, severe belly pain, leg swelling and pain, severe swelling of hands or face, and thoughts of self harm. Tell clinicians you recently gave birth.

whatToDo.action: Seek medical care immediately.
Call your clinician and keep describing the problem until heard.

seeClinicianIf: This topic is the red flag list; do not wait for the 6 week check.
evidenceNote: CDC list; its postpartum-specific timeframes vary by sign.

sources.title: CDC Hear Her: Urgent maternal warning signs

title: Potty training: readiness and methods
parentQuestions: When should I start potty training?
Can I train at 1 year?
whatToKnow: Most children start between 21 and 36 months; only about 40 to 60 percent finish by 36 months. The child-oriented method (AAP draws on Brazelton) waits for readiness; intensive early methods work in small studies but no head-to-head trial exists. Pressure can cause stool refusal and constipation.

whatToDo.action: Stays dry 2 hours, shows interest, follows simple instructions, tells you.
Praise success; keep accidents neutral.

seeClinicianIf: Pain with stooling, hiding to poop, stool refusal over weeks, or still wet by day after 4.
evidenceNote: AAP guidance: US training usually starts between 2 and 3 and most children are trained by 4; start on readiness signs and avoid power struggles. Mott 2025 poll gives parent experience data.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
AAFP American Family Physician: Toilet Training (2008)
Navigating the path to potty training (Mott Poll, 2025)

title: Self-esteem and praise
parentQuestions: How do I build confidence?
My child says nobody likes him
How should I praise my toddler?
whatToKnow: The AAP lists signs of low self-esteem such as avoiding tasks, lying or cheating when losing, bossiness, harsh self-criticism or withdrawal. It advises time together on activities without winners and losers, listening, age-appropriate decisions, and saying 'I love you' unconditionally.

whatToDo.action: Ten minutes of one-on-one time.
Praise effort, not only outcome.
Name the specific behavior you liked.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent low mood, withdrawal or falling grades.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

title: Depression and anxiety in pregnancy
parentQuestions: Is it normal to feel anxious or sad in pregnancy?
Can I get depression before the baby arrives?
What help is available?
whatToKnow: Depression and anxiety can appear during pregnancy, not only after birth, and some people have them for the first time. The USPSTF found convincing evidence that counselling such as cognitive behavioural therapy prevents perinatal depression in people at higher risk, and it estimates up to 1 in 7 women are affected. The NHS suggests talking to a midwife or GP and says antenatal classes, exercise and talking can help.

whatToDo.action: Tell the midwife how you are feeling.

whatToDo.when: If low mood lasts more than 2 weeks
whatToDo.action: Ask for a mental health assessment and talk therapy.

seeClinicianIf: Seek help the same day for thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, severe hopelessness or panic.
evidenceNote: USPSTF and NHS agree; access to therapy varies widely.

sources.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms (CDC Hear Her)
Mental health in pregnancy (NHS)
Interventions to prevent perinatal depression: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement (JAMA 2019, via Europe PMC)

title: Pretend play and war games
parentQuestions: My son plays with toy guns, should I worry?
Is pretend fighting normal?
whatToKnow: The AAP says pretend violence like 'bang, bang' at age four is typically a competitive, confidence-building outlet, not aggression. Parents can join pretend play to help work through feelings, letting the child control the story.

whatToDo.action: Set limits for real hurting; allow pretend play.
Suggest scenarios and follow their lead.

seeClinicianIf: Pretend play that is rigid, repeated trauma themes, or real harm to others.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).
