HealthyChildren.org (AAP): The power of play

title: Vaccines for a premature baby
parentQuestions: Does a premature baby get vaccines at the usual time?
Does a low birth weight baby need a different hepatitis B plan?
What about RSV protection for a preemie?
whatToKnow: The CDC schedule notes mention prematurity in a few places. For hepatitis B, babies under 2,000 grams whose mother tests negative get a dose at 1 month of age or hospital discharge, whichever is earlier. Babies of mothers who test positive or unknown get hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth, then more doses. For RSV, the notes say infants with a long birth hospital stay for prematurity who leave between October and March should be immunized before or soon after discharge. The notes give no separate general schedule for preterm babies.

whatToDo.action: Ask the neonatal team which vaccines and RSV protection your baby has had or is due for.
Bring the vaccine record and ask what is next.

seeClinicianIf: If a dose was missed or you are unsure of timing, ask the pediatrician for a catch-up plan.
evidenceNote: CDC notes were opened and quoted for the three situations above only. We opened no page showing a general rule for other vaccines, and the NHS vaccination page we opened does not mention premature babies.

sources.title: CDC: Child and adolescent immunization schedule notes

title: Premature baby: what preterm means
parentQuestions: What counts as a premature baby?
Is a baby born at 35 weeks preterm?
Why do babies get born early?
whatToKnow: A baby is preterm when born before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy. WHO splits this into extremely preterm (under 28 weeks), very preterm (28 to under 32 weeks) and moderate to late preterm (32 to 37 weeks). AAP says about 11 to 13 percent of US pregnancies end in preterm birth, and almost 60 percent of twin, triplet and other multiple births are preterm. Often no cause is found; multiple pregnancy, infections, and long-term conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure are among the known causes.

whatToDo.action: Ask the baby's team which group your baby falls in and what extra care that group usually needs.
Do not blame yourself: WHO and AAP both say a cause is often never found.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician or neonatal team about anything you are unsure of at each visit. See the other preterm topics for corrected age, NICU, going home and vaccines.
evidenceNote: WHO defines the groups and gives the 37-week cutoff; AAP gives the US figures. Survival and outcomes depend heavily on the country and the care available, as WHO notes.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Preemie
ACOG: Multiple Pregnancy
WHO: Preterm birth fact sheet

title: Signs of preterm labour
parentQuestions: What are the signs of preterm labour?
What should I do if my waters break early?
Can preterm labour be stopped?
whatToKnow: The NHS says labour before 37 weeks is premature, about 8 in 100 babies. Warning signs include regular tightenings, period-like pain, fluid leaking and unusual backache. Staff check the cervix, infection and the baby, and may offer steroid injections for the baby's lungs, magnesium sulphate or medicines to slow labour. Babies born early may need a neonatal unit.

whatToDo.action: Call your unit right away for any of the signs, or if unsure.
Know which hospital has a neonatal unit.

seeClinicianIf: Call at once for regular tightenings, leaking fluid, bleeding or backache that is new.
evidenceNote: Official NHS advice; individual treatment varies.

sources.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms (CDC Hear Her)
Premature labour and birth (NHS)

title: Puberty signs and talking about puberty
parentQuestions: When does puberty start?
What should I tell my daughter about periods?
whatToKnow: NHS says puberty can start anywhere from about 8 to 14, for both boys and girls. Signs include body hair, breast development and periods for girls, and larger genitals and deeper voice for boys. Start talking before it begins.

whatToDo.action: Explain the changes and hygiene.
Share supplies and a plan.

seeClinicianIf: Signs before 8 or none by 15: ask the GP.
evidenceNote: NHS (opened).

sources.title: NHS: Puberty
KidsHealth (Lurie Children's): Precocious puberty

title: Pumping at work: your US federal break-time rights (PUMP Act)
parentQuestions: Does my employer have to give me time to pump?
Where can I pump at work?
Are pumping breaks paid?
whatToKnow: US federal law, as DOL Fact Sheet #73 describes it: nearly all employees covered by the FLSA, in private and public sectors, may take reasonable break time each time they need to express milk, for one year after the child's birth. The employer must give a place that is not a bathroom, shielded from view and free from intrusion. Break time is paid if other breaks are paid; otherwise it must be fully relieved from duty, and any work done while pumping must be paid. Employers with fewer than 50 employees can claim undue hardship, and some rail and motorcoach employees and airline crew are excluded or may be exempt.

whatToDo.action: Tell your manager or HR when you will need breaks and ask where the space is.
The page says you can file a complaint with the Wage and Hour Division or sue; retaliation for complaining is prohibited.
State or local law may protect you even where federal law does not.

evidenceNote: Official DOL fact sheet. It describes US federal law only; it is a legal summary, not legal advice.

sources.title: US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet #73, Break Time for Nursing Mothers under the FLSA

title: Workplace accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth and lactation (PWFA)
parentQuestions: Can my employer refuse changes to my job after birth?
Is postpartum recovery leave an accommodation?
What does the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act cover?
whatToKnow: The EEOC page says the US Pregnant Workers Fairness Act applies to employers with 15 or more employees and requires reasonable accommodation for a known limitation related to pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, unless it causes significant difficulty or expense. Lactation and postpartum depression are listed as related conditions. Examples include extra breaks, schedule changes, telework, light duty and leave to recover from childbirth. Expressing milk at work is handled by the PUMP Act; the page does not explain how the two laws interact.

whatToDo.action: Tell your employer about the limitation and what you need; the page says the worker must have told the employer.
The page says employers cannot always demand it and may ask only for limited information, which must stay confidential.
More than 30 states and many cities have their own protections.

seeClinicianIf: If you have low mood or anxiety after birth that affects work, tell your clinician; PWFA can cover accommodations related to it.
evidenceNote: Official EEOC summary of US federal law; not legal advice.

sources.title: EEOC: What You Should Know About the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act

title: The glass test: a rash that does not fade
parentQuestions: How do I do the glass test?
My child has a fever and a rash, is it serious?
What does a meningitis rash look like?
whatToKnow: NHS lists a rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass among the signs of meningitis, and says it can also be a sign of serious illness with a fever. The meningitis rash usually starts as small red pinpricks, then spreads into red or purple blotches, and is harder to see on brown or black skin, where you check paler areas such as palms, soles, the mouth and inside the eyelids. NHS also says not everyone with meningitis gets a rash and that the rash is rare in sepsis, so a missing rash does not rule it out.

whatToDo.when: When a sick child has a rash
whatToDo.action: Press the side of a clear glass firmly on the spots. If they stay visible through the glass, treat it as an emergency.
Stiff neck, bothered by light, floppy, very sleepy, fast breathing, cold hands and feet, blue or blotchy skin, a weak or high-pitched cry.
Do not wait for the rash or for a fever to appear if your child seems seriously unwell.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says call your local emergency number (911 in the US) or go to the ER if a rash does not fade under a glass, or the child has a stiff neck, light bothers their eyes, is confused, floppy or hard to wake, is breathing fast or with effort, has blue or blotchy skin, or a fit for the first time. Do not drive yourself, and open the app's Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: NHS meningitis, sepsis, rashes and fever pages agree on the glass test as an emergency sign.

sources.title: NHS: Meningitis symptoms
NHS: Sepsis
NHS: Rashes in babies and children
NHS: High temperature (fever) in children

title: Common rashes
parentQuestions: Is this rash dangerous?
What is the red rash on my baby's cheeks?
whatToKnow: Many baby rashes are harmless: heat rash, eczema, nappy rash, cradle cap, viral rashes. A rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass, with fever and unwell, is an emergency. AAP says food does not cause eczema, though many children with eczema also have food allergies.

whatToDo.action: Note fever, appetite, itching and spread; take a photo.
Use fragrance-free emollients; avoid scalding baths.

seeClinicianIf: Rash that does not fade on pressing, with fever, drowsiness or stiff neck; swelling of lips or face; rapid spread; blisters.
evidenceNote: NHS says a rash that does not fade under a pressed glass is an emergency (call your local emergency number, 911 in the US) and can be harder to see on dark skin. AAP describes roseola and eczema as common and usually manageable. Heat rash, nappy rash and cradle cap were not covered by pages opened.

sources.title: Roseola in Babies and Toddlers (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
Eczema in Babies and Children: Symptoms and Causes (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)
Meningitis: symptoms (NHS)

title: Learning to read, and why reading aloud still matters
parentQuestions: How do I help my child learn to read?
Should I keep reading aloud when my child can read?
My child hates reading
When should I start reading to my baby?
whatToKnow: The AAP recommends reading aloud daily, even for a few minutes, letting the child pick the book, and continuing after they can read alone. The aim is to show reading is enjoyable, not just schoolwork. Use nonfiction, poetry and rhymes as well as stories.

whatToDo.action: Ten minutes of shared reading, with pauses to ask what might happen next.
Let them read back familiar books; keep it fun, not a test.
Read 10 to 15 minutes, let child choose, point and name.
Make a book part of routine.

seeClinicianIf: Slow progress in letter sounds or reading by age 6 to 7 despite practice: ask the school or pediatrician (see dyslexia signs).
evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance; the broader literacy evidence is large but we only opened this page.

HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Ten tips for your child's success in school

About (Reach Out and Read)

title: Baby's movements and kick counting
parentQuestions: How many kicks should I feel?
Should I count kicks?
What do I do if movements slow down?
whatToKnow: The NHS says there is no set number of movements and you do not need to count kicks; the key is learning your baby's usual pattern. A large trial (AFFIRM) found that a care package built around reduced-movement awareness did not reduce stillbirth. Formal counting is debated, but the point everyone shares is to seek help promptly if the pattern changes. Do not rely on a home Doppler.

whatToDo.action: Notice your baby's usual pattern at a quiet time.
Call the maternity unit the same day; do not wait until morning.

seeClinicianIf: Call the same day for reduced or changed movements, even if you called before.
evidenceNote: The NHS does not advise counting. A big randomised trial found no reduction in stillbirth from the awareness package, but the trial does not mean ignoring changes. Some clinics and apps use formal count protocols; I did not open a source for those.

sources.title: Your baby's movements (NHS)
Awareness of fetal movements and care package to reduce fetal mortality (AFFIRM): a stepped wedge, cluster-randomised trial (Lancet 2018, via Europe PMC)

title: Reggio Emilia approach
parentQuestions: What is the Reggio Emilia approach?
Is a 'Reggio-inspired' kindergarten really Reggio?
Does Reggio give better outcomes?
Реджио-подход в детском саду
whatToKnow: Reggio Emilia is an early childhood approach that grew in Reggio Emilia, Italy, centered on child-led projects, documentation of children's work, art and the idea of the environment as a teacher. A 2017 study of Reggio, Parma and Padova (non-experimental) found that compared with no formal care, Reggio was associated with better adult outcomes, but there were no strong differences compared with other forms of childcare, and the authors warn of self-selection. A 2021 integrative review of 51 studies of 'Reggio Inspired' practice found little outcome research, so claims are mostly based on philosophy and qualitative reports rather than controlled trials.

whatToDo.action: Ask how projects are chosen, how teachers document learning and what the training is; 'Reggio-inspired' has no certification.
Offer open-ended materials (clay, paper, loose parts), follow the child's interest for a week, and display their work.
Do a small project with questions ('What do we want to find out?') and photograph the process.

evidenceNote: Outcome evidence is limited and mostly observational; supporters and researchers agree the method is well described but not well tested. The 2021 integrative review of Reggio Inspired practice (Emerson and Linder) is described here from its abstract and is not separately cited.

sources.title: Biroli et al. 2017, Evaluation of the Reggio Approach to Early Education, NBER Working Paper 23390

title: Daily regime and schedules
parentQuestions: Do I need a strict schedule?
whatToKnow: A predictable routine helps toddlers feel safe and sleep better. A rigid feeding or sleep clock from birth is not required; responsive feeding for the first months, then a gentler rhythm.

whatToDo.action: Build a loose routine with consistent wake, meals, naps and bed.

evidenceNote: A study in many countries found a consistent bedtime routine linked to earlier bedtimes, faster sleep onset, fewer night wakings and longer sleep, with more benefit the more consistent it was. It is observational and covers bedtime, not feeding clocks.

sources.title: Bedtime routines for young children: a dose-dependent association with sleep outcomes (Mindell et al., Sleep 2015)

title: Repeating a grade
parentQuestions: The teacher suggests my child repeat the year, should we?
Does holding back help weak students?
whatToKnow: The AAP says grade retention has not been shown to help learning, can contribute to low self-esteem, and does not fix underlying learning or attention problems. Children tend to do best advancing with peers while reasons for struggling are found and supported. Options include academic supports, extra tutoring or summer programs.

whatToDo.action: Ask for a full evaluation (learning, language, attention, vision and hearing) before deciding.
Request targeted support and regular progress checks.

seeClinicianIf: Persistent struggles despite good attendance warrant a developmental or learning assessment.
evidenceNote: AAP guidance (opened); US data, so local systems differ.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Should my child repeat a grade?

title: Planning the return to work: leave, childcare, cost
parentQuestions: When should I start looking for childcare?
How do we plan returning to work after the baby?
How do we afford childcare?
whatToKnow: Leave rights are in the related topics; this one is the planning side. ChildCare.gov lays out a sequence: learn the options and how licensing works, search your state's tool, review inspection reports, contact programs, visit several, then weigh how each felt. It says the cost of child care is often the biggest part of a family's budget and that help depends on where you live. The AAP says paid leave of at least 12 weeks supports parents and babies and that FMLA is unpaid and excludes many workers.

whatToDo.action: Run the ChildCare.gov steps, since good programs may have limited space, and check hours against your commute.
Use the Paying for Child Care pages and your state resources to see what assistance exists; the pages we opened give no dollar figures.
Do visits and a short trial with the caregiver, plan pumping and milk storage if breastfeeding, and agree who handles drop-off, pickup and sick days.

evidenceNote: Steps are from ChildCare.gov; we found no official source for an ideal start date, so the app should not claim one.

title: Rh negative blood group and anti-D injections
parentQuestions: I am Rh negative, is that a problem?
What is the anti-D injection?
When is anti-D given?
whatToKnow: A blood test at about 8 to 12 weeks shows your Rh type. If you are Rh negative and the baby is Rh positive, anti-D injections stop your body forming antibodies that could harm a later baby. The NHS page says anti-D will not help if you already have antibodies, in which case you get extra scans and blood tests. Timing details vary, and extra doses are given after bleeding or procedures.

whatToDo.action: Ask for your blood group and Rh result.
Ask whether anti-D is needed.

seeClinicianIf: Report any bleeding, abdominal injury or procedure promptly if you are Rh negative.
evidenceNote: The NHS page confirms the principle but I could not confirm exact gestations from it; local policy decides timing.

sources.title: Rhesus disease (NHS)

title: RIE (Magda Gerber): respectful infant care
parentQuestions: What is RIE parenting?
Should I let my baby play alone without toys that do things?
Is narrating every diaper change helpful?
Метод Магды Гербер и RIE
whatToKnow: Resources for Infant Educarers (RIE), founded by Magda Gerber and Tom Forrest in Los Angeles in 1978, asks caregivers to treat babies as capable people, observe before acting, build routines around caregiving and favor uninterrupted free play. RIE describes itself as based on research and practice, but its own pages cite no specific trials, and I found no controlled outcome studies. Its core ideas (responsiveness, observation, relationship during routines) match mainstream advice on sensitive care; some specifics, such as how long to leave a baby to fuss, are matters of opinion.

whatToDo.action: Tell the baby what you are about to do before lifting or changing, and give a moment to respond.
Offer floor time with a few safe objects and watch rather than direct; stay close and respond if the baby is distressed.
Let the child try dressing or feeding, offer simple choices, and keep routines predictable.
Follow AAP safe sleep rules and the pediatrician's advice; respect for the baby does not replace them.

seeClinicianIf: Concerns about development, feeding or sleep; ask the pediatrician instead of waiting for a baby to 'work it out'.
evidenceNote: A philosophy with plausible overlap with research on sensitive care but no direct outcome evidence found. Supporters see respectful care as core; critics see parts as unproven.

sources.title: Educaring in Childcare Settings (Resources for Infant Educarers)
Serve and Return: Back-and-forth exchanges (Center on the Developing Child, Harvard)

title: Rooming-in: baby in the same room
parentQuestions: Should the baby stay with me at night?
Is it ok to send the baby to the nursery?
Will rooming-in wear me out?
whatToKnow: WHO Baby-Friendly practice keeps mother and baby together 24 hours a day. A review of 7 studies found no clear difference in exclusive breastfeeding at 3 to 6 months, and the evidence quality was low. It is often chosen because it makes it easier to notice early feeding cues, but a mother who is exhausted or unwell may reasonably ask for a few hours of help.

whatToDo.action: Ask whether the hospital offers rooming-in and whether the other parent can stay.
Ask for a nurse to watch the baby if you need to sleep.

seeClinicianIf: Never sleep with the baby on a sofa or armchair; if you feel drowsy, ask staff to take the baby or place the baby in the cot.
evidenceNote: WHO recommends it as a standard; the best available evidence does not prove a breastfeeding benefit, so it is a guideline-led practice rather than a proven one.

sources.title: Effect of rooming-in on duration of breastfeeding: systematic review (PMC)
WHO: Infant and young child feeding fact sheet

title: How often are prenatal visits and what happens at them?
parentQuestions: How many prenatal visits will I have?
What is checked at each visit?
When should I register?
whatToKnow: The NHS offers at least 10 appointments for a first baby (7 for later births) plus 2 scans, starting with a booking visit at 8 to 12 weeks. Later visits cover blood pressure, urine, bump growth and baby movements. WHO recommends at least 8 contacts, the first before 12 weeks, then at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks. You may contact the team any time you are worried.

whatToDo.action: Register for pregnancy care and book the first visit by week 12.
Bring questions and your partner if you wish.

seeClinicianIf: Do not wait for the next visit for bleeding, leaking fluid, severe headache or reduced movements.
evidenceNote: Both are official; the numbers differ between the UK and WHO and national schedules vary, so follow your local clinic.

title: RSV vaccine in pregnancy
parentQuestions: Should I get the RSV vaccine while pregnant?
When is it given?
How long does it protect my baby?
whatToKnow: The NHS offers an RSV vaccine from 28 weeks of pregnancy in every pregnancy to protect the baby for the first 6 months, when RSV is most likely to cause serious illness. It is best given as soon as possible from 28 weeks and can be given until labour. Older adults have a separate programme.

whatToDo.action: Book the vaccine at the next visit.
It can still be given up to labour if you missed the window.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a clinician if you are unwell with fever or have had a serious allergy to vaccine ingredients.
evidenceNote: Official UK programme; availability and the alternative of an infant antibody injection differ by country.

title: Safe sleep basics for the first year
parentQuestions: What is the safest way for a baby to sleep?
Back or side?
Should the cot be in our room?
Can I use a pillow or bumper?
How should my baby sleep?
Can my baby sleep on his stomach?
whatToKnow: For every sleep, including naps, put the baby on the back on a firm, flat mattress with nothing soft in the sleep space. Keeping the cot or bassinet in the parents' room for at least the first 6 months lowers risk. Pillows, duvets, bumpers, loose blankets, soft toys and nests or pods are not advised.

whatToDo.action: Back to sleep, feet to the foot of the cot, firm flat mattress with fitted sheet only.
Keep the cot in your room for all sleeps, day and night.
Move onto the back until the baby can roll both ways alone.
Back, flat, bare crib, room-share.
Stop swaddling at first rolling.

seeClinicianIf: Call the pediatrician if the baby has trouble breathing or looks blue or limp; use emergency services in that case.
evidenceNote: CDC and NHS agree on back sleeping, firm flat surface, room sharing, and a clear sleep space (AAP guidance on the same points was not directly opened).

title: Safe sleep in childcare: what to tell and check
parentQuestions: How do I make sure my baby sleeps safely at daycare?
What should I tell the nanny or grandparent about sleep?
Can daycare put my baby to sleep on their tummy?
whatToKnow: The AAP says to share its safe sleep guidance with everyone who cares for your baby, including babysitters and child care center staff. For babies up to 1 year that means back sleeping for every nap and at night, a firm flat surface that meets current CPSC standards and has not been recalled, a tight-fitting sheet, and no sleeping on armchairs, sofas, water beds, cushions or sheepskin. A baby who falls asleep in a car seat, stroller, swing or carrier should be moved to a firm flat surface as soon as possible. The AAP page links to 'A Child Care Provider's Guide to Safe Sleep' but we did not open it.

whatToDo.action: Ask where babies sleep, what position they are put in, and whether the provider follows back-to-sleep for every nap.
Look at the cribs: firm mattress, fitted sheet, nothing soft in them. Ask whether babies ever sleep in swings, car seats or on sofas.
Hand them the safe sleep rules in writing, including grandparents and nannies.

seeClinicianIf: If a baby is limp, not breathing or blue, call your local emergency number (911 in the US) at once; the app's Urgent help screen is fixed and does not depend on this topic. Raise any provider sleep practices that conflict with AAP guidance with the provider first, then your pediatrician.
evidenceNote: Safe sleep rules are AAP guidance for the first year. The AAP page did not detail provider-specific rules; the provider guide it links was not opened.

title: Same-sex parents: what the evidence says
parentQuestions: Are children of same-sex parents okay?
What does the AAP say?
Do we both need to be legal parents?
whatToKnow: The AAP 2013 policy states that children's well-being is affected much more by their relationships with parents, the parents' sense of competence and security, and social and economic support for the family than by the gender or sexual orientation of the parents. It says scientific evidence affirms that children have similar developmental and emotional needs and receive similar parenting. The AAP supports both parents in a same-gender couple having legal rights and responsibilities, for example through second-parent or coparent adoption, and says US laws on marriage and adoption are a patchwork. Laws differ by country; we opened no Kazakhstan source, so we make no claim on legal steps there.

whatToDo.action: Find out what legal recognition your country or state gives the non-birth parent, and ask a family lawyer about steps.
Stable relationships and community support matter most per AAP; build both.

seeClinicianIf: Not a medical matter. See a pediatrician or counsellor for stress, bullying or mood concerns, as for any family.
evidenceNote: AAP policy statement, which says it is based on a review of the literature. The statement dates from 2013, and AAP policies lapse after 5 years unless reaffirmed; we did not check for a newer version.

title: Tummy aches, headaches and school avoidance
parentQuestions: My child has tummy aches every school morning
Is it real or a way to skip school?
whatToKnow: NHS says recurrent abdominal pain is common, often linked with headaches and sleep problems, made worse by stress, anxiety or low mood, and that most children grow out of it. The AAP lists frequent headaches or stomachaches and school avoidance as warning signs of bullying. The pain is real.

whatToDo.action: Reassure, distract, keep to routines and school as much as possible.
Ask about bullying, worries and friendships.

seeClinicianIf: Weight loss, blood in stool, vomiting, fever, night pain, or pain with no pattern.
evidenceNote: NHS and AAP pages (opened).

title: School readiness: skills or maturity?
parentQuestions: Is my child ready for first grade?
What should a child be able to do before school?
Does my child need to read before school?
whatToKnow: The AAP says readiness includes focus, impulse control, taking turns, making friends, language, early literacy, early math, pencil and movement skills and toilet use, not only letters and numbers. Children develop at different rates, so there is no single ready age. In Kazakhstan the Ministry description states that reading, writing and counting are taught from the start of grade 1 and are not required on entry.

whatToDo.action: Practice self-care (dressing, toilet, zips), turn-taking and listening, and read together daily.
Visit the school and its route; talk about it positively.

seeClinicianIf: Concerns about speech, hearing, vision, attention, or very delayed play and social skills should be raised with the pediatrician before school starts.

title: Screen time for babies and toddlers
parentQuestions: How much screen time is OK for a 2 year old?
whatToKnow: AAP's 2016 advice: avoid screens under 18 months except video calls; 18 to 24 months only high-quality, with a caregiver; 2 to 5 about an hour. AAP now emphasizes quality, context and co-viewing over simple limits and warns about screens used to calm children.

whatToDo.action: Video calls only; talk and play instead.
Co-view short high-quality content; no screens at meals or one hour before sleep.

seeClinicianIf: Delayed speech with heavy screen use; screens used to stop every tantrum.
evidenceNote: AAP HealthyChildren updated page opened; the 2016 numbers came from search summaries.

title: Screen time and first devices
parentQuestions: How much screen time is OK for a 6 year old?
When to give a tablet?
How to set screen rules?
whatToKnow: The AAP's 2026 policy moves from fixed time limits to the quality, context and what media crowds out. Advice includes making a Family Media Plan, screen-free zones and times (meals, bedtime, bedrooms), co-viewing, a shared family tablet, delaying personal tablets, and modeling by parents. CDC's parenting tips for 3 to 5 still say about 1 hour of quality programming and no TV in the bedroom.

whatToDo.action: Write a family media plan; set screen-free meals and the hour before bed.
Revisit at the start of each school year.

seeClinicianIf: Screens replacing sleep, play and school, strong distress when stopped, or social withdrawal.
evidenceNote: AAP 2026 policy summary (HealthyChildren) and CDC tips; causal evidence remains limited, which the AAP itself notes.

title: Screen time for babies, toddlers and preschoolers: guidance and research
parentQuestions: How much screen time is okay for a toddler?
Is video chat with grandparents okay for a baby?
Does the AAP still say one hour a day?
Сколько времени можно ребёнку в мультики до 3 лет?
whatToKnow: WHO (2019) advises no screen time for infants and 1-year-olds, and no more than 1 hour a day for ages 2 to 4. AAP's 2016 statement for ages 0 to 5 stresses shared viewing, quality content and not crowding out sleep and play. In January 2026 the AAP replaced fixed limits with a broader 'digital ecosystem' policy and a Family Media Plan. A Canadian cohort (Madigan 2019) found more screen time at 24 and 36 months predicted lower developmental screening scores later; this is an association, small in size.

whatToDo.action: Avoid solo screens; live video chat with relatives is generally treated as a different case when an adult interacts with the child.
If you use media, choose high-quality content and watch together, talking about what you see.
Keep it limited (WHO: max 1 hour), choose calm content, and keep screens out of meals and the hour before bed.
Write a Family Media Plan together: screen-free times and places, content rules, review at school-year start.
Model it: put your phone away at meals and during play; turn off autoplay and notifications.

seeClinicianIf: Raise with the pediatrician if a child's screen use causes severe distress when stopped, sleep problems, loss of social interest or speech skills, or if you have concerns about language, eye contact or play.
evidenceNote: WHO (2019) and AAP (2016, 2026) are official guidance. The research base is mostly observational (Madigan 2019, cross-lagged, small effects), so the guidance is precautionary. The AAP 2026 policy dropped a fixed daily limit; the 2016 detail on video chat is from secondary summaries because the full text was blocked.

title: Separation anxiety and stranger anxiety
parentQuestions: Why does my baby cry when I leave?
whatToKnow: Distress at separation and with strangers can start at 4 to 5 months, is strongest around 9 months, often returns at 15 to 18 months and is rare after the preschool years (AAP). It signals healthy attachment and memory. Quick, calm goodbyes and predictable routines help.

whatToDo.action: Say a short goodbye; never sneak away.
Short separations with a trusted caregiver first.

seeClinicianIf: Extreme distress lasting months, refusal to eat or sleep, or anxiety continuing past age 4 and limiting daily life.
evidenceNote: AAP parent guidance describes onset after object permanence develops, short goodbyes, a ritual, returning when promised, and practice separations. It is guidance, not a trial-based guideline.

sources.title: How to Ease Your Child's Separation Anxiety (HealthyChildren.org, AAP)

title: Serve and return: back-and-forth with your baby
parentQuestions: How do I talk to a baby who cannot talk back?
Does responding to babbling really matter?
What are the best brain-building activities for my baby?
Как общаться с младенцем, чтобы развивать мозг?
whatToKnow: Serve and return is the Harvard Center on the Developing Child's name for the back-and-forth exchange when a baby babbles, points or cries and an adult responds with eye contact, words or a hug. The Center says these exchanges help build neural connections for communication and social skills, and that the developing brain expects them. It is an easy practice that needs no equipment, and it is consistent with attachment research; the claims about brain wiring are plausible but come from a summary of research, not a single trial of the five steps.

whatToDo.action: Look at the baby, copy sounds and faces, and pause so the baby can reply.
Notice what the baby points to or looks at, name it, and wait for the next turn.
Talk about what the child is doing, add one word to what they say, read together and ask simple questions.
Follow the child's lead in play, extend with a question, and keep screens off during meals and play.

seeClinicianIf: No eye contact, no response to sounds or voice, no babbling or gestures by the typical times, or loss of earlier skills; ask the pediatrician about hearing and development checks.
evidenceNote: The concept is promoted by Harvard's Center and rests on developmental and neuroscience research; the official page does not list effect sizes, and the effect of the five steps has not been tested as a package.

title: Sex, contraception and fertility after birth
parentQuestions: When can we have sex?
Can I get pregnant while breastfeeding?
How long before another pregnancy?
whatToKnow: NHS says there is no rule on timing; soreness and dryness are common, lubricant may help, and it can take time. You can get pregnant from about 3 weeks after birth, including while breastfeeding, so contraception is needed unless you want another pregnancy. NHS suggests waiting at least 12 months before the next pregnancy.

whatToDo.action: Discuss contraception with your midwife.
Go slowly and say if it hurts.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician for persistent pain.
evidenceNote: NHS. I did not open sources on lactational amenorrhea, IUDs or pills while breastfeeding, so they are not covered here.

title: Where do babies come from? Sex education by age
parentQuestions: What do I say when my child asks where babies come from?
When should I explain sex?
What should an 8 year old know?
whatToKnow: The AAP says let questions guide you, stay calm, keep answers short and honest. At 4 to 5 a simple answer is enough; at 5 to 7 children link sexuality to making babies and may invent explanations or turn to friends or the internet; at 8 to 9 explain that sex is between consenting people and begin consent, contraception and STI topics. Parents can ask the pediatrician for help.

whatToDo.action: Sperm and an egg join and a baby grows in the uterus; no details needed.
Start puberty and consent talks.

seeClinicianIf: Sexualized behavior beyond curiosity, or exposure to explicit content.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

title: Sex during pregnancy
parentQuestions: Is sex safe during pregnancy?
Can it cause miscarriage?
When should I avoid it?
whatToKnow: Sex is generally considered safe in a healthy pregnancy. The source I opened (Tommy's, linked from the NHS) advises avoiding penetrative sex if you have a low-lying placenta, your waters have broken or you have had several miscarriages, and to get any bleeding checked. Libido often changes, and it is a good topic for partners to discuss openly.

whatToDo.action: Talk about comfort, positions and changes in desire.
Use other ways of intimacy and check with the midwife.

seeClinicianIf: Ask if you have bleeding, pain after sex, leaking fluid, a low placenta or recurrent miscarriage.
evidenceNote: Consistent mainstream advice with specific exceptions; no evidence that normal sex causes miscarriage.

title: Shaken baby syndrome and coping with crying
parentQuestions: What if I lose my patience with a crying baby?
Why is shaking so dangerous?
How can I stop myself?
whatToKnow: The PURPLE program teaches that early crying is normal, soothing does not work every time, and a frustrated caregiver should never shake a baby. The page stresses having action steps ready for inconsolable crying. Putting the baby down safely and stepping away for a few minutes is widely advised, though the pages I opened do not spell that step out.

whatToDo.action: Agree with your partner on a plan: who takes over, where the baby can safely be put down.
Put the baby on their back in the cot, step away, breathe, call someone.

seeClinicianIf: Seek help urgently if a baby has been shaken or dropped; call the pediatrician or emergency services.
evidenceNote: PURPLE is an educational program; I did not open outcome studies, so its measured effect is not assessed here.

title: Sharing the baby's photos online
parentQuestions: Should we post our baby's photos?
What risks come with it?
whatToKnow: UNICEF lists risks: strangers can target children, data brokers can profile them, photos can be misused or altered, and children may later object. Advice includes avoiding naked or embarrassing images, checking privacy settings, leaving out location and school details, and agreeing with relatives what they may post.

whatToDo.action: Decide with the other parent what you will and will not share.
Review old posts and ask the child's view as they grow.

evidenceNote: Mostly commentary and expert guidance; no formal guideline exists in many countries.

title: Sibling rivalry
parentQuestions: My kids fight all the time
Is jealousy normal?
whatToKnow: Jealousy and regression are normal when siblings change. AAP advice includes one-on-one time, giving roles, keeping routines, and not telling a child to 'act your age'. We did not open a dedicated sibling rivalry page, so conflict tactics are limited to the friendship and anger pages.

whatToDo.action: Protect one-on-one time for each child.
Coach repair; do not always referee who started it.

seeClinicianIf: Violence or very persistent aggression.
evidenceNote: Mostly new-baby guidance (opened); thin for school-age sibling fights.

title: Sick child and daycare: when to stay home and what leave covers
parentQuestions: When should I keep my child home from daycare?
Can I take time off work when my child is sick?
Does fever mean no daycare?
whatToKnow: The AAP says a child with a respiratory illness and fever should stay home until the fever has been gone for at least 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine, and also lists diarrhea, repeated vomiting, rash with fever and some infections as reasons to stay home. Colds without fever and runny noses generally do not keep a child home if the child feels well enough to join activities. In the US, the DOL's FMLA page describes up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in 12 months for eligible employees, which includes caring for a child with a serious health condition; eligibility needs 12 months of work, 1,250 hours and a worksite with 50 or more employees within 75 miles.

whatToDo.action: Read the daycare's sick policy and line up a backup caregiver or flexible work.
Check the symptom against the AAP stay-home list and call the pediatrician for fever with other symptoms; dose any medicine by current weight from the official dosing table.
Check FMLA eligibility and ask HR about employer sick or family leave; the DOL page does not describe short single-day absences.

seeClinicianIf: Call 911 (or your local emergency number) for trouble breathing or a rapidly spreading purple, bruise-like rash; the AAP page names the rash case. Infants under 2 months with unexplained fever need a health professional right away. The app's Urgent help screen is fixed.
evidenceNote: AAP exclusion guidance and the DOL FMLA page. FMLA is US federal; it is unpaid and excludes many workers, as the AAP leave page also says.

title: SIDS and SUID: what raises the risk
parentQuestions: What is SIDS?
Can I prevent SIDS?
Does smoking matter?
whatToKnow: SIDS is the sudden unexplained death of an apparently healthy baby, most often in the first 6 months. Known risk factors include smoke exposure, sleeping on a sofa or soft surface, prematurity or low birth weight, and overheating. Breastfeeding, pacifier use at sleep, up to date vaccines and no smoke exposure are linked with lower risk.

whatToDo.action: Do not smoke or use nicotine and avoid alcohol and drugs.
Follow back-to-sleep, room sharing and clear sleep space; keep vaccines on schedule.

seeClinicianIf: Emergency help right away for a baby who is not breathing or is unresponsive; ask the clinician about extra advice if born early.
evidenceNote: The cause is unknown; recommendations are risk reduction, not a guarantee.

title: Single parents: support and what matters
parentQuestions: Is it worse for a child to have one parent?
How do I cope alone?
What help should I ask for?
whatToKnow: We could not open a dedicated AAP single-parenting page, so this is limited. The AAP 2013 policy notes many children are raised by single or cohabiting parents, by choice or circumstance, and affirms that children's well-being depends much more on relationships with parents, parents' sense of competence and security, and social and economic support than on the form of the family. AAP also supports adoption by single parents and lists single parents among valid family forms. We opened no page that compares outcomes of one-parent and two-parent homes, so we make no claim either way.

whatToDo.action: Name two or three people who can help with childcare, an emergency, or a break.
Keep routines steady and use parent groups or services your area offers.

seeClinicianIf: If exhaustion, low mood or isolation is heavy, tell your clinician; see the parent wellbeing and burnout topics.
evidenceNote: AAP states the evidence about relationships and support. Not a head-to-head outcome comparison, and a single-parent page was not available to us.

title: The first hour after birth: skin-to-skin, first feed, checks, placenta
parentQuestions: What happens right after the baby is born?
Can I hold my baby straight away?
When does the placenta come out?
When is the first feed?
Should the baby be on my chest right after birth?
What if I have a cesarean?
Can the other parent do skin-to-skin?
whatToKnow: The NHS suggests having the baby lifted onto you before the cord is cut, dried and covered while you hold them. A Cochrane review (2025) found skin-to-skin contact probably increases exclusive breastfeeding and helps keep newborns warm with higher blood sugar, regardless of mode of birth. The NHS says the first feed ideally comes within 1 hour, and the placenta usually comes within 30 minutes with an oxytocin injection or can take up to an hour without. A midwife also examines the baby, offers vitamin K, and checks you for bleeding.

whatToDo.action: Discuss delayed cord clamping, skin-to-skin, vitamin K and the placenta choice (active or physiological) with your midwife.
Keep your baby on your chest, ask for a feed when they show cues, and keep visitors for later.
Ask which newborn checks the unit does before you leave and who to call about feeding.
Ask the team to dry the baby on your chest and delay routine weighing and measuring until after the first feed.
Ask whether skin-to-skin can happen in theatre or recovery, or with the other parent first.

seeClinicianIf: Baby is limp, blue, not breathing well, or cannot be kept warm; or you have heavy bleeding, faintness or a retained placenta. The team will act.
evidenceNote: NHS and NICE support skin-to-skin; the Cochrane evidence is moderate certainty for breastfeeding.

title: Room temperature, overheating and sleep sacks
parentQuestions: How warm should the baby's room be?
Should the baby wear a hat while sleeping?
Are sleep sacks safe?
whatToKnow: Overheating raises SIDS risk. NHS advice is a room around 16 to 20 degrees C, using light layers, and checking the chest or back of the neck for heat; cool hands and feet are normal. Sheets and blankets tucked firmly below shoulder level or a baby sleeping bag are safe, and a head should not be covered while sleeping.

whatToDo.action: Dress in light layers, check the chest or neck, and remove a layer if the skin feels hot or sweaty.
Use a sleep sack or tucked blanket, no duvet, no hat indoors for sleep.

seeClinicianIf: Contact the pediatrician if the baby feels very hot or very cold, has a fever, or is unusually drowsy.

title: Soothing a newborn: what actually helps
parentQuestions: How do I calm a crying baby?
Can I spoil a baby by holding?
Why does my baby cry after feeds?
whatToKnow: Common reasons for crying are hunger, a wet nappy, tiredness, wind, being too hot or cold, boredom or overstimulation. NHS suggests holding, a sling, rocking, a walk, background noise and a warm bath, and notes too much stimulation can keep a baby awake. Crying that is inconsolable or sounds different can signal illness.

whatToDo.when: Crying with a fever or not feeding
whatToDo.action: Seek medical help the same day.

title: Sore throat and strep in children
parentQuestions: My child has a sore throat, is it strep?
Does a sore throat need antibiotics?
What does tonsillitis mean?
whatToKnow: NHS says sore throats usually get better in a week and antibiotics are not normally needed. CDC says viruses cause most sore throats and only about 3 in 10 children with a sore throat have strep. Cough, runny nose, hoarseness or pink eye point to a virus. Strep often brings a sudden sore throat, fever, red swollen tonsils, and in children headache, nausea, vomiting or stomach pain. A quick test from a clinician can tell, and strep is treated with antibiotics.

whatToDo.action: Cool or soft foods, fluids, rest, and paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed (see fever-medicine-by-weight). Children should not gargle salt water per NHS.
Small hard sweets to young children due to choking. No aspirin under 16.
Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says see a GP if a child under 5 needs help for a sore throat, it does not improve in a week, or it keeps coming back, and get urgent advice for a very high temperature or signs of dehydration. Call your local emergency number or go to the ER for trouble breathing, drooling or being unable to swallow.
evidenceNote: CDC and NHS agree that most sore throats are viral and that only a test can tell strep apart. CDC page we opened did not give school return timing.

title: Spanking: what the AAP says
parentQuestions: Is spanking OK?
Does a smack hurt?
whatToKnow: The AAP advises that parents should not spank or hit. Research links it to more aggression and anger, not better self-control, and raises injury risk. It also says harsh verbal discipline is ineffective and harmful.

whatToDo.action: Use calm limits, consequences, time outs and praise.
Apologize and reset; consider a parenting class.

seeClinicianIf: Anger you cannot manage or a child hurt.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): What's the best way to discipline my child?

title: Speech sounds and lisps
parentQuestions: My child cannot say R
Is a lisp normal at 5?
When should my child see a speech therapist?
whatToKnow: ASHA says most speech sounds are usually acquired by age 5, with wide variation, and some error patterns resolve later (for example gliding by 6 to 7). Dialect differences are not errors. Persistent or unusual patterns past the typical age are a reason for evaluation.

whatToDo.action: If many sounds are still unclear to strangers, ask the pediatrician about speech-language therapy.
Model the correct word without making the child repeat.

seeClinicianIf: Speech hard to understand at 5, a lisp that persists after the early school years, or errors that do not match peers.
evidenceNote: ASHA page is a clinical topic overview; we did not open norm tables, so exact ages per sound are not given here.

sources.title: ASHA Practice Portal: Selected phonological patterns

title: Spitting up versus reflux in babies
parentQuestions: Is it normal for my baby to spit up?
When is it reflux?
Should I raise the head of the cot?
whatToKnow: Reflux, where a baby brings up milk during or after feeds, usually starts before 8 weeks and improves by about a year. A happy baby who is gaining weight does not usually need treatment. Holding upright after feeds, burping and checking position help; do not raise the cot head and keep the baby sleeping flat on the back.

whatToDo.action: Burp regularly and hold the baby upright during and for a while after feeds.
Keep the baby flat on the back, not on the side or front or on a wedge.

seeClinicianIf: See a clinician if the baby is not gaining weight, refuses feeds, has distress with feeds, blood or green vomit, or projectile vomiting.
evidenceNote: NHS advice; unsettled babies with reflux symptoms sometimes need review for other causes.

sources.title: NHS: Reflux in babies

title: Starting solids
parentQuestions: When do I start solid food?
Baby led weaning or purees?
whatToKnow: Start around 6 months when the baby sits steady, can pick up food and swallows rather than pushes it out; chewing fists and night waking are not readiness. Breast milk or formula remain the main nutrition. Avoid honey before 1, added salt and sugar, whole nuts, and hard raw pieces.

whatToDo.action: Offer iron-rich foods and finger foods or purees with milk feeds.
Iron-rich foods daily.

seeClinicianIf: Gagging that turns to choking, persistent vomiting, rash or swelling after a new food.
evidenceNote: NHS opened. Baby-led weaning vs purees: neither shows clear superiority in trials.

sources.title: NHS: Your baby's first solid foods

title: Storing and sending pumped milk to childcare
parentQuestions: How long can pumped milk sit out?
How do I label milk for daycare?
How do I thaw frozen breast milk safely?
whatToKnow: CDC guidance for freshly expressed milk: up to 4 hours at room temperature of 77 F or colder, up to 4 days in the refrigerator, and in the freezer about 6 months is best and up to 12 months is acceptable. Thaw in the refrigerator overnight, in warm or lukewarm water, or under lukewarm running water; use refrigerator-thawed milk within 24 hours of full thaw and warmed milk within 2 hours; never refreeze thawed milk. Do not microwave milk, store it in the door, or use disposable bottle liners or bags not made for breast milk.

whatToDo.action: Freeze in amounts for one feeding (the CDC page says 2 to 4 ounces) with about an inch of space at the top, and label each container with the date.
Add the child's name and ask the provider about their own requirements; milk can travel in an insulated cooler with frozen ice packs for up to 24 hours.
Whether they support continued breastfeeding, let you nurse on site and handle pumped milk properly, as the AAP checklist suggests.

evidenceNote: Times and temperatures are from the CDC page, which is for healthy full-term babies at home and childcare; hospital rules differ.

CDC: Breast Milk Storage and Preparation

title: Stranger safety
parentQuestions: How do I teach my child about strangers?
What if someone offers a ride?
whatToKnow: CDC says teach preschoolers how to stay safe around strangers. The AAP body safety tips add a simple rule, telling a trusted adult, and reassurance that the child will be believed. Most harm comes from known people, so teach body rules and permission rather than only 'stranger danger'.

whatToDo.action: Practice 'check first' and a family code word.
Role-play what to do if lost.

evidenceNote: CDC and AAP pages (opened); the 'known people' point is common guidance from the AAP tips.

sources.title: AAP: 10 tips for parents to teach children about body safety and boundaries
CDC: Positive parenting tips, preschoolers 3 to 5 years

title: Strollers, bouncers, swings, carriers and infant seats: where baby may not sleep
parentQuestions: Can my baby sleep in the car seat, bouncer or swing?
Is a stroller safe for a newborn?
How do I use a baby carrier safely?
whatToKnow: AAP says swings, rockers, bouncers and gliders are fine for play when used as directed but not for sleep, because a sleeping baby's head can drop and block breathing. Car seats are for vehicle travel: a baby may doze in a moving car, but should be moved to a firm flat surface as soon as possible, and AAP says seats should not be used for sleeping or feeding away from the car. NHS says a pushchair for a young baby needs a fully reclining seat, and carriers are safe only when the T.I.C.K.S. checks are met.

whatToDo.action: Check the product is for play or travel, not sold as a sleeper. Round padded loungers and inclined sleepers are not safe for sleep, and AAP warns old or secondhand banned products still turn up; check recalls on the CPSC site.
For a young baby use a fully reclining seat (NHS), a harness, working brakes and a strong frame; wait for an upright seat until baby can sit unaided.
Use T.I.C.K.S.: tight, in view, close enough to kiss, chin off chest, supported back. Keep fabric away from baby's face and take baby out to feed.

whatToDo.when: Baby falls asleep in a seat
whatToDo.action: Move them to a flat firm sleep surface on their back as soon as you can, and do not leave a car seat sitting around as a bed.

seeClinicianIf: If a baby was found limp, blue or not breathing in a seat, swing or carrier, call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the ER, and use the app's fixed Urgent help screen.
evidenceNote: AAP and NHS, plus the Lullaby Trust, agree on the main points. We could not open CPSC product pages (404), so recall checks are only mentioned as AAP advises.

title: Stuttering (stammering)
parentQuestions: My child repeats words, is he stuttering?
Will my child outgrow stuttering?
whatToKnow: NHS says about 1 in 12 young children goes through a stammering phase and about two in three eventually speak fluently. Treatment is often successful in preschool children, so early referral helps. Parents can contact the GP or health visitor for referral to a speech and language therapist.

whatToDo.action: Listen patiently, do not finish sentences, slow your own speech.
Ask for a speech-language therapy assessment early.

seeClinicianIf: Stammering lasting more than a few months, getting worse, with tension or avoidance, or with family history.
evidenceNote: NHS (opened).

title: Sun safety
parentQuestions: What SPF for kids?
How often to reapply sunscreen?
Can toddlers use sunscreen?
whatToKnow: Under 6 months, keep babies in shade and clothing first; AAP allows a little sunscreen on small areas when that is not enough. From then on, the AAP says use broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 15 or higher (SPF 30 for most), apply 15 to 30 minutes before going out, reapply every 2 hours and after swimming, and use shade and hats, especially 10 am to 4 pm.

whatToDo.action: Sunscreen, hat, shade at midday.
Reapply after water.
Shade, hat, and reapply every 2 hours.

seeClinicianIf: Blistering sunburn or unusual moles.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Sun safety, sunburn and sunscreen

title: Swaddling: how to do it safely and when to stop
parentQuestions: Is swaddling safe?
When should I stop swaddling?
Should I swaddle tight like grandma did?
Can swaddled babies sleep on their side?
whatToKnow: AAP says swaddling can calm a baby but is not a SIDS prevention tool. A swaddled baby must sleep on the back, and swaddling should stop at the first signs of trying to roll, which can be as early as 2 months. Swaddling can add to overheating, and weighted swaddles or blankets are not advised.

whatToDo.action: Place the swaddled baby on the back on a firm flat surface; leave the hips free to bend up and out and keep the wrap snug only around chest and arms.
Watch for early rolling attempts. At the first sign, stop swaddling and switch to a sleep sack that leaves the arms free.
Check for sweating, damp hair, flushed cheeks or fast breathing as signs of overheating and remove a layer.
Swaddle loosely with hips free; stop at first rolling.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if the baby seems to be rolling earlier than expected, or if a swaddle seems to affect the legs or hips.
evidenceNote: AAP and IHDI both advise hip-healthy technique. There is no evidence that swaddling lowers SIDS risk.

sources.title: AAP HealthyChildren: Swaddling, is it safe?

AAP news release: Updated safe sleep recommendations 2022

title: Swelling, back pain and sleep
parentQuestions: Is swelling normal?
Why does my back hurt?
How should I sleep?
whatToKnow: Some swelling of ankles and fingers is normal, but sudden swelling can signal pre-eclampsia. Back pain is common; ask the GP or midwife about a pregnancy physiotherapist. A pooled analysis of studies found that going to sleep on the back was linked to higher odds of late stillbirth, and left and right side looked equally safe, though the absolute risk is low and the data are observational.

whatToDo.action: Try going to sleep on your side.
Keep active, ask about obstetric physiotherapy.

seeClinicianIf: Seek help for sudden swelling, severe headache, back pain with bleeding or fever, or pain that comes in waves before 37 weeks.
evidenceNote: Observational meta-analysis supports side sleeping advice; it cannot prove cause. NHS pages give symptom guidance.

title: Swimming lessons and drowning prevention
parentQuestions: When should my child learn to swim?
Are floaties safe?
How can toddlers drown?
whatToKnow: The AAP says drowning is the leading cause of death for ages 1 to 4, recommends swim lessons after the first birthday depending on readiness, fencing pools on four sides, close supervision, life jackets near open water (not floaties), and CPR knowledge. The AAP 7 year checklist asks about swimming skills.

whatToDo.action: Enroll in lessons; supervise within arm's reach for young children.
Use a US Coast Guard approved life jacket or local equivalent.
Stay within arm's reach.
Fence, gate, remove toys.

seeClinicianIf: Any submersion even if the child seems fine: emergency.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

title: How to take a baby's temperature
parentQuestions: How do I take my newborn's temperature?
Which thermometer is best?
Is a forehead thermometer reliable?
whatToKnow: A normal temperature is about 36.4 C. NHS advises a digital thermometer in the armpit for children under 5, held for about 15 seconds or until it beeps. Ear thermometers can be misleading in babies and strip thermometers are not accurate. Never use a mercury glass thermometer.

whatToDo.action: Hold the baby comfortably, keep the arm against the body and follow the thermometer instructions.
Let a baby who has been bathed or bundled cool a few minutes before measuring.

seeClinicianIf: Same day care for 38 C or higher under 3 months or under 36 C at any age under 5.
evidenceNote: NHS recommends axillary; some US sources use rectal. Ask your clinician which method they trust.

sources.title: AAP HealthyChildren: Fever, when to call the pediatrician
NHS: How to take your baby's temperature

title: Tantrums and emotion regulation
parentQuestions: How do I handle tantrums?
Why does my toddler scream?
whatToKnow: Tantrums peak between 1 and 3 years; prevalence was about 87 percent at 18 to 24 months and fell by 42 to 48 months (Potegal, seen via summaries). Most last under 5 minutes and mix anger and sadness. They reflect immature self-regulation; fatigue, hunger and frustration are triggers.

whatToDo.action: Stay calm, keep the child safe, name the feeling, avoid arguing or giving in.
Offer comfort and a short, simple talk.

seeClinicianIf: Frequent tantrums over 25 minutes, self-harm, aggression to others several times a day, or after age 5.
evidenceNote: Sullivan and Lewis 2012 opened (small sample); Potegal data via secondary summary.

sources.title: Sullivan and Lewis 2012, Infancy: Early goal blockage response and subsequent tantrum behavior (PMC3293480)

title: Whooping cough (Tdap) vaccine in pregnancy
parentQuestions: Do I need a whooping cough vaccine while pregnant?
When is the best time?
Does it protect my newborn?
whatToKnow: The NHS recommends the whooping cough vaccine in every pregnancy, usually around 20 weeks and from 16 weeks. It is ideally given before 32 weeks, and antibodies pass to the baby, protecting them until their own vaccine at 8 weeks. The vaccine is inactivated and does not contain live bacteria.

whatToDo.action: Have the vaccine, often at the 20-week scan visit.
Still worth having, though less protective for the baby.

seeClinicianIf: Ask a clinician if you have had a severe reaction to a vaccine before or are acutely unwell.
evidenceNote: NHS is official; I could not open a current CDC page, so US timing is not stated here.

title: Teething symptoms vs. things blamed on teething
parentQuestions: Does teething cause fever?
Is diarrhoea from teething?
whatToKnow: Teething can bring sore gums, drooling, chewing, fussiness and a slightly raised temperature (under 38C). The NHS says there is no evidence teething causes diarrhoea. A real fever, vomiting or a rash is not just teething.

whatToDo.action: Offer a cold (not frozen) teething ring or a clean cool washcloth; rub gums with a clean finger.
Amber necklaces and teething gels with numbing agents are not recommended; ask your clinician before using any gel.

seeClinicianIf: Fever of 38C or more, diarrhoea, vomiting, or a baby who seems very unwell: treat as illness, not teething.
evidenceNote: NHS lists the symptoms; the claim about amber and gels comes from general pediatric advice and is not verified by a page opened here.

sources.title: NHS: Baby teething symptoms

title: Teething and the first teeth timeline
parentQuestions: When do babies get their first tooth?
Is my baby late with teeth?
whatToKnow: Most babies get the first tooth around 6 months, but earlier or later (even 12 months) can be normal. Typical order: front teeth about 6 months, next teeth about 8, first molars about 12, canines about 18, second molars about 24. Most children have all 20 baby teeth by 2 to 3 years.

whatToDo.action: Start cleaning teeth with a soft brush (see fluoride topic).

whatToDo.when: By 12 to 15 months with no teeth
whatToDo.action: Mention it at the next check-up; late eruption is often familial.

seeClinicianIf: No teeth by about 15 to 18 months, teeth erupting very asymmetrically, or a child who seems unwell. Ask the clinician.
evidenceNote: NHS gives the timeline as a typical pattern with wide normal variation.

sources.title: NHS: Baby teething symptoms

title: Temperament and the 'difficult' child
parentQuestions: My child is so intense
Why is my child different from siblings?
whatToKnow: The AAP says much difficult behavior reflects temperament; it is not purposeful and not anyone's fault. Notice your own reactions, respond neutrally, and adjust your style.

whatToDo.action: Observe triggers and plan for transitions.
Check your own temperament match.

seeClinicianIf: Behavior that is extreme, dangerous or causing school failure.
evidenceNote: AAP (opened).

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP): Strategies and solutions for handling a difficult child

title: Terrible twos and the 'threenager': normal tantrums and when to ask
parentQuestions: Is my toddler's tantrum normal?
How many tantrums a day is too many?
Why is my 3 year old so defiant?
Кризис трёх лет: это нормально, что ребёнок всё делает наперекор?
Are the terrible twos real?
whatToKnow: 'Terrible twos' and 'threenager' are Western pop terms for a stage when children want autonomy but cannot yet regulate big feelings or say what they need. In a US preschool sample, most children (about 84 percent) had tantrums sometimes and about 9 percent had them daily. Tantrums are most common between ages 1 and 3 and generally ease after age 3. Concerning patterns are unpredictable, prolonged or destructive tantrums, not the loud ones in expected situations.

whatToDo.action: Prevent triggers: plan snacks and naps, give choices of two, redirect. Keep home safe so you can say yes more often.
During a tantrum stay near and calm, name the feeling, and wait. Hold limits on hitting, biting and throwing and stop them immediately.
Teach words and a calm-down routine (breathing, a cozy spot) when everyone is calm, and praise any use of it.
Do not reward a tantrum with the thing refused; comfort is fine, changing the answer is the lesson.
Set a few clear limits, offer choices, and give plenty of outdoor play.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if tantrums are frequent daily and last long, often involve hurting people or breaking things, self-harm, trouble calming down at all, happen mostly at daycare or school, or come with low mood, loss of skills or constant irritability. Research shows these features matter more than tantrum count alone.
evidenceNote: Tantrum frequency data come from parent-report community samples (Wakschlag 2012) and clinic comparisons (Belden 2008, preliminary). The HealthyChildren page is practical guidance, not a diagnostic tool. 'Threenager' is a cultural label, not a clinical concept.

title: Threadworms
parentQuestions: My child itches at night
Are worms common in kids?
whatToKnow: NHS says threadworms appear as white threads in stool, with night itching, irritability and sleep waking. Treat all household members over 2 with pharmacist medicine and good hygiene. No need to stay off school.

whatToDo.action: See a pharmacist.
Short nails, hand washing, hot wash of bedding.

seeClinicianIf: Under 2, pregnancy, or symptoms continuing.
evidenceNote: NHS (opened).

title: Thumb and finger sucking
parentQuestions: Should I stop my child from thumb sucking?
whatToKnow: Sucking is a natural self-soothing reflex and is of little dental concern in infancy. Prolonged digit sucking can cause open bite, crossbite and increased overjet; finger habits are more associated with overjet than pacifiers. Pressure and criticism can prolong the habit, positive rewards work better.

whatToDo.action: Do not worry; offer other comfort (cuddle toy, routine).
Praise days without it; talk to the dentist about help.

seeClinicianIf: Habit continues past about 4 to 5, or teeth are moving visibly: dentist or orthodontist.
evidenceNote: AAPD pacifier policy covers finger habits in comparison; the 4 to 5 age cut-off is common but not verified in a page I opened.

sources.title: AAPD: Policy on Pacifiers (2024 revision, Reference Manual 2026)

title: Discipline: time-outs, limits and positive parenting
parentQuestions: Is spanking OK?
How do time outs work?
whatToKnow: AAP says avoid spanking, hitting, shaming and threatening; use praise, limits, redirection and clear expectations. Spanking under 18 months raises injury risk and is linked to more aggression later. Brief time-outs (about 1 minute per year) are widely suggested but evidence is limited.

whatToDo.action: Catch good behavior with specific praise; give clear, short rules.
Use a calm time-in or short time-out.

seeClinicianIf: Discipline problems that frighten you or an urge to hurt your child: ask for help.
evidenceNote: AAP spanking position opened; the time-out duration rule from general advice.

title: Tongue-tie and lip-tie
parentQuestions: Does my baby have a tongue-tie?
Should it be cut?
Will it affect speech or feeding?
whatToKnow: Tongue-tie is a short or tight band under the tongue. It often causes no problems; if it affects feeding, options include feeding help from a trained professional and a minor snip, usually without anaesthesia in young babies. An umbrella review of 15 systematic reviews found the evidence for breastfeeding benefit inconclusive and warned of overdiagnosis. Evidence on lip-tie is even weaker, and rare complications of cutting include bleeding, infection and feeding difficulty.

whatToDo.action: Ask for a feeding assessment first, not only a procedure.
Ask who does it, what evidence they rely on, and the plan afterwards.

seeClinicianIf: Contact your midwife or pediatrician about painful feeding, poor weight gain, or long, frequent feeds.
evidenceNote: UK NHS describes the snip as an option when feeding is affected; reviews find weak and inconsistent evidence, so views differ.

title: Travelling and flying while pregnant
parentQuestions: Can I fly while pregnant?
When is the best time to travel?
What about long trips?
whatToKnow: The NHS says mid-pregnancy, between 4 and 6 months, is often the best time to travel, and flying itself is not harmful. CDC notes some airlines let you fly until 36 weeks and others stop earlier, and that cruises may stop at 24 to 28 weeks. Long journeys over 4 hours raise clot risk; move often and drink water. Avoid destinations with Zika or malaria risk.

whatToDo.action: Check airline cut-offs and travel insurance.
Move every 30 minutes and carry your maternity notes.

seeClinicianIf: Ask before travel if you have complications or are near term.
evidenceNote: NHS and CDC agree on the core points; airline rules vary.

title: Travel with toddlers
parentQuestions: Is it OK to fly with a baby?
whatToKnow: Plan around nap times, bring snacks and a familiar comforter, use an approved car seat, and check vaccines and insurance. For flights, children under 2 may be a lap passenger but a seat is safer.

whatToDo.action: Check the vaccination record, medications, and sun and water safety at the destination.

seeClinicianIf: Fever or illness before travel.

title: Erikson: trust vs mistrust (0 to 1 year)
parentQuestions: What is Erikson's trust vs mistrust?
whatToKnow: Erikson proposed that reliable care in the first year builds basic trust. It has influenced thinking but there is little empirical support for the stages and ages as stated; most research is on adolescence.

whatToDo.action: Respond consistently to a baby's needs.

evidenceNote: APA defines it as Erikson's first stage, birth to about 18 months, in which responsive care builds basic trust. This is a description of the theory, not evidence that it holds; no empirical support was opened.

title: Trying again after a miscarriage
parentQuestions: When can we try for another baby after a miscarriage?
Will I have a healthy pregnancy next time?
Where do I find support?
whatToKnow: NHS says you can try to get pregnant again when you feel ready, after your symptoms have gone. A period may take up to 8 weeks to return, and cycles can take a few months to settle. NHS says most women who have had a miscarriage go on to have a successful pregnancy. A miscarriage can be hard emotionally; GP surgeries or pregnancy units can offer counselling and support, partners can get support too, and national charities offer helplines. NHS advises seeing a GP after 3 or more miscarriages, when tests for a treatable cause are usually offered. We opened no official page about the feelings of a rainbow baby pregnancy.

whatToDo.action: Rest, talk with your partner, family or friends, and ask your GP or pregnancy unit about counselling.
Try again after your symptoms have gone; ask your clinician if you are unsure.

seeClinicianIf: See a GP after 3 or more miscarriages. For worrying symptoms or emotional distress that does not ease, contact your clinician; for an emergency use your local emergency number.
evidenceNote: NHS page opened. It says little about anxiety in the next pregnancy.

title: Tummy time
parentQuestions: When do I start tummy time?
My baby hates tummy time
How long per day?
How much tummy time?
whatToKnow: NHS says tummy time can start from birth, on your chest while you are awake, then on the floor when ready. It strengthens the neck, back and shoulders. It is only for awake, supervised time; sleep stays on the back.

whatToDo.action: Short sessions on your chest or lap, building up gradually.
Floor time with toys.
Several short sessions on the floor when baby is awake.

seeClinicianIf: Talk to the pediatrician if the baby cannot lift the head at all or is stiff or floppy.
evidenceNote: NHS and GOSH agree on supervised tummy time; no exact daily minutes are agreed.

title: Twins: feeding and daily rhythm in the first months
parentQuestions: How do I feed two babies at once?
Should I wake the second twin?
Can I breastfeed twins?
whatToKnow: AAP advice: when one twin wakes to eat, wake the other too, and feed both at once if you can with burp breaks. A large U-shaped feeding pillow helps for breast or bottle; after a C-section wait about a week before using it because the edge can press on the wound. AAP also suggests noting the clock when they wake to eat, since newborns usually stay awake about 1 to 1.5 hours, to bring both onto the same schedule. ACOG says breastfeeding twins is possible but may take practice, and lactation specialists can help.

whatToDo.action: Wake the second twin to feed and ask for help positioning at first.
Protect your back with good posture and support.
Ask a lactation specialist or your pediatrician if feeding is not going well.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician if either twin is not gaining weight, feeds poorly, or you cannot cope. The AAP page does not give sleep safety detail; see the safe sleep topic.
evidenceNote: Both are official bodies. The AAP page is a practical guide, not a trial. We found no opened page on sharing attention between twins, so that is left out.

title: Twin pregnancy: what changes in care
parentQuestions: Is a twin pregnancy high risk?
Do I need more scans with twins?
Will I give birth early with twins?
whatToKnow: ACOG says the most common complication of multiple pregnancy is preterm birth: more than half of twins and nearly all triplets or more are born preterm. Visits are usually more frequent, and from the second trimester ultrasound may be every 4 to 6 weeks. Preeclampsia and gestational diabetes are more common, growth can differ between babies, and blood screening for genetic conditions is less accurate. Ultrasound early on shows whether twins share a placenta, which changes the level of monitoring. NICE has a separate guideline on twin and triplet care in addition to routine care, aimed at lowering complications.

whatToDo.action: Ask your ob-gyn or midwife how many babies, and whether they share a placenta.
Keep all scans and visits, and ask about activity and weight gain advice for twins.

whatToDo.when: In the second half of pregnancy
whatToDo.action: Learn the signs of preterm labour and who to call.

seeClinicianIf: Ask your care team about anything that worries you and about signs of preterm labour. Postpartum depression may be more likely with multiples, so tell your team about intense sadness or anxiety.
evidenceNote: ACOG's FAQ and NICE overview opened. We could not open the NICE recommendation chapter, so we give none of its numbers.

title: Umbilical cord stump care
parentQuestions: How do I clean the cord?
Should I use alcohol or chlorhexidine?
When does it fall off?
whatToKnow: WHO recommends clean, dry cord care for facility births and low-mortality settings, and daily 4% chlorhexidine for home births where neonatal mortality is above 30 per 1000. Keeping the stump clean and exposed to air is the usual advice; it dries and separates by itself. A few spots of blood are normal.

whatToDo.action: Keep the stump clean and dry, following your midwife's instructions.
Put home remedies or dung on the stump.

seeClinicianIf: Contact a clinician for redness or swelling around the base, yellow pus, a foul smell, fever of 38 C or more, or more than a little bleeding.
evidenceNote: WHO 2013 guidance is clear; chlorhexidine is common in facility births in some countries despite WHO scope.

title: Caring for the uncircumcised penis and normal phimosis
parentQuestions: Should I pull back my baby's foreskin?
When does the foreskin retract?
Is a tight foreskin a problem?
whatToKnow: No special care is needed in infancy: wash the outside gently and never force the foreskin back. The foreskin is retractable in about 4% of newborns, about half of boys by the end of year one and about 89% by age three; phimosis is still seen in about 9 to 20% of 5 to 13 year olds and about 1% at 16 to 18. Forced retraction can cause scarring and a pathological phimosis.

whatToDo.action: Wash the outside only; leave the foreskin alone.

Offer fluids and watch for dehydration.

title: Vitamin K injection at birth, and what refusing it risks
parentQuestions: Why does my newborn need a shot of vitamin K?
Can we choose oral drops?
How dangerous is it to refuse?
whatToKnow: Newborns have little vitamin K, which is needed for blood clotting. One 1 mg injection in the thigh, ideally within 6 hours of birth, prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding. CDC says unvaccinated babies who skip the shot have about 81 times the risk of this bleeding, and late cases (about 2 to 8 weeks) can involve the brain, often with no warning signs. AAP says oral vitamin K is not a reliable substitute, and a 1990s link to childhood cancer was not confirmed.

whatToDo.action: Decide in advance and tell the midwife; the shot can wait up to 6 hours for the first feed.
Tell the pediatrician; the baby will need close watching and any later procedure (including circumcision) carries bleeding risk.

title: Vomiting and diarrhea in children: oral rehydration
parentQuestions: My child keeps vomiting, what should I give?
How long does a stomach bug last?
Should I stop diarrhea with medicine?
whatToKnow: NHS says vomiting and diarrhea are usually a stomach bug, and the main job is fluid to avoid dehydration. Diarrhea usually stops in 5 to 7 days and vomiting in 1 or 2 days. Keep breast or bottle feeding going with smaller, more frequent feeds, and use formula at usual strength. A pharmacist can recommend oral rehydration powder you mix with water.

whatToDo.action: Give small sips often. For babies, offer small feeds more often than usual, and give sips of water between feeds if on formula or solids.
No fruit juice or fizzy drinks, which can worsen diarrhea. Do not make formula weaker. NHS says do not give medicine to stop diarrhea to children under 12, and no aspirin under 16.
Use oral rehydration solution as directed on the packet.
Wash hands with soap, wash soiled laundry hot, and keep the child home until 2 days without vomiting or diarrhea.

seeClinicianIf: NHS says to call for urgent advice if the baby is under 12 months, the child stops feeding, a child under 5 shows dehydration such as fewer wet nappies, vomiting continues and fluid will not stay down, there is blood in the stool, diarrhea lasts over 7 days or vomiting over 2 days. Call your local emergency number or go to the ER for green vomit, vomit with blood or like coffee grounds, a stiff neck, a severe headache or tummy ache, blue or blotchy skin, severe breathing difficulty, or unusual confusion or floppiness. Open the app's Urgent help screen.
