title: Vygotsky's age crises: the 'crisis of 3' and 'crisis of 7'
parentQuestions: Is my 3-year-old in the crisis of three years and how long does it last?
Why does my 7-year-old suddenly answer back and lose spontaneity?
Is the crisis of 3 real or just terrible twos?
Кризис 3 лет: что делать и когда он закончится?
Кризис 7 лет: как помочь первокласснику?
What are the age crises in children?
Do all children go through crises at 1, 3, 7?
Is the crisis of 3 years the same as terrible twos?
whatToKnow: In his lectures on child psychology Vygotsky described short turning points at the newborn stage, around 1, 3, 7 and 13 years, when a child's relation to the social world is rebuilt; at 3 the child shows negativism, stubbornness and self-will, at 7 mood is unsteady and the child becomes more independent. He saw the negative behavior as the other side of real developmental gains. It is a theoretical framework rather than a measured diagnosis, and Western research does not use the word 'crisis'. It describes the same period as toddler autonomy: tantrums are most frequent between ages 1 and 3 and ease after 3, anger and distress are the two main components, and school entry is studied as a self-regulation and relationship challenge.

whatToDo.action: Give small real choices, say 'yes' to safe independence ('you do the buttons'), keep two or three firm rules, warn before transitions, and protect sleep and snacks since tiredness and hunger raise tantrum risk.
Stay near and calm, name the feeling in a few words, do not argue; always stop hitting, biting and throwing at once and never ignore dangerous behavior.
Keep routines and sleep steady, expect a tired and moody first term, give the child a role and responsibility, and listen for school worries without interrogating.
Treat 'crisis' as a prompt to look at routine, stress and expectations, not as a label for the child.
Use the idea as a prompt to offer choices, predictable routines and calm limits, not as a prediction that behavior must worsen.
Compare with what the AAP says about the age, and ask your pediatrician if behavior is extreme or lasts months.

seeClinicianIf: Tantrums that are very frequent and long, regularly cause injury to the child or others, last well beyond the preschool years, come with loss of skills, or leave you worried about your child's behavior; the AAP advises talking to the pediatrician when you are concerned.
evidenceNote: Vygotsky's crises are a theoretical framework from the 1930s; no modern study confirms a discrete 'crisis'. Tantrum research (Potegal and Davidson) and AAP guidance support the observation that toddler tantrums are common and peak between ages 1 and 3.

title: W-sitting
parentQuestions: Is W sitting bad?
whatToKnow: W-sitting is common and often just a comfortable position for flexible toddlers. There is no good evidence it harms hips, but if it is the only way a child sits or comes with weak core control or tightness, a therapist can check. Encourage varied positions.

whatToDo.action: Offer other sitting positions and gently change it sometimes.

seeClinicianIf: Always W-sits and avoids other positions, with clumsy walking, pain, or tight legs.
evidenceNote: The belief that W-sitting harms hips or development is folk: a systematic review found no evidence to advise against it and no link to hip dysplasia, and a cohort of 104 children found the same hip dysplasia rate in W-sitters (9%) and others (10%). Persistent W-sitting alongside other motor concerns still deserves a clinician's look.

title: Waking a newborn for feeds: when to wake, when to let sleep
parentQuestions: Should I wake my newborn to feed?
How long can a newborn sleep between feeds?
My baby is too sleepy to feed, what do I do?
whatToKnow: AAP gives no fixed schedule: feed as often as the baby is willing, aiming for 8 to 12 feeds in 24 hours, and not letting the baby go much beyond about 2 to 3 hours in the day or about 4 hours at night. NHS says a baby should feed at least 8 times in 24 hours in the first weeks. Newborns lose some weight in the first days (the AAP page says up to roughly 8 to 10 percent) and should then start gaining, which is why feeds and the first weight check matter.

whatToDo.action: Wake the baby if the gap is getting long. If baby does not feed right away, wait about 30 minutes and try again. Some babies nurse while drowsy, so they do not need to be fully awake.
Watch early hunger cues (lip smacking, sucking motions, rooting, squirming) and feed on those; crying is a late sign.
Check for at least 6 wet diapers a day with pale urine and several loose yellow stools. Book the first pediatric visit within 48 hours of leaving hospital for a weight check.
Keep lights dim and voices quiet so night stays for sleeping.

seeClinicianIf: Contact your doctor, midwife or health visitor if baby will not wake for feeds or will not feed after repeated tries, or has too few wet diapers. NHS says to contact your doctor or local health advice line if a baby seems unwell, for example with a high temperature or not wanting to feed, and to call emergency services for a fit, blue or pale skin, breathing difficulty, or no wet nappy in 8 hours.
evidenceNote: AAP and NHS agree on 8 or more feeds per day. The AAP page gives the wake-and-retry advice and the gap limits; NHS pages we opened did not cover waking. The how-to-tell-enough-milk page does not say when to wake.

title: Waldorf (Steiner) education
parentQuestions: Is Waldorf kindergarten good for my child?
Why no reading until 7 in Waldorf?
Is Waldorf based on a spiritual belief system?

whatToKnow: Waldorf education was founded by Rudolf Steiner in 1919 and is rooted in his anthroposophy worldview. Typical features are play-based early years, rhythm and routine, arts and crafts, storytelling, limited technology and later formal reading instruction. A 2026 systematic review of 37 studies found no consistent pattern for academic achievement, a pattern favoring Waldorf for socio-emotional outcomes and creativity, but very low certainty and high risk of bias, and the authors say it shows differences between school groups, not causal effects. A 2024 survey of empirical research notes the field is growing but much of it is not in English.

whatToDo.action: Visit a class, ask how reading and maths are taught, how technology and health topics are handled, and how the school relates to anthroposophy.

whatToDo.when: If you like the style at home
whatToDo.action: Keep a daily rhythm, stories, outdoor play and simple toys.
Whatever the school, check that the child is progressing in language and early literacy; talk to the teacher if reading is far behind.
Do not delay medical or developmental assessments because of a school philosophy; follow the pediatrician's schedule.

seeClinicianIf: Concerns about speech, hearing, attention, or reading difficulty should be raised with the pediatrician and not left to 'later readiness' ideas.
evidenceNote: Evidence is thin and low in certainty; supporters and critics disagree, and some of the research is produced by Waldorf-affiliated groups. Descriptive group differences do not prove causation.

title: Wonder Weeks and developmental leaps: what is proven
parentQuestions: Is my baby in a leap? Leap 5 fussiness
Are the Wonder Weeks real?
Why is my 8 week old suddenly so clingy and cranky?
Что такое скачки развития у младенцев и правда ли они по неделям?
whatToKnow: The Wonder Weeks book (Van de Rijt, Plooij) says babies have 10 predictable leaps in the first 20 months, each starting with a fussy, clingy regression period, with timing counted from the due date. The original human data came from a small Dutch study of 15 mothers. The one early replication attempt (de Weerth) did not find the predicted pattern and the authors dispute each other's methods. Babies do change fast and have fussy spells, but a calendar of exact weeks is not established.

whatToDo.action: Fussy evenings and growth changes are common; respond with feeds, holding and sleep, and do not wait for a specific week.
If your baby is clingier or sleeps worse, check the usual causes first: hunger, illness, teething, a new skill, routine changes. Offer extra closeness.
Use leap apps for fun, but do not let them override what you see in your own child or delay a check-up.
Write down when fussy spells start and what changed that week; a pattern of your own child is more useful than a generic calendar.

seeClinicianIf: Do not explain these signs by a 'leap': fever, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, vomiting, unusual sleepiness or floppiness, inconsolable crying lasting many hours, or loss of skills. Contact the pediatrician promptly.
evidenceNote: The theory has limited independent support and one failed replication attempt that its authors dispute; sample sizes were small on both sides. No major pediatric body endorses fixed leap weeks. Treat the idea as unproven rather than proven false.

title: The '30 million word gap': what holds up and what does not
parentQuestions: Do I need to talk to my baby all day?
Is the 30 million word gap true?
How many words should a toddler hear?
Нужно ли постоянно разговаривать с малышом, пока он не говорит?
whatToKnow: Hart and Risley (1995) reported that children in welfare families hear about 30 million fewer words by age 3 than children in professional families, from 42 families. The figure is extrapolated, and Sperry and colleagues (2019) did not replicate it in five US communities, finding large variation within income groups. A LENA study estimated a gap nearer 4 million by age 4. What holds up: back-and-forth conversation and child-directed speech matter. Conversational turns at 18 to 24 months predicted IQ and vocabulary 10 years later after controlling for family income (Gilkerson 2018).

whatToDo.action: Talk during feeds, diaper changes and walks; pause for the baby's coos and answer them.
Name what you both look at, read picture books daily, and sing.
Take turns: wait, repeat what the child says, add one word. Aim for conversations, not word counts.
Ask open questions, follow the child's interests, and read together every day.
Include grandparents and siblings in talking time, and read together every day.

seeClinicianIf: Ask the pediatrician about hearing and language screening if the baby does not babble by about 9 months, has few words by 18 months, or does not combine two words by about 2 years, or if any language is lost. Bilingual children may mix languages but should still show progress.
evidenceNote: The 30 million figure is widely criticized; defenders (Golinkoff and colleagues) say the core finding about talk quantity and quality still stands, and critics (Sperry) say it is culturally narrow. Conversational turns are the more robust predictor, though LENA studies are observational and company-linked.

title: Youth sports, safety gear and injuries
parentQuestions: When should my child start sports?
How do I prevent sports injuries?
whatToKnow: CDC says children 6 to 17 need at least 60 minutes of activity a day, with muscle and bone-strengthening on 3 days. Helmets, mouthguards and properly fitted gear reduce injury. The AAP overuse report page was blocked, so we cite no specific advice on early specialization here.

whatToDo.action: A variety of sports and play.
Helmet for biking and wheeled sports; mouthguard for contact sports.

title: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
parentQuestions: How much should I help my child with a puzzle or homework?
Should I let my child struggle or step in?
What is scaffolding in parenting?
Зона ближайшего развития: как применять дома?
How much should I help my child with schoolwork?
Should I let my child struggle?
whatToKnow: Vygotsky defined the zone of proximal development as the gap between what a child can do alone and what the child can do with help from a more capable person. Wood, Bruner and Ross later used the word scaffolding for support that is adjusted to the child and gradually withdrawn. It is a useful rule of thumb for helping with tasks, but the original tutoring study was small and the concept is more detailed in Vygotsky's own work than in popular summaries. Harvard's executive function guidance gives the same practical advice: support more at first, then reduce it as the child seems ready.

whatToDo.action: Do the hard part and let the child do the last step (you start the stacking, they place the top block).
Wait a few seconds before helping, give a hint instead of the answer, show once, then step back.
Ask 'what have you tried?' first, break homework into small steps, and let the child do the step they can do; stop helping when they succeed alone.
Watch for frustration: if the child is stuck for a long time, lower the task; if bored, raise it a notch.
Help just enough to get the child unstuck, then step back.
Show once, do together, then let them do it alone.

evidenceNote: ZPD is a theoretical construct from Vygotsky; scaffolding has support in classroom and tutoring research, but the founding 1976 study had a very small sample and one tutor.
